positive_text: Sea $ABCD$ un rectángulo con $AB > BC$, y $O$ el punto donde se cruzan las diagonales $AC$ y $BD$. La bisectriz del ángulo $B\hat{A}C$ intersecta a $BD$ en $E$. Sea $M$ el punto medio de $AB$. Por $E$ se traza una perpendicular a $AB$, que corta a $AB$ en $F$; también por $E$ se traza una perpendicular a $AE$, que corta a $AC$ en $H$. Si $OH = a$ y $MF = \frac{4}{3}a$, halla el área de $ABCD$ en función de $a$.

negatives.text: Sean $ABCD$ un rectángulo con $AB > BC$, y $O$ el punto de intersección de sus diagonales $AC$ y $BD$. La bisectriz del ángulo $B\hat{A}C$ corta a $BD$ en $E$. Llamamos $M$ al punto medio de $AB$. Se traza por $E$ la perpendicular a $AB$, que corta a $AB$ en $F$; se traza por $E$ la perpendicular a $AE$, que corta a $AC$ en $H$. Si $OH = a$ y $MF = -\frac{4}{3}a$, calcula el área del rectángulo $ABCD$ en términos de $a$.

Sean $ABCD$ un rectángulo con $AB > BC$, y $O$ el punto de intersección de sus diagonales $AC$ y $BD$. La bisectriz del ángulo $B\hat{A}C$ corta a $BD$ en $E$. Llamamos $M$ al punto medio de $AB$. Se traza por $E$ la perpendicular a $AB$, que corta a $AB$ en $F$; se traza por $E$ la perpendicular a $AE$, que corta a $AC$ en $H$. Si $OH = a$ y $MF = \frac{4}{3}a^2$, calcula el área del rectángulo $ABCD$ en términos de $a$.

Sean $ABCD$ un rectángulo con $AB > BC$, y $O$ el punto de intersección de sus diagonales $AC$ y $BD$. La bisectriz del ángulo $B\hat{A}C$ corta a $BD$ en $E$. Llamamos $M$ al punto medio de $AB$. Se traza por $E$ la perpendicular a $AB$, que corta a $AB$ en $F$; se traza por $E$ la perpendicular a $AE$, que corta a $AC$ en $H$. Si $OH = a$ y $MF = \frac{4}{3}a + 1$, calcula el área del rectángulo $ABCD$ en términos de $a$.

positive_text: \text{Sean } a, b, c \text{ números reales positivos tales que } a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 1. \text{ Pruebe que} \quad a^2 b + a b^2 + c^2 b + c^2 a + 2 a b c \le \frac{1}{3}

negatives.text: \text{Sean } x, y, z \text{ números reales positivos tales que } x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1. \text{ Pruebe que} \quad x^2 y + x y^2 + z^2 y + z^2 x + 2 x y z \ge \frac{1}{3}
\text{Sean } x, y, z \text{ números reales positivos tales que } x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1. \text{ Pruebe que} \quad x^2 y + x y^2 + z^2 y + z^2 x + 2 x y z^2 \le \frac{1}{3}

positive_text:
Sea $p > 3$ un número primo. Si
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{p-1} \frac{1}{k^2} = \frac{a}{b}
$$
donde $\gcd(a, b) = 1$, demuestre que $p^3$ divide a $a$.

negatives.text:
Sea $p > 3$ un número primo. Si
$$
\frac{1}{1^2} + \frac{1}{2^2} + \dots + \frac{1}{(p-1)^2} = \frac{n}{m}
$$
donde $\gcd(n, m) = 1$, demuestre que $p$ divide a $n$.

Sea $p > 3$ un número primo. Si
$$
\frac{1}{1^2} + \frac{1}{2^2} + \dots + \frac{1}{(p-1)^2} = \frac{n}{m}
$$
donde $\gcd(n, m) = 1$, demuestre que $p^3$ divide a $m$.

positive_text: \text{a) Dado } k \ge 3, \text{ encontrar un número entero positivo } n \text{ que sea igual a la suma de exactamente } k \text{ divisores positivos de } n \text{ distintos.}\\\text{b) Si } n \text{ puede escribirse como la suma de exactamente } k \ge 3 \text{ divisores positivos de } n \text{ distintos, y } p \text{ es el menor número primo que divide a } n, \text{ probar que}\\\left(\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{p+1} + \dots + \frac{1}{p+k-1}\right) \ge 1.

negatives.text: \text{a) Para cada } k \ge 3, \text{ hallar un entero positivo } n \text{ que se pueda representar como suma de exactamente } k^2 \text{ divisores positivos de } n \text{ distintos entre sí.}\\\text{b) Supongamos que } n \text{ se puede expresar como suma de exactamente } k^2 \text{ divisores positivos de } n \text{ distintos entre sí, para algún } k \ge 3. \text{ Sea } p \text{ el menor divisor primo de } n. \text{ Demostrar que}\\\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{p+1} + \dots + \frac{1}{p+k-1} \ge 1.

\text{a) Para cada } k \ge 3, \text{ hallar un entero positivo } n \text{ que se pueda representar como suma de exactamente } k \text{ divisores positivos de } n \text{ distintos entre sí.}\\\text{b) Supongamos que } n \text{ se puede expresar como suma de exactamente } k \ge 3 \text{ divisores positivos de } n \text{ distintos entre sí. Sea } p \text{ el mayor divisor primo de } n. \text{ Demostrar que}\\\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{p+1} + \dots + \frac{1}{p+k-1} \ge 1.

\text{a) Para cada } k \ge 3, \text{ hallar un entero positivo } n \text{ que se pueda representar como suma de exactamente } k \text{ divisores positivos de } n \text{ distintos entre sí.}\\\text{b) Supongamos que } n \text{ se puede expresar como suma de exactamente } k \ge 3 \text{ divisores positivos de } n \text{ distintos entre sí. Sea } p \text{ el menor divisor primo de } n. \text{ Demostrar que}\\\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{p+1} + \dots + \frac{1}{p+k-1} < 1.

positive_text: Sea $(a_n)_{n \ge 1}$ una sucesión infinita de enteros positivos que cumple la relación de recurrencia $$a_{n+2} = \gcd(a_{n+1}, a_n) + c,$$ para cada $n = 1, 2, \dots$, donde $c = 2006$. ¿Es posible que tal sucesión tenga exactamente $10^{c}$ valores distintos?

negatives.text: Consideramos todas las sucesiones infinitas $(x_n)_{n \ge 1}$ de enteros positivos que satisfacen la recurrencia $$x_{n+2} = \text{mcd}(x_{n+1}, x_n) - 2006,$$ para todo $n = 1, 2, \dots$. ¿Puede ocurrir que una sucesión de este tipo contenga exactamente $10^{2006}$ números distintos?

Consideramos todas las sucesiones infinitas $(x_n)_{n \ge 1}$ de enteros positivos que satisfacen la recurrencia $$x_{n+2} = \text{mcd}(x_{n+1}, x_n) + 2006,$$ para todo $n = 1, 2, \dots$. ¿Puede ocurrir que una sucesión de este tipo contenga exactamente $2^{2006}$ números distintos?

Consideramos todas las sucesiones infinitas $(x_n)_{n \ge 1}$ de enteros positivos que satisfacen la recurrencia $$x_{n+2} = \text{mcd}(x_{n+1}, x_n^2) + 2006,$$ para todo $n = 1, 2, \dots$. ¿Puede ocurrir que una sucesión de este tipo contenga exactamente $10^{2006}$ números distintos?

positive_text: Sea $n = 2k+1$ con $k \ge 1$. En un conjunto de $n$ personas, algunas son honestas (siempre dicen la verdad) y el resto son impredecibles (no se puede confiar en sus respuestas). Se conoce que hay a lo sumo $k$ impredecibles. Un observador externo puede elegir pares de individuos $A$ y $B$ y preguntarle a $A$ si $B$ es honesto. Demostrar que con $3k$ preguntas de este tipo, el observador puede identificar con precisión a cada individuo como honesto o impredecible.

negatives.text: Sea $k \ge 1$ un entero. En un grupo de $2k+1$ personas algunas son sinceras (siempre dicen la verdad) y las restantes son impredecibles (a veces dicen la verdad y a veces mienten). Se sabe que las impredecibles son a lo sumo $k$. Alguien ajeno al grupo debe determinar quién es sincero y quién impredecible mediante una secuencia de pasos. En cada paso elige dos personas $A$ y $B$ del grupo y le pregunta a $A$ ¿es $B$ impredecible? Demostrar que al cabo de $3k$ pasos el forastero podrá clasificar con certeza a las $2k+1$ personas del grupo.

Sea $k \ge 1$ un entero. En un grupo de $2k+1$ personas algunas son sinceras (siempre dicen la verdad) y las restantes son impredecibles (a veces dicen la verdad y a veces mienten). Se sabe que las impredecibles son a lo sumo $k$. Alguien ajeno al grupo debe determinar quién es sincero y quién impredecible mediante una secuencia de pasos. En cada paso elige dos personas $A$ y $B$ del grupo y le pregunta a $A$ ¿es $B$ impredecible? Demostrar que al cabo de $3k - 1$ pasos el forastero podrá clasificar con certeza a las $2k+1$ personas del grupo.

Sea $k \ge 1$ un entero. En un grupo de $2k+1$ personas, algunas son mentirosas (siempre mienten) y las restantes son impredecibles (a veces dicen la verdad y a veces mienten). Se sabe que las impredecibles son a lo sumo $k$. Alguien ajeno al grupo debe determinar quién es mentiroso y quién impredecible mediante una secuencia de pasos. En cada paso elige dos personas $A$ y $B$ del grupo y le pregunta a $A$ ¿es $B$ mentiroso? Demostrar que al cabo de $3k$ pasos el forastero podrá clasificar con certeza a las $2k+1$ personas del grupo.

positive_text:
Sea $m$ un entero positivo y defínase una secuencia $\{b_n\}$ mediante:
$$
b_1 = \frac{m}{2}, \quad b_{n+1} = b_n \lceil b_n \rceil, \text{ para } n \ge 1.
$$
Hallar todos los valores de $m$ tales que $b_{2007}$ es el primer término entero de la secuencia.
Nota: $\lceil x \rceil$ denota el menor entero mayor o igual a $x$.

negatives.text:
Dado un entero positivo $m$, se define la sucesión $\{a_n\}$ como:
$$
a_1 = \frac{m}{2}, \quad a_{n+1} = a_n \lfloor a_n \rfloor, \text{ para } n \ge 1.
$$
Determinar todos los valores de $m$ para los cuales $a_{2007}$ es el primer entero que aparece en la sucesión.
Nota: $\lfloor x \rfloor$ denota al mayor entero menor o igual a $x$.

Dado un entero positivo $m$, se define la sucesión $\{a_n\}$ como:
$$
a_1 = \frac{m}{2}, \quad a_{n+1} = a_n + [a_n], \text{ para } n \ge 1.
$$
Determinar todos los valores de $m$ para los cuales $a_{2007}$ es el primer entero que aparece en la sucesión.
Nota: $[x]$ es el menor entero no menor que $x$.

Dado un entero positivo $m$, se define la sucesión $\{a_n\}$ como:
$$
a_1 = \frac{m}{2}, \quad a_{n+1} = a_n [a_n], \text{ para } n \ge 1.
$$
Determinar todos los valores de $m$ para los cuales $a_{2007}$ es el primer término que no es entero en la sucesión.
Nota: $[x]$ es el menor entero no menor que $x$.

positive_text: Sea $n > 2$ un entero par. En un cuadrado de $n \times n$, distribuir fichas de manera que cada fila contenga un número impar de fichas y cada columna tenga un número par y no nulo. Determinar el mínimo número total de fichas necesarias para satisfacer estas condiciones. Dar un ejemplo de distribución con esa cantidad y explicar por qué no es posible con menos.

negatives.text: Sea $n > 2$ un entero par. En las casillas de un tablero de $n \times n$ se deben colocar fichas de modo que en cada columna la cantidad de fichas sea impar y distinta de cero, y en cada fila la cantidad de fichas sea par. Determinar la menor cantidad de fichas que hay que colocar en el tablero para cumplir esta regla.

Sea $n > 2$ un entero par. En las casillas de un tablero de $n \times n$ se deben colocar fichas de modo que en cada columna la cantidad de fichas sea par y distinta de cero, y en cada fila la cantidad de fichas sea impar. Determinar la mayor cantidad de fichas que se pueden colocar en el tablero sin repetir ninguna.

Sea $n > 2$ un entero par. En las casillas de un tablero de $n \times n$ se deben colocar fichas de modo que en cada columna la cantidad de fichas sea par y distinta de cero, y en cada fila la cantidad de fichas sea impar. Determinar la menor cantidad de fichas que hay que colocar en el tablero para cumplir esta regla, pero permitiendo que una fila tenga cero fichas.

positive_text:
Sea $p > 3$ un número primo y $x_1, x_2,..., x_k$ ($2 < k < p$) números enteros distintos módulo $p$ y no congruentes a cero módulo $p$. Denotamos por $r(x) \in \{0,1,..., p-1\}$ al resto de $x$ módulo $p$.

Un entero $a \in \{1,2,..., p-1\}$ se llama bueno si:
$$
r(a x_1) < r(a x_2) < \dots < r(a x_k).
$$

Muestre que el número de tales $a$ buenos no excede $\frac{2p}{k+1} - 1$.

negatives.text:
Dados un primo $p > 3$ y $x_1, x_2,..., x_k$ ($2 < k < p$) enteros distintos módulo $p$ y no nulos, denotamos por $r(x)$ al residuo de $x$ módulo $p$ en $\{0,1,..., p-1\}$.

Decimos que $a \in \{1,2,..., p-1\}$ es bueno si:
$$
r(a x_1) > r(a x_2) > \dots > r(a x_k).
$$

Demuestre que hay como máximo $\frac{2p}{k+1} - 1$ números buenos.

Dados un número primo $p > 3$ y $x_1, x_2,..., x_k$ ($2 < k < p$) enteros distintos módulo $p$ y no nulos, denotamos por $r(x)$ al residuo de $x$ módulo $p$ en $\{0,1,..., p-1\}$.

Decimos que $a \in \{1,2,..., p-1\}$ es bueno si:
$$
r(a x_1^2) < r(a x_2^2) < \dots < r(a x_k^2).
$$

Demuestre que hay como máximo $\frac{2p}{k+1} - 1$ números buenos.

Dados un número primo $p > 3$ y $x_1, x_2,..., x_k$ ($2 < k < p$) enteros distintos módulo $p$ y no nulos, denotamos por $r(x)$ al residuo de $x$ módulo $p$ en $\{0,1,..., p-1\}$.

Decimos que $a \in \{1,2,..., p-1\}$ es bueno si:
$$
r(a x_1) + r(a x_2) + \dots + r(a x_k) < p.
$$

Demuestre que hay como máximo $\frac{2p}{k+1} - 1$ números buenos.

positive_text: Sobre una circunferencia, dos equipos $A$ y $B$ colocan $n$ banderas cada uno ($n \ge 2$), alternadamente, con $A$ iniciando. Cada bandera se coloca en un punto distinto y no se puede mover. Al final, el territorio se divide según quién tenga la bandera más cercana a cada punto. Si hay empate, el punto es neutro. El equipo cuya área controlada sea mayor gana. Demostrar que $B$ tiene una estrategia ganadora para cualquier $n$.

negatives.text: Dos equipos, $A$ y $B$, disputan el territorio limitado por una circunferencia. $A$ tiene $n$ banderas azules y $B$ tiene $n$ banderas blancas ($n \ge 2$). Juegan alternadamente y $B$ comienza el juego. Cada equipo, en su turno, coloca una de sus banderas en un punto de la circunferencia que no se haya usado en una jugada anterior. Un punto del territorio es del equipo $A$ si la bandera más próxima a él es azul, y es del equipo $B$ si la bandera más próxima a ese punto es blanca. Si la bandera azul más próxima a un punto está a la misma distancia que la bandera blanca más próxima a ese punto, entonces el punto es neutro. Un equipo gana si sus puntos cubren un área mayor que el área cubierta por los puntos del otro equipo. Demostrar que, para todo $n$, el equipo $B$ tiene estrategia para ganar el juego.

Dos equipos, $A$ y $B$, disputan el territorio limitado por una circunferencia. $A$ tiene $n$ banderas azules y $B$ tiene $n$ banderas blancas ($n \ge 2$). Juegan alternadamente y $A$ comienza el juego. Cada equipo, en su turno, coloca una de sus banderas en un punto de la circunferencia que no se haya usado en una jugada anterior. Un punto del territorio es del equipo $A$ si la bandera más próxima a él es azul, y es del equipo $B$ si la bandera más próxima a ese punto es blanca. Si la bandera azul más próxima a un punto está a una distancia menor que la bandera blanca más próxima a ese punto, entonces el punto es neutro. Un equipo gana si sus puntos cubren un área mayor que el área cubierta por los puntos del otro equipo. Demostrar que, para todo $n$, el equipo $B$ tiene estrategia para ganar el juego.

Dos equipos, $A$ y $B$, disputan el territorio limitado por una circunferencia. $A$ tiene $n+1$ banderas azules y $B$ tiene $n$ banderas blancas ($n \ge 2$). Juegan alternadamente y $A$ comienza el juego. Cada equipo, en su turno, coloca una de sus banderas en un punto de la circunferencia que no se haya usado en una jugada anterior. Un punto del territorio es del equipo $A$ si la bandera más próxima a él es azul, y es del equipo $B$ si la bandera más próxima a ese punto es blanca. Si la bandera azul más próxima a un punto está a la misma distancia que la bandera blanca más próxima a ese punto, entonces el punto es neutro. Un equipo gana si sus puntos cubren un área mayor que el área cubierta por los puntos del otro equipo. Demostrar que, para todo $n$, el equipo $B$ tiene estrategia para ganar el juego.

positive_text:
Given a semicircle with diameter $AB$, center $O$, and radius $r$, let point $C$ lie on segment $AB$ such that $AC = \frac{2}{3}r$. A line perpendicular to $AB$ at $C$ intersects the semicircle at $D$. Let $H$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to $AD$, and let $E$ be the intersection of $CD$ and $OH$.

a) Determine an expression for $AD$ in terms of $r$.

b) If $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $AE$ and $OD$, respectively, compute $\angle MHN$.

negatives.text:
Consider a semicircle with diameter $AB$, center $O$ and radius $r$. Let $C$ be the point on segment $AB$ such that $AC = \frac{r}{3}$. Line $l$ is perpendicular to $AB$ at $C$ and $D$ is the common point of $l$ and the semicircle. Let $H$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to $AD$ and $E$ the intersection of lines $CD$ and $OH$.

a) Express $AD$ as a function of $r$.

b) If $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $AE$ and $OD$ respectively, find the measure of angle $\angle MHN$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, point $P$ lies on side $AB$ such that $\frac{AP}{PB} = \frac{1}{4}$. The perpendicular bisector of $PB$ intersects side $BC$ at point $Q$. Given that $\text{area}(PQC) = \frac{4}{25}\text{area}(ABC)$ and $AC = 7$, determine the length of $BC$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, point $P$ divides side $AB$ in ratio $\frac{AP}{PB} = \frac{1}{4}$. The perpendicular bisector of segment $PB$ intersects side $AC$ at point $Q$. If $\text{area}(PQC) = \frac{4}{25}\text{area}(ABC)$ and $AC = 7$, find $BC$.

In triangle $ABC$, point $P$ divides side $AB$ in ratio $\frac{AP}{PB} = \frac{1}{4}$. The perpendicular bisector of segment $PB$ intersects side $BC$ at point $Q$. If $\text{area}(PQC) = \frac{4}{25}\text{area}(ABC)$ and $AB = 7$, find $BC$.

In triangle $ABC$, point $P$ divides side $AB$ in ratio $\frac{AP}{PB} = \frac{1}{4}$. The perpendicular bisector of segment $PB$ intersects side $BC$ at point $Q$. If $\text{area}(PQC) = \frac{4}{25}\text{area}(ABC)$ and $AC = 49$, find $BC$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram and let $G$ lie on side $AB$. A circle passing through $A$ and $G$ is tangent to the extension of $CB$ beyond $B$ at point $P$. If the line $DG$ intersects the circle again at $L$ and $GLBC$ is cyclic, show that $AB = PC$.

negatives.text: In the parallelogram $ABCD$, point $G$ is chosen on side $AB$. Consider the circle through $A$ and $G$ that is tangent to the extension of $CB$ beyond $B$ at point $P$. The extension of $DG$ beyond $G$ intersects the circle at $L$. If the quadrilateral $GLBC$ is cyclic, prove that $AB = 2PC$.

In the parallelogram $ABCD$, point $G$ is chosen on side $AB$. Consider the circle through $A$ and $G$ that is tangent to the extension of $CB$ beyond $B$ at point $P$. The extension of $DG$ beyond $G$ intersects the circle at $L$. If the quadrilateral $GLBC$ is cyclic, prove that $AB = PB$.

In the parallelogram $ABCD$, point $G$ is chosen on side $AB$. Consider the circle through $A$ and $G$ that is tangent to the extension of $CB$ beyond $B$ at point $P$. The extension of $DG$ beyond $G$ intersects the circle at $L$. If the quadrilateral $GLBC$ is cyclic, prove that $AB = DP$.

positive_text: Let $N \ge 4$ be a fixed integer. Players $A$ and $B$ alternately append $+k$ or $-k$ to a growing sequence, starting with $A$ at $k = 1$. After each move, the player aims to ensure that there exists a consecutive subsequence whose sum is divisible by $N$. Determine for which values of $N$ one of the players has a guaranteed winning strategy.

negatives.text: Let $N \ge 4$ be a fixed integer. Two players $A$ and $B$ write down numbers, each number in continuation to the previous expression. First $A$ writes $+1$ or $-1$, then $B$ writes $+2$ or $-2$, then $A$ writes $+3$ or $-3$ etc.; at step $k$ the player to move must write $+k$ or $-k$. The objective of each one is that after a move of his several non-consecutive numbers in the obtained expression, taken with their signs, have sum divisible by $N$. For each $N$ determine which of the players has a winning strategy, if any.

Let $N \ge 4$ be a fixed integer. Two players $A$ and $B$ write down numbers, each number in continuation to the previous expression. First $A$ writes $+1$ or $-1$, then $B$ writes $+2$ or $-2$, then $A$ writes $+3$ or $-3$ etc.; at step $k$ the player to move must write $+k$ or $-k$. The objective of each one is that after a move of his several consecutive numbers in the obtained expression, taken with their signs, have sum equal to $N$, not divisible by $N$. For each $N$ determine which of the players has a winning strategy, if any.

Let $N \ge 4$ be a fixed integer. Two players $A$ and $B$ write down numbers, each number in continuation to the previous expression. First $A$ writes $+1$ or $-1$, then $B$ writes $+2$ or $-2$, then $A$ writes $+3$ or $-3$ etc.; at step $k$ the player to move must write $+k$ or $-k$. The objective of each one is that after a move of his several consecutive numbers in the obtained expression, taken with their signs, have sum divisible by $N+1$. For each $N$ determine which of the players has a winning strategy, if any.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a trapezoid with $AB \parallel CD$, $AB > CD$, and such that $BC = CD = DA$. Points $E$ and $F$ lie on $AB$ such that $AE = EF = FB$. The lines $CF$ and $DE$ intersect at point $P$. Prove that $\angle APB = \angle DAB$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a trapezoid with $AB \parallel CD$, $AB > CD$, and $BC = CD = DA$. Points $E$ and $F$ divide $AB$ into three equal parts; $E$ is between $A$ and $F$. Lines $CE$ and $DF$ intersect at $P$. Prove that $\angle APB = \angle DAB$.

Let $ABCD$ be a trapezoid with $AB \parallel CD$, $AB > CD$, and $BC = CD = DA$. Points $E$ and $F$ divide $AB$ into three equal parts; $E$ is between $A$ and $F$. Lines $CF$ and $DE$ intersect at $P$. Prove that $\angle APB = \angle ADC$.

Let $ABCD$ be a trapezoid with $AB \parallel CD$, $AB > CD$, and $BC = CD = DA$. Points $E$ and $F$ divide $AB$ into three equal parts; $E$ is between $A$ and $F$. Lines $CF$ and $DE$ intersect at $P$. Prove that $\angle APB = \angle CDA$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABP$ be acute with $AB > BP$. The altitudes from $B$, $P$, and $A$ are $BH$, $PQ$, and $AS$ respectively. Extending $QS$ meets $AP$ at $C$, and extending $HS$ meets $BC$ at $L$. Given that $HS = SL$ and $HL \perp BC$, determine the value of $\frac{SL}{SC}$.

negatives.text: In the acute-angled triangle $ABP$ ($AB > BP$) the altitudes are $BH$, $PQ$ and $AS$. The extension of $QS$ intersects line $AP$ at $C$. The extension of $HS$ intersects $BC$ at $L$. If $HS = SL$ and $HL$ is parallel to $BC$, compute $\frac{SL}{SC}$.

f(a + b) = f(a) + f(b)

positive_text:
Let there be a round-robin football tournament with $n \ge 4$ teams, where every team plays every other team once. If the final scores of the teams form a sequence of $n$ consecutive integers, determine the largest possible score of the highest-ranked team.

**NOTE:** 3 points are awarded for a win, 1 for a draw, and 0 for a loss.

positive_text:

$$
a^n + 1, a^{n+1} + 1, \dots, a^{2n-2} + 1,
$$

negatives.text:

$$
a^n + 1, a^{n+1} + 1, \dots, a^{2n-2} + 1,

$$
a^n - 1, a^{n+1} - 1, \dots, a^{2n-2} - 1,

positive_text: Alan plays a solitaire game with a number $n$. He begins by selecting a positive odd divisor $d$ of $n$. If $d = 1$, the computer updates $n$ to $n+1$. Otherwise, if $d > 1$, the computer updates $n$ to $n/d$. The process repeats using the new number. For example: $$ 20 \xrightarrow{\{d=1\}} 21 \xrightarrow{\{d=3\}} 7 \xrightarrow{\{d=1\}} 8 \xrightarrow{\{\dots\}} $$ Is there a starting value $n$ such that Alan can play the game so that the number $n$ is never a power of 3 at any step?

negatives.text: Alan plays a solitaire game in his computer. To begin, Alan chooses a positive integer $n$. Then he chooses a positive odd divisor of $n$. If the chosen divisor is $d=1$, the computer replaces $n$ with $n+1$. If the chosen divisor is a number $d$ greater than 1, the computer replaces $n$ with $n/d$. Alan continues the game by choosing a divisor $d$ of the new number. For instance: $$ 20 \xrightarrow{\{d=1\}} 21 \xrightarrow{\{d=3\}} 7 \xrightarrow{\{d=1\}} 8 \xrightarrow{\{\dots\}} $$ Can Alan choose an appropriate starting number $n$ and play in such a way that the computer never shows a power of 2?

Alan continues the game by choosing a divisor $d$ of the new number. For instance: $$ 20 \xrightarrow{\{d=1\}} 19 \xrightarrow{\{d=3\}} 7 \xrightarrow{\{d=1\}} 6 \xrightarrow{\{\dots\}} $$ Can Alan choose an appropriate starting number $n$ and play in such a way that the computer never shows a power of 3?

For instance: $$ 20 \xrightarrow{\{d=1\}} 21 \xrightarrow{\{d=3\}} 7 \xrightarrow{\{d=1\}} 8 \xrightarrow{\{\dots\}} $$ Can Alan choose an appropriate starting number $n$ and play in such a way that the computer never shows a power of 3 or a power of 2?

The intersection of lines $PD$ and $BC$ is $Q$. If a line through $Q$ is perpendicular to $AC$ and intersects $AB$ at $R$, and $S$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $D$ to $AC$, show that $\angle PSQ = \angle RCP$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $\angle B = \angle D = 90^\circ$ and $AB > AD$. Let $P$ be the point on side $AB$ such that $AP = AD$. Lines $PC$ and $BC$ intersect at $Q$. The perpendicular line to $AC$ through $Q$ intersects $AB$ at $R$. Let $S$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $D$ to $AC$. Prove that $\angle PSQ = \angle RCP$.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $\angle B = \angle D = 90^\circ$ and $AB > AD$. Let $P$ be the point on side $AB$ such that $AP = AD$. Lines $PD$ and $BC$ intersect at $Q$. The perpendicular line to $AB$ through $Q$ intersects $AC$ at $R$. Let $S$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $D$ to $AC$. Prove that $\angle PSQ = \angle RCP$.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $\angle B = \angle D = 90^\circ$ and $AB < AD$. Let $P$ be the point on side $AB$ such that $AP = AD$. Lines $PD$ and $BC$ intersect at $Q$. The perpendicular line to $AC$ through $Q$ intersects $AB$ at $R$. Let $S$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $D$ to $AC$. Prove that $\angle PSQ = \angle RCP$.

positive_text:
Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_m$ be positive real numbers. Define for each positive integer $j$,
$$
T_j = a_1^j + a_2^j + \dots + a_m^j.
$$
(a) Prove that if $T_1 < T_2$, then the sequence $T_1, T_2, T_3, \dots$ is strictly increasing.

(b) Prove that it is possible to have $T_1 > T_2$ while the sequence $T_1, T_2, T_3, \dots$ is not strictly decreasing.

negatives.text:
Let $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ be positive real numbers. For each positive integer $k$, define
$$
S_k = x_1^k + x_2^k + \dots + x_n^k.
$$
(a) Prove that if $S_1 > S_2$ then the sequence $S_1, S_2, S_3, \dots$ is strictly increasing.

(b) Prove that it is possible that $S_1 < S_2$ and yet the sequence $S_1, S_2, S_3, \dots$ is not strictly increasing.

Let $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ be positive real numbers. For each positive integer $k$, define
$$
S_k = x_1^k + x_2^k + \dots + x_n^k.
$$
(a) Prove that if $S_1 < S_2$ then the sequence $S_1, S_2, S_3, \dots$ is strictly decreasing.

(b) Prove that it is possible that $S_1 > S_2$ and yet the sequence $S_1, S_2, S_3, \dots$ is not strictly decreasing.

Let $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ be positive real numbers. For each positive integer $k$, define
$$
S_k = x_1^k + x_2^k + \dots + x_n^k.
$$
(a) Prove that if $S_1 < S_2$ then the sequence $S_1, S_2, S_3, \dots$ is strictly increasing.

(b) Prove that it is possible that $S_1 > S_2$ and yet the sequence $S_1, S_2, S_3, \dots$ is not strictly increasing.

positive_text:
Prove that the equation
$$
6\left(6 x^{2}+3 y^{2}+z^{2}\right)=5 w^{2}
$$
has no integer solutions other than $x=y=z=w=0$.

negatives.text:
Prove that the equation
$$
6\left(6 a^{2}+3 b^{2}+c^{2}\right)=5 n^{2}
$$
has integer solutions other than $a=b=c=n=0$.

Prove that the equation
$$
6\left(6 a^{2}+3 b^{2}+c^{2}\right)=5 n^{2}
$$
has solutions in positive integers other than $a=b=c=n=0$.

Prove that the equation
$$
6\left(6 a^{2}+3 b^{2}+c^{2}\right)=5 n
$$
has no solutions in integers other than $a=b=c=n=0$.

positive_text: Let three points $P$, $Q$, $R$ be given in the plane, and for convenience define $P_4 = P$, $P_5 = Q$. For $i = 1, 2, 3$, let $M_i$ be the midpoint of segment $P_i P_{i+1}$, and define $N_i$ as the midpoint of segment $P_i M_i$. Let the lines $P_i N_{i+1}$ and $M_i P_{i+2}$ intersect at point $X_i$, and the lines $P_i M_{i+1}$ and $N_i P_{i+2}$ intersect at point $Y_i$. Determine the ratio of the area of triangle $X_1 X_2 X_3$ to the area of triangle $Y_1 Y_2 Y_3$.

negatives.text: Let $A_{1}$, $A_{2}$, $A_{3}$ be three points in the plane, and for convenience, let $A_{4}=A_{1}$, $A_{5}=A_{2}$. For $n=1,2,3$, suppose that $B_{n}$ is the midpoint of $A_{n} A_{n+1}$, and suppose that $C_{n}$ is the midpoint of $B_{n} A_{n+1}$. Suppose that $A_{n} C_{n+1}$ and $B_{n} A_{n+2}$ meet at $D_{n}$, and that $A_{n} B_{n+1}$ and $C_{n} A_{n+2}$ meet at $E_{n}$. Calculate the ratio of the area of triangle $D_{1} D_{2} D_{3}$ to the area of triangle $E_{1} E_{2} E_{3}$.

Let $A_{1}$, $A_{2}$, $A_{3}$ be three points in the plane, and for convenience, let $A_{4}=A_{1}$, $A_{5}=A_{2}$. For $n=1,2,3$, suppose that $B_{n}$ is the midpoint of $A_{n} A_{n+1}$, and suppose that $C_{n}$ is the midpoint of $A_{n} B_{n}$. Suppose that $A_{n} C_{n+1}$ and $B_{n} A_{n+2}$ meet at $D_{n}$, and that $A_{n} C_{n+1}$ and $C_{n} A_{n+2}$ meet at $E_{n}$. Calculate the ratio of the area of triangle $D_{1} D_{2} D_{3}$ to the area of triangle $E_{1} E_{2} E_{3}$.

Let $A_{1}$, $A_{2}$, $A_{3}$ be three points in the plane, and for convenience, let $A_{4}=A_{1}$, $A_{5}=A_{2}$. For $n=1,2,3$, suppose that $B_{n}$ is the midpoint of $A_{n} A_{n+1}$, and suppose that $C_{n}$ is the midpoint of $A_{n} B_{n}$. Suppose that $A_{n} C_{n+1}$ and $B_{n} A_{n+2}$ meet at $D_{n}$, and that $A_{n+2} B_{n+1}$ and $C_{n} A_{n+2}$ meet at $E_{n}$. Calculate the ratio of the area of triangle $D_{1} D_{2} D_{3}$ to the area of triangle $E_{1} E_{2} E_{3}$.

positive_text: Prove that for any integer $n$ with $n \geq 6$, a convex hexagon exists that can be partitioned into $n$ triangles of equal size and shape.

negatives.text: Show that for every integer $n \geq 6$, there exists a convex hexagon which can be dissected into exactly $n$ similar triangles.
Show that for every integer $n \geq 6$, there exists a convex hexagon which can be dissected into at most $n$ congruent triangles.
Show that for every integer $n \geq 6$, there exists a convex pentagon which can be dissected into exactly $n$ congruent triangles.

positive_text:
Let $n$ be an integer such that $n>3$. Consider selecting three distinct numbers from the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ and forming all arithmetic expressions using these numbers exactly once with the operations of addition and multiplication. 

a. Prove that if the three selected numbers are all strictly greater than $\lfloor n / 2 \rfloor$, then the resulting expressions yield unique values.

b. Suppose $p$ is a prime number with $p \leq \sqrt{n}$. Prove that the number of such triplets where the smallest number is $p$ and at least two of the resulting expressions are equal is exactly the number of positive divisors of $p-1$.

negatives.text:
Let $n$ be an integer such that $n>3$. Suppose that we choose three numbers from the set $\{1,2, \ldots, n\}$. Using each of these three numbers only once and using addition, multiplication, and parenthesis, let us form all possible combinations.

a. Show that if we choose all three numbers greater than or equal to $n / 2$, then the values of these combinations are all distinct.

b. Let $p$ be a prime number such that $p \leq \sqrt{n}$. Show that the number of ways of choosing three numbers so that the smallest one is $p$ and the values of the combinations are all distinct is precisely the number of positive divisors of $p-1$.

Let $n$ be an integer such that $n>3$. Suppose that we choose three numbers from the set $\{1,2, \ldots, n\}$. Using each of these three numbers only once and using addition and multiplication, let us form all possible combinations.

a. Show that if we choose all three numbers less than $n / 2$, then the values of these combinations are all distinct.

b. Let $p$ be a prime number such that $p \leq \sqrt{n}$. Show that the number of ways of choosing three numbers so that the smallest one is $p$ and the values of the combinations are not all distinct is precisely the number of positive divisors of $p+1$.

Let $n$ be an integer such that $n>3$. Suppose that we choose three numbers from the set $\{1,2, \ldots, n\}$. Using each of these three numbers only once and using addition, multiplication, and parenthesis, let us form all possible combinations.

a. Show that if we choose all three numbers greater than $n / 2$, then the values of these combinations are all equal.

b. Let $p$ be a prime number such that $p \leq \sqrt{n}$. Show that the number of ways of choosing three numbers so that the smallest one is $p$ and the values of the combinations are all equal is precisely the number of positive divisors of $p-1$.

positive_text: Let $A, B, C, D$ be points such that $AB = BC = CD = DA$ and $\angle ABC = 60^\circ$. A line $\ell$ passes through $D$ and does not intersect the quadrilateral except at $D$. If $\ell$ intersects $AB$ and $BC$ at points $E$ and $F$ respectively, and $M$ is the intersection of $CE$ and $AF$, show that $CA^{2} = CM \cdot CE$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB = BC = CD = DA$ and $\angle ABC = 60^\circ$. Let $\ell$ be a line through $D$ that intersects the quadrilateral at another point. Let $E$ and $F$ be the points of intersection of $\ell$ with $AB$ and $BC$, and let $M = CE \cap AF$. Prove that $CA^{2} = CM \cdot CE$.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB = BC = CD = DA$ and $\angle ABC = 60^\circ$. Let $\ell$ be a line through $D$ not intersecting the quadrilateral except at $D$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the points of intersection of $\ell$ with $AD$ and $CD$, respectively. Let $M = CE \cap AF$. Prove that $CA^{2} = CM \cdot CE$.

positive_text: Let $b_{1}, b_{2}, \cdots$ be a sequence of real numbers such that $b_{i+j} \leq b_{i} + b_{j}$ for all $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$. Show that $$ \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{b_{k}}{k} \geq b_{n} $$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

negatives.text: Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots$ be a sequence of real numbers satisfying $a_{i+j} \leq a_{i} + a_{j}$ for all $i, j=1,2, \cdots$. Prove that $$ a_{1}+\frac{a_{2}}{2}+\frac{a_{3}}{3}+\cdots+\frac{a_{n}}{n} \leq a_{n} $$ for each positive integer $n$.

Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots$ be a sequence of real numbers satisfying $a_{i+j} \leq a_{i} + a_{j} + 1$ for all $i, j=1,2, \cdots$. Prove that $$ a_{1}+\frac{a_{2}}{2}+\frac{a_{3}}{3}+\cdots+\frac{a_{n}}{n} \geq a_{n} $$ for each positive integer $n$.

positive_text: Consider a grid of size $n \times n$ with each cell representing a house. Initially, the fire starts at the cell $(1, c)$, where $c \leq \frac{n}{2}$. In each time interval, the firefighters can choose one unburned house to protect. Simultaneously, the fire spreads to all adjacent (up, down, left, right) unburned and unguarded cells. A house is saved if it is not burned and remains unguarded. What is the maximum number of houses that can be saved?

negatives.text: In a $n \times n$ grid, a fire starts at position $(1, c)$, where $c \leq \frac{n}{2}$. At each time step, firefighters can defend one house while the fire spreads to all adjacent unguarded houses and diagonally adjacent unguarded houses. The process ends when the fire can no longer spread. What is the maximum number of houses that can be saved?

In a $n \times n$ grid, a fire starts at position $(1, c)$, where $c \leq \frac{n}{2}$. At each time step, firefighters can defend one house while the fire spreads to all adjacent unguarded houses. The process ends when the fire can no longer spread. What is the minimum number of houses that must be saved to prevent the fire from reaching the bottom row?

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $\angle A < 60^\circ$. Let $X$ lie on $AB$ and $Y$ on $AC$ such that $AX + AC = BX + BC$ and $AY + AB = CY + CB$. If point $P$ satisfies $PX \perp AB$ and $PY \perp AC$, show that $\angle BPC < 120^\circ$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $\angle A < 60^\circ$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be points on $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, such that $CA + AX = CB + BX$ and $BA + AY = BC + CY$. Let $P$ be the point such that $PX$ and $PY$ are perpendicular to $AB$ and $BC$, respectively. Prove that $\angle BPC < 120^\circ$.

Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $\angle A < 60^\circ$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be points on $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, such that $CA + AX = CB + BX$ and $BA + AY = BC + CY$. Let $P$ be the point such that $PX$ and $PY$ are parallel to $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Prove that $\angle BPC < 120^\circ$.

Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $\angle A < 60^\circ$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be points on $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, such that $CA + AX = CB + BX$ and $BA + AY = BC + CY$. Let $P$ be the point such that $PX$ and $PY$ are perpendicular to $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Prove that $\angle BPC > 120^\circ$.

positive_text: Given three non-intersecting, mutually external circles $\Gamma_{1}, \Gamma_{2}, \Gamma_{3}$ in the plane, define a point $P$ outside these circles as exceptional if the lines $A_{1} B_{1}, A_{2} B_{2}, A_{3} B_{3}$, where each $A_i, B_i$ are the tangency points from $P$ to $\Gamma_i$, are concurrent. Prove that all such exceptional points lie on a common circle.

negatives.text: Let three non-overlapping and mutually external circles $\Gamma_{1}, \Gamma_{2}, \Gamma_{3}$ be given in the plane. For any point $P$ outside the circles, construct six points $A_i, B_i$ as the tangents from $P$ to $\Gamma_i$. Call $P$ exceptional if the lines $A_1B_1, A_2B_2, A_3B_3$ are parallel. Prove that all such exceptional points lie on a single circle.

Let three mutually external circles $\Gamma_{1}, \Gamma_{2}, \Gamma_{3}$ be given in the plane. For a point $P$ outside the circles, construct six points $A_i, B_i$ such that $PA_i$ and $PB_i$ are tangents to $\Gamma_i$. Call $P$ exceptional if the lines $A_1B_1, A_2B_2, A_3B_3$ are concurrent. Show that all such exceptional points lie on a line.

Let three circles $\Gamma_{1}, \Gamma_{2}, \Gamma_{3}$ be given in the plane, which are overlapping and intersecting. For a point $P$ outside the circles, construct six points $A_i, B_i$ as the tangents from $P$ to $\Gamma_i$. Call $P$ exceptional if the lines $A_1B_1, A_2B_2, A_3B_3$ are concurrent. Show that all such exceptional points lie on the same circle.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $D$ be a point on segment $BC$. A line through $D$ meets $AB$ at $X$ and the extension of $AC$ at $Y$. If the circumcircle of triangle $BXD$ meets the circumcircle $\omega$ of triangle $ABC$ at a second point $Z$, and the lines $ZD$ and $ZY$ meet $\omega$ again at $V$ and $W$, respectively, show that $AB = VW$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle and let $D$ be a point on side $BC$. A line through $D$ intersects $AB$ at $X$ and the ray $AC$ at $Y$. The circumcircle of triangle $CXD$ intersects the circumcircle $\omega$ of triangle $ABC$ again at point $Z \neq C$. The lines $ZD$ and $ZY$ intersect $\omega$ again at $V$ and $W$, respectively. Prove that $AB = VW$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle and let $D$ be a point on side $BC$. A line through $D$ intersects $AB$ at $X$ and the ray $AC$ at $Y$. The circumcircle of triangle $BXD$ intersects the circumcircle $\omega$ of triangle $ABC$ again at point $Z \neq B$. The lines $ZD$ and $ZC$ intersect $\omega$ again at $V$ and $W$, respectively. Prove that $AB = VW$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle and let $D$ be a point on side $BC$. A line through $D$ intersects $AB$ at $X$ and the ray $AC$ at $Y$. The circumcircle of triangle $BXD$ intersects the circumcircle $\omega$ of triangle $ABC$ again at point $Z \neq B$. The lines $ZD$ and $ZY$ intersect $\omega$ again at $V$ and $W$, respectively. Prove that $AC = VW$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be called great if for every point $D$ on $BC$, and for $P$ and $Q$ being the feet of perpendiculars from $D$ to $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, the reflection of $D$ across the line $PQ$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Show that triangle $ABC$ is great if and only if it is a right isosceles triangle at vertex $A$.

negatives.text: Suppose triangle $ABC$ satisfies the condition that for all points $D$ on segment $BC$, and for $P$ and $Q$ being the feet of the perpendiculars from $D$ to $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, the reflection of $D$ over the line $PQ$ lies on the incircle of triangle $ABC$. Prove that triangle $ABC$ is great if and only if $\angle A = 90^\circ$ and $AB = AC$.

Suppose triangle $ABC$ satisfies the condition that for all points $D$ on segment $BC$, and for $P$ and $Q$ being the feet of the perpendiculars from $D$ to $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, the reflection of $D$ over the line $PQ$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Prove that triangle $ABC$ is great if and only if $\angle A = 90^\circ$ and $AB = 2AC$.

Suppose triangle $ABC$ satisfies the condition that for all points $D$ on segment $BC$, and for $P$ and $Q$ being the feet of the perpendiculars from $D$ to $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, the reflection of $D$ over the line $PQ$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Prove that triangle $ABC$ is great if and only if $\angle A = 60^\circ$ and $AB = AC$.

positive_text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R}^{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{+}$ such that
$$
(z+1) f(a+b) = f(a f(z) + b) + f(b f(z) + a)
$$
for all positive real numbers $a$, $b$, $z$.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R}^{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{+}$ such that
$$
(z+1) f(x+y) = f(x f(z) + y) - f(y f(z) + x)
$$
for all positive real numbers $x$, $y$, $z$.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R}^{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{+}$ such that
$$
(z+1) f(x+y) = f(x f(z) + y) + f(y f(z) + x)
$$
for all $x$, $y$, $z$ in the set of all real numbers.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R}^{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{+}$ such that
$$
(z+1) f(x+y) = f(x f(z^2) + y) + f(y f(z^2) + x)
$$
for all positive real numbers $x$, $y$, $z$.

positive_text: Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of all integers. Characterize all polynomials $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that for every permutation $\{a_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ of $\mathbb{Z}$, there are positive integers $i < j$ and some integer $k$ with $\sum_{n=i}^{j} a_n = P(k)$.

negatives.text: Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of all integers. Find all polynomials $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that for any infinite sequence $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ of integers in which each integer in $\mathbb{Z}$ appears exactly once, there exist indices $i < j$ and an integer $k$ with $\prod_{n=i}^{j} a_n = P(k)$.

Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of all integers. Find all polynomials $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that for any infinite sequence $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ of integers in which each integer in $\mathbb{Z}$ appears exactly once, there exist indices $i < j$ and an integer $k$ with $\sum_{n=i}^{j} a_n = P(k)^2$.

Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of all integers. Find all polynomials $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that for any infinite sequence $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ of integers in which each integer in $\mathbb{Z}$ appears exactly once, there exist indices $i < j$ and an integer $k$ with $\sum_{n=i}^{j} a_n < P(k)$.

positive_text: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be positive real numbers. Emerald walks in the coordinate plane from the origin $(0,0)$, moving either one unit right or one unit up each minute, while staying within the region $|x-y|<2025$. At each point $(x, y)$ she visits, she records the integer $\lfloor x \alpha + y \beta\rfloor$. If every non-negative integer is recorded exactly once, find all possible pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$ that allow such a journey.

negatives.text: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be positive real numbers. A traveler begins at $(0,0)$ and moves one unit either right or up each minute, staying within the region $|x - y| < 2025$. At every point $(x, y)$, the value $\lfloor x \alpha - y \beta\rfloor$ is recorded. If every non-negative integer is recorded exactly once, find all such pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$ for which this is possible.

Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be positive real numbers. A traveler begins at $(0,0)$ and moves one unit either right or up each minute, staying within the region $|x - y| < 2025$. At every point $(x, y)$, the value $\lfloor x^2 \alpha + y^2 \beta\rfloor$ is recorded. If every non-negative integer is recorded exactly once, find all such pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$ for which this is possible.

Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be positive real numbers. A traveler begins at $(0,0)$ and moves one unit either right or up each minute, staying within the region $|x - y| < 2025$. At every point $(x, y)$, the value $\lfloor x \alpha + y \beta\rfloor$ is recorded. If every positive integer is recorded exactly once, find all such pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$ for which this is possible.

positive_text:
Find all real solutions $(x, y, z)$ satisfying the equation
$$
4x^4 - x^2 (4y^4 + 4z^4 - 1) - 2xyz + (y^4 + z^4)^2 + y^2z^2 = 0
$$.

negatives.text:
Determine all real triples $(x, y, z)$ such that
$$
4x^4 - x^2 (4y^4 + 4z^4 - 1) + 2xyz + y^8 + 2y^4z^4 + y^2z^2 + z^8 = 0
$$.

Find all real triples $(x, y, z)$ satisfying
$$
4x^4 - x^2 (4y^4 + 4z^4 - 1) - 2xyz + y^8 - 2y^4z^4 + y^2z^2 + z^8 = 0
$$.

Find all real triples $(x, y, z)$ such that
$$
4x^4 - x^2 (4y^4 + 4z^4 - 1) - 2xyz + y^8 + 2y^4z^4 + y^2z^2 + z^8 = 1
$$.

positive_text: Find all triples $(x, y, z)$ of positive integers $x > y > z > 0$ such that $y \cdot 2^x + 1 = x^2$.

negatives.text: Find all triples $(x, y, z)$ of positive integers $x > y > z > 0$, such that $x^2 = y \cdot 2^x - 1$ holds.
Find all triples $(x, y, z)$ of positive integers $x > y > z > 0$, such that $x^2 = y \cdot 2^{x^2} + 1$ holds.

positive_text: Let $a$ and $b$ be positive real numbers with $a + b = 1$. Prove that $$\frac{(3a - 1)^2}{a} + \frac{(3b - 1)^2}{b} \geq 1.$$ For what values of $a$ and $b$ does equality occur?

negatives.text: Let $x$ and $y$ be positive real numbers such that $x + y = 1$. Prove that $$\frac{(3x - 1)^2}{x} + \frac{(3y - 1)^2}{y} \leq 1.$$ When does equality hold?
Let $x$ and $y$ be positive real numbers such that $x + y = 1$. Prove that $$\frac{(3x - 2)^2}{x} + \frac{(3y - 2)^2}{y} \geq 1.$$ When does equality hold?
Let $x$ and $y$ be positive real numbers such that $x + y = 2$. Prove that $$\frac{(3x - 1)^2}{x} + \frac{(3y - 1)^2}{y} \geq 1.$$ When does equality hold?

positive_text:
Determine the maximum value of the function
$$
f_k(x, y) = (x + y) - (x^{2k+1} + y^{2k+1})
$$
subject to the condition $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ for all $k \in \mathbb{Z}^+$.

negatives.text:
Determine the maximum value of the function
$$
f_k(x, y) = (x + y) - (x^{2k+1} + y^{2k+1})
$$
over all real numbers $x$ and $y$ satisfying the equation $x^2 + y^2 = 2$ for all positive integers $k$.

Determine the maximum value of the function
$$
f_k(x, y) = (x + y) + (x^{2k+1} + y^{2k+1})
$$
over all real numbers $x$ and $y$ satisfying the equation $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ for all positive integers $k$.

Determine the minimum value of the function
$$
f_k(x, y) = (x + y) - (x^{2k+1} + y^{2k+1})
$$
over all real numbers $x$ and $y$ satisfying the equation $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ for all positive integers $k$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $\angle ABC = \angle BAC$, and let $P$ be a point on the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ lying on the arc $CA$ not containing $B$. If $E$ and $F$ are the feet of perpendiculars from $C$ to $AP$ and $BP$, respectively, show that $AE = BF$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $\overline{AC} = \overline{BC}$, and let $P$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ on the arc $CA$ not containing $B$. If $E$ and $F$ are the projections of $C$ onto lines $AP$ and $BP$, respectively, prove that $AE + BF$ is constant.

Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $\overline{AC} = \overline{BC}$, and let $P$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ on the arc $CA$ not containing $B$. If $E$ and $F$ are the projections of $C$ onto lines $AP$ and $BP$, respectively, prove that $AE^2 + BF^2 = AB^2$.

positive_text: \text{Let } x, y, z \text{ and } w \text{ be four integers such that } 7x + 8y = 14z + 28w. \text{ Prove that } x \cdot y \text{ is a multiple of } 14.

negatives.text: \text{Let } a, b, c \text{ and } d \text{ be four integers such that } 7a + 8b = 14c - 28d. \text{ Prove that } a \cdot b \text{ is a multiple of } 14.
\text{Let } a, b, c \text{ and } d \text{ be four integers such that } 7a + 8b = 14c + 28d^2. \text{ Prove that } a \cdot b \text{ is a multiple of } 14.

positive_text:
Given $n$ packages with weights $1, 2, 3, \ldots, n$, can they be partitioned into three subsets with equal total weight? Determine if this is possible for

a. $n = 2011$

b. $n = 2012$

negatives.text:
A postman has $n$ parcels of weights $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, $\ldots$, $n$. He wants to divide the parcels into three groups of equal weight. Is this possible for

a. $n = 2011$

b. $n = 2013$?

A postman has $n$ parcels of weights $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, $\ldots$, $n$. He wants to divide the parcels into three groups such that the absolute difference between any two groups is less than 1. Is this possible for

a. $n = 2011$

b. $n = 2012$?

positive_text:
Find all integer pairs $(x, y)$ satisfying
$$
(x^2 - x) + (x + 1) + (y^2 - y) + (y + 1) = 24 - 9xy.
$$

negatives.text:
Find all integer solutions of
$$
(x - 1) \cdot x + (x + 1) + (y - 1) \cdot y + (y + 1) = 24 + 9xy.
$$

Determine all integer solutions of
$$
(x - 1) \cdot x + (x + 1) + (y - 1) \cdot y + (y + 1) = 24 - 9x^2y.
$$

Find all integer values of $x$ and $y$ such that
$$
(x - 1)^2 + (x + 1) + (y - 1)^2 + (y + 1) = 24 - 9xy.
$$

positive_text: Let $n \ge 3$ be an integer. Consider a convex $n$-gon $P_1P_2\dots P_n$. A line $\ell$ passes through $P_1$ but does not pass through any other vertex. Let $\ell'$ be perpendicular to $\ell$ and also passing through $P_1$. The $n$-gon is orthogonally projected onto $\ell'$, yielding points $Q_1, Q_2, \dots, Q_n$, where $Q_j$ is the projection of $P_j$. The line $\ell$ is valid if the projections $Q_j$ are distinct. Determine the number of distinct orderings of $Q_1, \dots, Q_n$ as $\ell$ and the $n$-gon vary over all such configurations.

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 3$ be an integer. For a convex $n$-gon $A_1A_2\dots A_n$, consider a line $g$ through $A_1$ that does not pass through any other vertex. Let $h$ be the line through $A_1$ parallel to $g$. We orthogonally project the $n$-gon onto $h$, and for $j = 1, \dots, n$, let $B_j$ be the projection of $A_j$. The line $g$ is valid if the projections $B_j$ are distinct. How many distinct orderings of $B_1, \dots, B_n$ can occur?

Let $n \ge 3$ be an integer. For a convex $n$-gon $A_1A_2\dots A_n$, consider a line $g$ through $A_1$ that does not pass through any other vertex. Let $h$ be the line through $A_1$ perpendicular to $g$. We orthogonally project the $n$-gon onto $h$, and for $j = 1, \dots, n$, let $B_j$ be the projection of $A_j$. The line $g$ is valid if the projections $B_j$ are distinct. How many distinct orderings of $B_1, \dots, B_n$ can occur if $g$ must pass through $A_2$?

Let $n \ge 3$ be an integer. For a convex $n$-gon $A_1A_2\dots A_n$, consider a line $g$ through $A_1$ that does not pass through any other vertex. Let $h$ be the line through $A_1$ perpendicular to $g$. We orthogonally project the $n$-gon onto $h$, and for $j = 1, \dots, n$, let $B_j$ be the projection of $A_j$. The line $g$ is valid if the projections $B_j$ are distinct. How many distinct orderings of $B_1, \dots, B_n$ can occur if the polygon is not convex?

positive_text: \text{Find all real values of } a \text{ and } b \text{ such that} \quad a^2 + a = b^3 - b, \quad b^2 + b = a^3 - a.

negatives.text: \text{Determine all real numbers } x \text{ and } y \text{ such that} \quad x^2 - x = y^3 - y, \quad y^2 + y = x^3 - x.
\text{Find all real numbers } x \text{ and } y \text{ such that} \quad x^2 + x = y^3 + y, \quad y^2 + y = x^3 - x.
\text{Determine all real numbers } x \text{ and } y \text{ such that} \quad x^2 + x = y^3 - y, \quad y^2 - y = x^3 - x.

positive_text: Let $p < q < r < s$ be real numbers. Arrange the values $u = pq + rs$, $v = qr + ps$, and $w = rp + qs$ in increasing order and justify your conclusion.

negatives.text: Let $a < b < c < d$ be real numbers. Arrange the values $x = ab + cd$, $y = bc + ad$, and $z = ca - bd$ in ascending order and prove your conclusion.
Let $a < b < c < d$ be real numbers. Arrange $x = ab + cd$, $y = bc + ad$, and $z = ca + bd$ in ascending order assuming $a, b, c, d$ are positive integers.
Let $a < b < c < d$ be real numbers. Arrange $x = ab + cd$, $y = bc + ad$, and $z = ca + bd$ in ascending order and prove the correctness, assuming $a + b + c + d = 0$.

positive_text: \text{Prove that} \quad (a^2 + b^2 c^2) \cdot (b^2 + a^2 c^2) \cdot (c^2 + a^2 b^2) \geq 8 a b^2 c^3 \quad \text{holds for all integer values of } a, b \text{ and } c. \text{ When does equality hold?}

negatives.text: \text{Prove that} \quad (x^2 + y^2 z^2) \cdot (y^2 + x^2 z^2) \cdot (z^2 + x^2 y^2) \leq 8 x y^2 z^3 \quad \text{holds for all integer values of } x, y, z. \text{ When does equality hold?}
\text{Prove that} \quad (x^2 + y^2 z^2) \cdot (y^2 + x^2 z^2) \cdot (z^2 + x^2 y^2) \geq 8 x^2 y z^3 \quad \text{holds for all integer values of } x, y, z. \text{ When does equality hold?}
\text{Prove that} \quad (x^2 + y^2 z^2) \cdot (y^2 + x^2 z^2) \cdot (z^2 + x^2 y^2) \geq 8 x y z^3 \quad \text{holds for all integer values of } x, y, z. \text{ When does equality hold?}

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB > AC$ and circumradius $R$. If $D$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$, and $T$ is a point on the line $AD$ such that $AT = 2R$ and $D$ lies between $A$ and $T$, and if $S$ is the midpoint of the arc $BC$ not containing $A$ on the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$, prove that $\angle AST = 90^\circ$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AC < AB$ and circumradius $R$. Let $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$, and let $T$ be a point on $AD$ such that $AT = 2R$ with $D$ between $A$ and $T$. Let $S$ be the midpoint of the arc $BC$ that does include $A$. Prove that $\angle AST = 90^\circ$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AC < AB$ and circumradius $R$. Let $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$, and let $T$ be a point on $AD$ such that $AT = R$ with $D$ between $A$ and $T$. Let $S$ be the midpoint of the arc $BC$ not containing $A$. Prove that $\angle AST = 90^\circ$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AC < AB$ and circumradius $R$. Let $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$, and let $T$ be a point on $AD$ such that $AT = 2R$ with $D$ between $A$ and $T$. Let $S$ be the midpoint of the arc $BC$ not containing $A$. Prove that $\angle SAT = 90^\circ$.

positive_text: Given a fixed integer $n \ge 3$, the integers $1, 2, 3, \dots, n$ are written on a board. At each step, two numbers are selected and replaced with their average. After $n-1$ such operations, only one number remains. What is the smallest integer that can be the final result using an optimal sequence of operations?

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 3$ be a fixed integer. The numbers $1, 2, 3, \dots, n$ are written on a board. In every move one chooses two numbers and replaces them by their geometric mean. This is done until only a single number remains on the board. Determine the least integer that can be reached at the end by an appropriate sequence of moves.

Let $n \ge 3$ be a fixed integer. The numbers $1, 2, 3, \dots, n$ are written on a board. In every move one chooses two numbers and replaces them by their sum. This is done until only a single number remains on the board. Determine the least integer that can be reached at the end by an appropriate sequence of moves.

Let $n \ge 3$ be a fixed integer. The numbers $1, 2, 3, \dots, n$ are written on a board. In every move one chooses two numbers and replaces them by their difference. This is done until only a single number remains on the board. Determine the least integer that can be reached at the end by an appropriate sequence of moves.

positive_text:
Let $x$, $y$, $z$ and $w$ be real numbers with $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + w^2 = 4$. Prove that
$$
(x+2)(y+2) \geq zw
$$
and find values $x$, $y$, $z$, and $w$ for which equality occurs.

negatives.text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ be real numbers with $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 = 4$. Prove the inequality
$$
(a+2)(b+2) \leq cd
$$
and give four numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ such that equality holds.

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ be real numbers with $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 = 4$. Prove the inequality
$$
(a+2)(b+2) \geq c^2 + d^2
$$
and give four numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ such that equality holds.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AC = BC$. Let $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $CD$. The line $BM$ meets $AC$ at point $E$. Prove that $AC = 3CE$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$ with $\overline{AC} = 2\overline{BC}$, let $D$ be the foot of the altitude through $C$. The midpoint of $CD$ is $M$. The line $BM$ intersects $AC$ at $E$. Prove that $AC = 3CE$.

positive_text: In einem gleichschenkligen Dreieck $ABC$ mit $\overline{AC} = \overline{BC}$ sei $D$ der Fußpunkt der Höhe von $C$ auf $AB$, und $M$ sei der Mittelpunkt der Strecke $CD$. Die Verbindungsgerade von $B$ und $M$ schneidet die Strecke $AC$ im Punkt $E$. Zeigen Sie, dass $\overline{AC} = 3\cdot \overline{CE}$ gilt.

negatives.text: Im gleichschenkeligen Dreieck $ABC$ mit $\overline{AC} = \overline{BC}$ sei $D$ der Fußpunkt der Höhe durch $C$, und $M$ sei der Mittelpunkt von $CD$. Die Gerade durch $B$ und $M$ schneidet $AB$ im Punkt $E$. Zeigen Sie, dass $\overline{AC} = 3\cdot \overline{CE}$ ist.

Im gleichschenkeligen Dreieck $ABC$ mit $\overline{AC} = \overline{BC}$ sei $D$ der Fußpunkt der Höhe durch $C$, und $M$ sei der Mittelpunkt von $CD$. Die Gerade durch $B$ und $M$ schneidet $AC$ im Punkt $E$. Zeigen Sie, dass $\overline{CE} = 3\cdot \overline{AC}$ ist.

positive_text:
The nonnegative integers $a$, $b$, and $n$ are written on a blackboard with $a = 2000$ and $b = 17$. Alice and Bob alternate turns, with Alice starting. On each turn, a player replaces one number with the absolute difference of the other two, provided the set of numbers does not remain unchanged. The player who cannot make a move loses.
* Prove that the game is finite for any $n$.
* Determine the winner when $n = 2017$.

negatives.text:
The nonnegative integers $2000$, $17$, and $n$ are written on a blackboard. Alice and Bob play the following game: Alice begins, then they play in turns. A move consists in replacing one of the three numbers with the sum of the other two. No moves are allowed where all three numbers remain unchanged. A player in turn who cannot make a legal move loses the game.
* Prove that the game will end for every number $n$.
* Who wins the game in the case $n = 2017$?

The nonnegative integers $2000$, $17$, and $n$ are written on a blackboard. Alice and Bob play the following game: Alice begins, then they play in turns. A move consists in replacing one of the three numbers by the absolute difference of the other two. No moves are allowed where the resulting number is equal to one of the existing numbers. A player in turn who cannot make a legal move loses the game.
* Prove that the game will end for every number $n$.
* Who wins the game in the case $n = 2017$?

The nonnegative integers $2000$, $17$, and $n$ are written on a blackboard. Alice and Bob play the following game: Alice begins, then they play in turns. A move consists in replacing one of the three numbers by the absolute difference of the other two. No moves are allowed where the resulting number is negative. A player in turn who cannot make a legal move loses the game.
* Prove that the game will end for every number $n$.
* Who wins the game in the case $n = 2017$?

positive_text:
Let $\alpha$ be a positive real number. Find the largest real constant $C$ such that the inequality
$$
\left(1 + \frac{\alpha}{x^2}\right) \left(1 + \frac{\alpha}{y^2}\right) \left(1 + \frac{\alpha}{z^2}\right) \geq C \cdot \left(\left(\frac{x}{z} + \frac{z}{x}\right) + 2\right)
$$
holds for all positive real numbers $x, y, z$ with $xy + yz + zx = \alpha$. For what values of $x, y, z$ does equality occur?

negatives.text:
Let $\alpha$ be a positive real number. Find the maximum real number $C$ such that the inequality
$$
\left(1 + \frac{\alpha}{x^2}\right) \left(1 + \frac{\alpha}{y^2}\right) \left(1 + \frac{\alpha}{z^2}\right) \geq C \cdot \left(\frac{x}{z} - \frac{z}{x} + 2\right)
$$
holds for all positive real numbers $x, y, z$ with $xy + yz + zx = \alpha$. When does equality occur?

Let $\alpha$ be a positive real number. Determine the largest real number $C$ such that the inequality
$$
\left(1 + \frac{\alpha}{x^2}\right) \left(1 + \frac{\alpha}{y^2}\right) \left(1 + \frac{\alpha}{z^2}\right) \geq C \cdot \left(\frac{x}{z} + \frac{z}{x} + 2\right)^2
$$
is valid for all positive real numbers $x, y, z$ with $xy + yz + zx = \alpha$. When does equality occur?

positive_text:
Let $S$ be a set of positive integers satisfying the following:
(i) $2018 \in S$.
(ii) If $n \in S$, then all divisors of $n$ are in $S$.
(iii) For all $a, b \in S$ with $1 < a < b$, the number $ab + 1$ is also in $S$.

Prove that $S = \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}$.

negatives.text:
Let $M$ be a set of positive integers such that:
(1) $2018 \in M$.
(2) If $m \in M$, then all positive divisors of $m$ are also elements of $M$.
(3) For all $k, m \in M$ with $1 < k < m$, the number $km - 1$ is also an element of $M$.

Prove that $M = \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}$.

Let $M$ be a set of positive integers such that:
(1) $2018 \in M$.
(2) If $m \in M$, then all positive divisors of $m$ are also elements of $M$.
(3) For all $k, m \in M$ with $1 < k < m$, the number $k + m$ is also an element of $M$.

Prove that $M = \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}$.

Let $M$ be a set of positive integers such that:
(1) $2018 \in M$.
(2) If $m \in M$, then all positive divisors of $m$ are also elements of $M$.
(3) For all $k, m \in M$ with $1 < k < m$, the number $km + 1$ is not an element of $M$.

Prove that $M = \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have an interior point $P$ such that the circumcenters $M_A$ of $\triangle BCP$ and $M_B$ of $\triangle ACP$ lie outside $\triangle ABC$. It is given that $A$, $P$, and $M_A$ are collinear, as are $B$, $P$, and $M_B$. A line through $P$ parallel to $AB$ intersects the circumcircles of $\triangle BCP$ and $\triangle ACP$ at $D$ and $E$ (other than $P$). Prove that $DE = AC + BC$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ have a point $P$ inside it such that the circumcenters of triangles $BCP$ and $ACP$, denoted $M_A$ and $M_B$, lie outside triangle $ABC$. It is given that $A$, $P$, $M_A$ are collinear and $B$, $P$, $M_B$ are collinear. A line through $P$ parallel to side $AB$ intersects the circumcircles of $\triangle BCP$ and $\triangle ACP$ at points $D$ and $E$, distinct from $P$. Prove that $DE = AC - BC$.

Let triangle $ABC$ have a point $P$ inside it such that the circumcenters of triangles $BCP$ and $ACP$, denoted $M_A$ and $M_B$, lie outside triangle $ABC$. It is given that $A$, $P$, $M_A$ are collinear and $B$, $P$, $M_B$ are collinear. A line through $P$ perpendicular to side $AB$ intersects the circumcircles of $\triangle BCP$ and $\triangle ACP$ at points $D$ and $E$, distinct from $P$. Prove that $DE = AC + BC$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with altitudes $AD$ and $BE$, where $D$ and $E$ are the feet on $BC$ and $AC$, respectively. Points $F$ and $G$ lie on $AD$ and $BE$, respectively, such that $$\frac{AF}{FD} = \frac{BG}{GE}.$$ The line $CF$ intersects $BE$ at $H$, and the line $CG$ intersects $AD$ at $I$. Prove that $F, G, H, I$ lie on a common circle.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with altitudes $AD$ and $BE$, where $D$ and $E$ are the feet on $BC$ and $AC$, respectively. Points $F$ and $G$ lie on $AD$ and $BE$, respectively, such that $$\frac{AF}{FD} = -\frac{BG}{GE}.$$ The line $CF$ intersects $BE$ at $H$, and the line $CG$ intersects $AD$ at $I$. Prove that $F, G, H, I$ lie on a circle.

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with altitudes $AD$ and $BE$, where $D$ and $E$ are the feet on $BC$ and $AC$, respectively. Points $F$ and $G$ lie on $AD$ and $BE$, respectively, such that $$\frac{AF}{FD} = \frac{BG}{GE}.$$ The line $CF$ intersects $AD$ at $H$, and the line $CG$ intersects $BE$ at $I$. Prove that $F, G, H, I$ lie on a circle.

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with altitudes $AD$ and $BE$, where $D$ and $E$ are the feet on $BC$ and $AC$, respectively. Points $F$ and $G$ lie on $AD$ and $BE$, respectively, such that $$\frac{AF^2}{FD^2} = \frac{BG^2}{GE^2}.$$ The line $CF$ intersects $BE$ at $H$, and the line $CG$ intersects $AD$ at $I$. Prove that $F, G, H, I$ lie on a circle.

positive_text: Let $a$ and $b$ be real numbers such that $(a + 1)(b + 2) = 8$. Prove that $$(ab - 10)^2 \geq 64.$$ Also, find all such pairs $(a, b)$ for which equality is achieved.

negatives.text: Let $x$ and $y$ be real numbers such that $(x + 1)(y + 2) = 8$. Prove that $$(xy + 10)^2 \geq 64.$$ Also, find all pairs $(x, y)$ for which equality is achieved.
Let $x$ and $y$ be real numbers satisfying $(x + 1)(y + 2) = 8$. Show that $$(xy - 10)^3 \geq 64.$$ Determine all pairs $(x, y)$ for which equality holds.

positive_text: Let $a$ and $b$ be real numbers such that $(a - 1)(b - 2) = -8$. Prove that $$(ab - 10)^2 \geq 64.$$ Determine all values of $(a, b)$ where equality occurs.

negatives.text: Let $x$ and $y$ be real numbers such that $(x + 1)(y + 2) = 9$. Prove that $$(xy - 10)^2 \geq 64.$$ Find all pairs $(x, y)$ for which equality holds.
Let $x$ and $y$ be real numbers satisfying $(x + 1)(y + 2) = 8$. Show that $$(xy - 9)^2 \geq 64.$$ Determine all pairs $(x, y)$ for which equality holds.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle. Define a point $X$ such that $AX = AB$ and $X$ lies on the ray opposite to $AC$ at $A$. Similarly, define $Y$ such that $BY = AB$ and $Y$ lies on the ray opposite to $BC$ at $B$. Prove that the circumcircles of $ACY$ and $BCX$ intersect again at a point other than $C$ that lies on the internal bisector of $\angle BCA$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ denote a triangle. The point $X$ lies on the extension of $AC$ beyond $A$, such that $AX = AB$. Similarly, the point $Y$ lies on the extension of $BC$ beyond $B$ such that $BY = AB$. Prove that the circumcircles of $ABY$ and $BCX$ intersect a second time in a point different from $C$ that lies on the bisector of the angle $\angle BCA$.

Let $ABC$ denote a triangle. The point $X$ lies on the extension of $AC$ beyond $A$, such that $AX = AB$. Similarly, the point $Y$ lies on the extension of $BC$ beyond $B$ such that $BY = AB$. Prove that the circumcircles of $ACY$ and $BCX$ intersect a second time in a point different from $C$ that lies on the external bisector of the angle $\angle BCA$.

Let $ABC$ denote a triangle. The point $X$ lies on the extension of $AC$ beyond $A$, such that $AX = AB$. Similarly, the point $Y$ lies on the extension of $BC$ beyond $B$ such that $BY = AB$. Prove that the circumcircles of $ACY$ and $BCX$ intersect a second time in a point different from $C$ that lies on the perpendicular bisector of segment $AB$.

positive_text: \text{Let } x, y, z \text{ be distinct positive integers. Prove that } \frac{x^3 + y^3 + z^3}{3} - xyz \ge x + y + z. \text{ When does equality hold?}

negatives.text: \text{Let } a, b, c \text{ be pairwise distinct natural numbers. Prove that } \frac{a^3 + b^3 + c^3}{3} \le abc + a + b + c. \text{ When does equality hold?}
\text{Let } a, b, c \text{ be pairwise distinct natural numbers. Prove that } \frac{a^3 + b^3 + c^3}{3} \ge abc + a^2 + b^2 + c^2. \text{ When does equality hold?}
\text{Let } a, b, c \text{ be pairwise distinct natural numbers. Prove that } \frac{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}{3} \ge abc + a + b + c. \text{ When does equality hold?}

positive_text: Let $\alpha$ be a real number. Determine all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying $$ f(f(a) + b) = f(a^2 - b) + \alpha f(a) b $$ for all $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$.

negatives.text: Let $\alpha$ be a real number. Determine all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying $$ f(f(x) + y) = f(x^2 - y) + \alpha f(x) y^2 $$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.
Let $\alpha$ be a real number. Determine all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying $$ f(f(x) + y) = f(x^2 - y) + \alpha f(x) y + f(y) $$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.
Let $\alpha$ be a real number. Determine all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying $$ f(f(x) + y) = f(x^2 + y) + \alpha f(x) y $$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

positive_text: \text{Let } x \text{ and } y \text{ be positive integers and } z \text{ be a positive real number such that} \quad \frac{x+1}{y+z} = \frac{y}{x}. \text{ Show that } z \ge 1 \text{ holds.}

negatives.text: \text{Let } a, b \in \mathbb{Z}^+ \text{ and } c \in \mathbb{R}^+ \text{ satisfy } \frac{a-1}{b+c} = \frac{b}{a}. \text{ Prove that } c \ge 1 \text{ holds.}
\text{Let } a, b \in \mathbb{Z}^+ \text{ and } c \in \mathbb{R}^+ \text{ satisfy } \frac{a+1}{b-c} = \frac{b}{a}. \text{ Prove that } c \ge 1 \text{ holds.}
\text{Let } a, b \in \mathbb{Z}^+ \text{ and } c \in \mathbb{R}^+ \text{ satisfy } \frac{a+1}{b+\sqrt{c}} = \frac{b}{a}. \text{ Prove that } c \ge 1 \text{ holds.}

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $AC = BC$, and let $k$ be its circumcircle. Point $D$ is on the arc $BC$ of $k$ not containing $A$, and $E$ is the intersection of $CD$ with $AB$. Show that $BC$ is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $BDE$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $AC = BC$, and let $k$ be its circumcircle. Let $D$ be a point on the arc $BC$ of $k$ not containing $A$, and let $E$ be the intersection of $BD$ with $AC$. Prove that the line $BC$ is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $BDE$.

Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $AC = BC$, and let $k$ be its circumcircle. Let $D$ be a point on the arc $BC$ of $k$ not containing $A$, and let $E$ be the intersection of $CD$ with $AB$. Prove that the line $BC$ is a chord of the circumcircle of triangle $BDE$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be given. Construct points $P$ and $Q$ on the line $BC$ such that $BP = BA$ and $CQ = CA$, with $P$ lying on the extension of $BC$ beyond $B$ and $Q$ on the extension beyond $C$. Show that the center $O$ of the circle passing through $A$, $P$, and $Q$ lies on the bisector of $\angle BAC$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be given. Let $P$ be the point on the extension of $BC$ beyond $B$ such that $BP = BA$, and let $Q$ be the point on the segment $BC$ such that $CQ = CA$. Prove that the circumcenter $O$ of triangle $APQ$ lies on the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$.

positive_text:
Determine whether there exists a real number $ c $ such that the equation
$$
 x^3 - 2023x^2 - 2023x + c = 0
$$
has three distinct rational roots.

negatives.text:

$$
has three different rational solutions.

Determine whether there exists a real number $ r $ such that the equation
$$
 x^3 - 2023x^2 - 2023x + r = 0
$$
has three different integer solutions.

positive_text: Alice and Bob play a game on a linear board of $n \ge 3$ cells, with Alice's piece at the leftmost cell and Bob's at the rightmost cell. Players take turns moving their piece one or two cells toward the opponent's piece, ensuring the move lands on an unoccupied cell and does not leap over the opponent. Alice moves first. A player loses if they cannot move. Determine all $n$ for which Bob has a winning strategy regardless of Alice's play, and all $n$ for which Alice has a winning strategy regardless of Bob's play.

negatives.text: Alice and Bob play a game on a strip of $n \ge 3$ squares with two game pieces. Alice's piece is on the first square, Bob's on the last square. Players alternate, and on their turn, they move their piece by 1 or 2 squares in the direction of the opponent, landing on an empty square or passing over the opponent's piece. Alice moves first. If a player cannot move, they lose. For which $n$ can Bob ensure a win no matter how Alice plays? For which $n$ can Alice ensure a win no matter how Bob plays?

positive_text:
Let $a$ and $b$ be positive real numbers such that $a + b = 1$. Prove that
$$
\frac{a+1}{b} + \frac{b+1}{a} \geq 6.
$$
When does equality occur?

negatives.text:
Let $x$ and $y$ be positive real numbers with $x + y = 1$. Prove that
$$
\frac{x^2 + 1}{y} + \frac{y^2 + 1}{x} \geq 6.
$$
When does equality hold?

positive_text:
Find the minimal value of $ C $ such that the inequality
$$
(a + b)^2 (a^2 + b^2 + C) + (1 - ab)^2 \geq 0
$$
is valid for all real numbers $ a $ and $ b $. What are the values of $ a $ and $ b $ for which equality is achieved?

negatives.text:
Find the minimal constant $ C $ such that the inequality
$$
(X + Y)^2 (X^2 + Y^2 + C) + (1 - XY)^2 \leq 0
$$
holds for all real numbers $ X $ and $ Y $. For which $ X $ and $ Y $ does equality occur?

Find the minimal constant $ C $ such that the inequality
$$
(X + Y)^2 (X^2 + Y^2 + C) + (1 + XY)^2 \geq 0
$$
holds for all real numbers $ X $ and $ Y $. For which $ X $ and $ Y $ does equality occur?

Find the minimal constant $ C $ such that the inequality
$$
(X + Y)^2 (X^2 + Y^2 + C) + (1 - XY)^2 \geq 1
$$
holds for all real numbers $ X $ and $ Y $. For which $ X $ and $ Y $ does equality occur?

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB > AC$. Let the altitudes from $A$, $B$, and $C$ meet $BC$, $AC$, and $AB$ at $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively. Let $S$ be the intersection point of $EF$ and $BC$. Prove that the circles passing through $A, E, F$ and $D, E, S$ are tangent at $E$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with $AB > AC$. Let $D$, $E$, and $F$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $A$, $B$, and $C$ to the opposite sides. Let $S$ be the intersection point of lines $EF$ and $BC$. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $AED$ and $AFS$ are tangent at $E$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with $AB > AC$. Let $D$, $E$, and $F$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $A$, $B$, and $C$ to the opposite sides. Let $S$ be the intersection point of lines $EF$ and $BC$. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $AEF$ and $DES$ intersect at $E$ and another point.

positive_text: Let $k$ be a positive integer. Show that $c(k) = k^5 + 5^k$ is divisible by $11$ if and only if $d(k) = k^5 \cdot 5^k + 1$ is divisible by $11$.

negatives.text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Prove that $a(n) = n^5 + 5^n$ is divisible by $11$ if and only if $b(n) = n^5 \cdot 5^n - 1$ is divisible by $11$.
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Prove that $a(n) = n^5 + 5^n$ is divisible by $11$ if and only if $b(n) = n^5 \cdot 5^{n+1} + 1$ is divisible by $11$.

positive_text:

3^{x} - 5^{y} = z^{3}
$$

$$

positive_text:
Let $N$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f, g: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ be functions such that $f(n) = g(n) = 0$ for all $|n| \geq N$. Define $h: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ by
$$
h(n) = \sup \{f(k)g(n-k) : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}
$$
for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Prove that
$$
\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} h(n) \geq \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (f(n))^p \right)^{1/p} \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (g(n))^q \right)^{1/q}
$$
for all positive real numbers $p$ and $q$ satisfying $1/p + 1/q = 1$.

negatives.text:
Let $N$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f, g: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ be functions such that $f(n) = g(n) = 0$ for all $|n| \geq N$. Define $h: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ by
$$
h(n) = \min \{f(k)g(n-k) : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}
$$
for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Prove that
$$
\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} h(n) \geq \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (f(n))^p \right)^{1/p} \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (g(n))^q \right)^{1/q}
$$
for all positive real numbers $p$ and $q$ satisfying $1/p + 1/q = 1$.

Let $N$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f, g: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ be functions such that $f(n) = g(n) = 0$ for all $|n| \geq N$. Define $h: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ by
$$
h(n) = \max \{f(k)g(n-k) : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}
$$
for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Prove that
$$
\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} h(n) \geq \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (f(n))^p \right)^{1/p} + \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (g(n))^q \right)^{1/q}
$$
for all positive real numbers $p$ and $q$ satisfying $1/p + 1/q = 1$.

Let $N$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f, g: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ be functions such that $f(n) = g(n) = 0$ for all $|n| \geq N$. Define $h: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ by

$$
for all positive real numbers $p$ and $q$ satisfying $1/p + 1/q = 1$.

positive_text: Find all positive integer solutions $(x, y, z, t)$ such that $$2013^t + 14^z = 12^x + 13^y.$$

negatives.text: Determine all quadruplets $(x, y, z, t)$ of positive integers such that $$12^x + 13^y + 14^z = 2013^t.$$
Determine all quadruplets $(x, y, z, t)$ of positive integers such that $$12^x + 13^y - 14^z = 2013^t + 1.$$
Determine all quadruplets $(x, y, z, t)$ of positive integers such that $$12^x + 13^y - 14^z = 2013^{t+1}.$$

positive_text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $x$, $y$, and $z$ be positive real numbers such that
$$
(a - x)(b - y)(c - z) = abc - xyz.
$$
Prove that
$$
(a + x)(b + y)(c + z) \geq 8abc.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $m_1$, $m_2$, $m_3$, $n_1$, $n_2$ and $n_3$ be positive real numbers such that
$$
(m_1 - n_1)(m_2 - n_2)(m_3 - n_3) = m_1 m_2 m_3 + n_1 n_2 n_3.
$$
Prove that
$$
(m_1 + n_1)(m_2 + n_2)(m_3 + n_3) \geq 8m_1 m_2 m_3.
$$

Let $m_1$, $m_2$, $m_3$, $n_1$, $n_2$ and $n_3$ be positive real numbers such that
$$
(m_1 - n_1)(m_2 - n_2)(m_3 - n_3) = m_1 m_2 m_3 - n_1 n_2 n_3.
$$
Prove that
$$
(m_1 + n_1)(m_2 + n_2)(m_3 + n_3) < 8m_1 m_2 m_3.
$$

Let $m_1$, $m_2$, $m_3$, $n_1$, $n_2$ and $n_3$ be positive real numbers such that
$$
(m_1 - n_1)(m_2 - n_2)(m_3 - n_3) = m_1^2 m_2 m_3 - n_1 n_2 n_3.
$$
Prove that
$$
(m_1 + n_1)(m_2 + n_2)(m_3 + n_3) \geq 8m_1 m_2 m_3.
$$

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have $AB = AC$. Let points $D$ and $E$ lie on segment $BC$ such that $D$ lies between $B$ and $E$, and $E$ lies between $D$ and $C$, with $2\angle DAE = \angle BAC$. Show that there exists a triangle $XYZ$ with side lengths $XY = BD$, $YZ = DE$, and $ZX = EC$. Determine $\angle BAC + \angle YXZ$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ have $AB = AC$. Let points $D$ and $E$ lie on side $BC$ such that $D$ is between $B$ and $E$, and $E$ is between $D$ and $C$, with $2\angle DAE = 2\angle BAC$. positive_text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Isaac has $2^n$ integers $x_1, \dots, x_{2^n}$. positive_text: Let $AB$ be a diameter of a circle ($\omega$) with center $O$. Let $M$ lie on $AB$ such that $AM < MB$. If the common chord of the circumcircles of triangles $CED$ and $CFG$ intersects $\omega$ at $K$ and $L$, and $\omega_2$ at $N$ (with $N$ closer to $L$), prove that $KC = NL$.

negatives.text: Let $AB$ be a diameter of a circle ($\omega$) with center $O$. Let $M$ be a point on $AB$ such that $MA < MB$. positive_text: \text{Let } a, b, c \text{ be positive real numbers. Prove that } \sqrt{a^3(b + c)} + \sqrt{b^3(c + a)} + \sqrt{c^3(a + b)} \geq \frac{4}{3}(ab + bc + ca)

negatives.text: \text{Let } a, b, c \text{ be positive real numbers. Prove that } \sqrt{a^3 b - a^3 c} + \sqrt{b^3 c - b^3 a} + \sqrt{c^3 a - c^3 b} \geq \frac{4}{3}(ab + bc + ca)

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $AB < AC$. Take points $F$ and $E$ on the extensions of $BA$ and $CA$ beyond $A$ such that $BF = CE = BC$. Let $M, N, H$ be the midpoints of $BF, CE, BC$ respectively, and let $O$ and $K$ be the circumcenters of triangles $MNH$ and $ABC$. positive_text: Given a set of $n$ points $P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n$ in the plane, let $r(P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n)$ denote the radius of the smallest enclosing circle. Show that for $n \ge 3$, there exist three points $P_i, P_j, P_k$ such that $$ r(P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n) = r(P_i, P_j, P_k). $$

negatives.text: Let $r(P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n)$ be the radius of the largest circle that fits inside the convex hull of the points $P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n$. Prove that if $n \ge 3$, there exist three points $P_i, P_j, P_k$ such that $$ r(P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n) = r(P_i, P_j, P_k). $$
