Given trapezoid $ABCD$ with $BC \parallel AD$ and diagonals intersecting at $O$ such that $CD = AO$ and $BC = OD$. If $CA$ bisects $\angle CBD$, find the angles of $ABCD$.

positive_text: Let there be $N$ children ($N \ge 3$), all with distinct heights, placed in a circular formation. A child is called *middle* if he is neither the tallest nor the shortest among himself and his two adjacent neighbors. Show that if $N$ is odd, then at least one *middle* child must exist in every such circular arrangement.

negatives.text: Let $N$ boys ($N \ge 3$) with distinct heights be arranged in a circle. A boy is called *middle* if he is taller than one of his neighbors and shorter than the other one. Prove that if $N$ is an even number, then there exists at least one *middle* boy in any arrangement of the boys along the circle.

Let $N$ boys ($N \ge 3$) with distinct heights be arranged in a circle. A boy is called *middle* if he is taller than both of his neighbors. Prove that if $N$ is an odd number, then there exists at least one *middle* boy in any arrangement of the boys along the circle.

Let $N$ boys ($N \ge 3$) with distinct heights be arranged in a circle. A boy is called *middle* if he is taller than one of his neighbors and shorter than the other one. Prove that if $N$ is an odd number, then there exists exactly one *middle* boy in any arrangement of the boys along the circle.

positive_text: \text{Given } N \geq 3 \text{ people, each with unique heights, arranged in a circle, define a person as *tall* if they are taller than their immediate neighbors. Determine all possible values of the number of such *tall* individuals.}

negatives.text: \text{Let } N \geq 3 \text{ boys, all of different heights, be arranged in a circle. A boy is called *tall* if he is taller than at least one of his neighbors. Determine all possible numbers of *tall* boys.}

\text{Let } N \geq 3 \text{ boys, all of different heights, be arranged in a circle. A boy is called *tall* if he is taller than both his neighbors. Determine the maximum number of *tall* boys in such an arrangement.}

\text{Let } N \geq 3 \text{ boys, all of different heights, be arranged in a circle. A boy is called *tall* if he is taller than both his neighbors. Determine all possible numbers of *tall* boys in a line instead of a circle.}

positive_text: Let $N$ children ($N \ge 3$), each with distinct heights, be placed in a circular arrangement. A child is considered *middle* if they are taller than one neighbor and shorter than the other. Determine all possible counts of middle children in such an arrangement.

negatives.text: Let $N$ boys ($N \ge 3$), no two of them having the same height, be arranged in a circle. A boy is said to be *middle* if he is taller than both of his neighbors. Determine all possible numbers of middle boys in such an arrangement.

Let $N$ boys ($N \ge 3$), no two of them having the same height, be arranged in a circle. A boy is said to be *middle* if he is taller than one neighbor and equal to the other. Determine all possible numbers of middle boys in such an arrangement.

Let $N$ boys ($N \ge 3$), no two of them having the same height, be arranged in a line instead of a circle. A boy is said to be *middle* if he is taller than one neighbor and shorter than the other. Determine all possible numbers of middle boys in such an arrangement.

negatives.text: \text{Let } N \geq 3 \text{ boys, all of different heights, be arranged in a circle. A boy is called *tall* if he is taller than at least one of his neighbors. Determine all possible numbers of *tall* boys.}

\text{Let } N \geq 3 \text{ boys, all of different heights, be arranged in a circle. A boy is called *tall* if he is taller than both his neighbors. Determine the maximum number of *tall* boys in such an arrangement.}

\text{Let } N \geq 3 \text{ boys, all of different heights, be arranged in a circle. A boy is called *tall* if he is taller than both his neighbors. Determine all possible numbers of *tall* boys in a line instead of a circle.}

positive_text: Let three points $P$, $Q$, and $R$ lie on the curve $xy = 1$ such that triangle $PQR$ is equilateral. Determine all possible values of the product of the sum of the $x$-coordinates and the sum of the $y$-coordinates of the triangle's vertices.

negatives.text: Three points $A$, $B$, $C$ lie on the hyperbola $y = 1/x$ so that the triangle $ABC$ is isosceles. Find all possible values of the product of the sum of abscissae and the sum of ordinates of the vertices of $ABC$.

Three points $A$, $B$, $C$ lie on the hyperbola $y = 1/x$ so that the triangle $ABC$ is equilateral. Find all possible values of the product of the sum of abscissae and the sum of the squares of the ordinates of the vertices of $ABC$.

Three points $A$, $B$, $C$ lie on the parabola $y = x^2$ so that the triangle $ABC$ is equilateral. Find all possible values of the product of the sum of abscissae and the sum of ordinates of the vertices of $ABC$.

positive_text: Let three points $P$, $Q$, and $R$ lie on the curve $xy = 1$ such that triangle $PQR$ is equilateral. Determine all possible values of the product of the sum of the $x$-coordinates and the sum of the $y$-coordinates of the triangle's vertices.

negatives.text: Three points $A$, $B$, $C$ lie on the hyperbola $y = 1/x$ so that the triangle $ABC$ is isosceles. Find all possible values of the product of the sum of abscissae and the sum of ordinates of the vertices of $ABC$.

Three points $A$, $B$, $C$ lie on the parabola $y = x^2$ so that the triangle $ABC$ is equilateral. Find all possible values of the product of the sum of abscissae and the sum of ordinates of the vertices of $ABC$.

positive_text: Given four points $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ lying on the hyperbola $y = 1/x$, suppose the quadrilateral $PQRS$ is a parallelogram with $PQ \parallel RS$ and the length of $PQ$ is twice the length of $QR$. Determine all possible areas of $PQRS$.

negatives.text: Four points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ lie on the hyperbola $y = 1/x$ such that $ABCD$ is a parallelogram with $AB \parallel CD$ and $AB = 3 \cdot BC$. Find all possible values of the area of $ABCD$.
Four points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ lie on the hyperbola $y = 1/x$ such that $ABCD$ is a parallelogram with $AB \parallel CD$ and $AB = 2 \cdot AD$. Find all possible values of the area of $ABCD$.
Four points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ lie on the hyperbola $y = 1/x$ such that the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is a rectangle with $AB = 2 \cdot BC$. Find all possible values of the area of $ABCD$.

positive_text: Consider two chords $AB$ and $CD$, parallel to each other, on the hyperbola $xy = 1$. Let the lines $AC$ and $BD$ intersect the $y$-axis at $A_1$ and $D_1$ respectively, and intersect the $x$-axis at $C_1$ and $B_1$ respectively. Show that the triangles $A_1OC_1$ and $D_1OB_1$ have equal areas.

negatives.text: Let $AB$ and $CD$ be two chords on the hyperbola $y = 1/x$ such that they are not parallel. If the lines $AC$ and $BD$ intersect the $y$-axis at $A_1$ and $D_1$, and the $x$-axis at $C_1$ and $B_1$, respectively, prove that the areas of the triangles $A_1OC_1$ and $D_1OB_1$ are equal.

Let $AB$ and $CD$ be two chords on the hyperbola $y = 1/x$ such that they are parallel. If the lines $AC$ and $BD$ intersect the $y$-axis at $A_1$ and $D_1$, and the $x$-axis at $C_1$ and $B_1$, respectively, prove that the areas of the triangles $A_1OD_1$ and $C_1OB_1$ are equal.

positive_text: Consider two chords $AB$ and $CD$, parallel to each other, on the hyperbola $xy = 1$. Show that the triangles $A_1OC_1$ and $D_1OB_1$ have equal areas.

negatives.text: Two parallel chords $AB$ and $CD$ are constructed on the hyperbola $y = 1/x$. The lines $AC$ and $BD$ meet the ordinate axis $Oy$ at points $A_1$ and $D_1$ respectively, and meet the abscissae axis $Ox$ at points $C_1$ and $B_1$ respectively. Prove that the areas of the triangles $A_1OB_1$ and $D_1OC_1$ are equal.

Two parallel chords $AB$ and $CD$ are constructed on the hyperbola $y = x$. The lines $AC$ and $BD$ meet the ordinate axis $Oy$ at points $A_1$ and $D_1$ respectively, and meet the abscissae axis $Ox$ at points $C_1$ and $B_1$ respectively. Prove that the perimeters of the triangles $A_1OC_1$ and $D_1OB_1$ are equal.

positive_text: Determine all positive integer pairs $(m, n)$ such that for any polynomial $P(x)$ with real coefficients and degree $m$, there exists a polynomial $Q(x)$ with real coefficients and degree $n$ where $Q(x)$ divides $Q(P(x))$.

negatives.text: Find all pairs $(m, n)$ of positive integers such that for all polynomial $P(x)$ with real coefficients and $\deg P(x) = m$, there exists a polynomial $Q(x)$ with real coefficients and $\deg Q(x) = n$ such that $P(Q(x))$ is divisible by $Q(x)$.

Find all pairs $(m, n)$ of positive integers such that for all polynomial $P(x)$ with real coefficients and $\deg P(x) = m$, there exists a polynomial $Q(x)$ with real coefficients and $\deg Q(x) = n$ such that $Q(P(x))$ is divisible by $x - Q(x)$.

Find all pairs $(m, n)$ of positive integers such that for all polynomial $P(x)$ with real coefficients and $\deg P(x) = m$, there exists a polynomial $Q(x)$ with real coefficients and $\deg Q(x) = n$ such that $Q(P(x))$ is divisible by $Q(x^2)$.

positive_text: Consider the hyperbola $ y = \frac{1}{x} $ on the Cartesian plane $ Oxy $. Three points $ A(t) $, $ B(t) $, and $ C(t) $ lie on the hyperbola such that their $ x $-coordinates are proportional to three distinct constant velocities $ v_1, v_2, v_3 $ times time $ t $. Prove that the area of triangle $ ABC $ is time-independent.

negatives.text: Let $ A(t) = (a t, \frac{1}{a t}) $, $ B(t) = (b t, \frac{1}{b t}) $, $ C(t) = (c t, \frac{1}{c t}) $, where $ a, b, c $ are distinct positive constants. Prove that the area of triangle $ ABC $ is proportional to $ t $.

positive_text: Let $ A, B, C $ be three points on the parabola $ y = x^2 $. The median from $ B $ to the midpoint $ M $ of side $ AC $ is vertical and has a length of $ 2 $. Determine the area of triangle $ ABC $.

negatives.text: Let $ A, B, C $ be three points on the parabola $ y = x^2 $. The median from $ B $ to the midpoint $ M $ of side $ AC $ is horizontal and has a length of $ 2 $. Find the area of triangle $ ABC $.

positive_text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be positive real numbers such that $ab + bc + ca \ge a + b + c$. Prove that

$$a(ab+bc+ca) + b(ab+bc+ca) + c(ab+bc+ca) + 3abc \ge 4(ab+bc+ca).$$

positive_text: Find all integer pairs $(x, y)$ such that $(y^2 + 7(x - y))^2 = x^3 y$.

negatives.text: Find all integer pairs $(a, b)$ such that $(b^2 + 7(a - b))^2 = a^3 + b$.
Find all integer pairs $(a, b)$ such that $(b^2 + 7(a + b))^2 = a^3 b$.
Find all integer pairs $(a, b)$ such that $(b^2 + 7(a - b))^2 = a^2 b$.

positive_text:
Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram, and let $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ lie on sides $AD$, $AB$, and $BC$, respectively, with the condition $AX = CZ$.
a) Prove that at least one of the following is true:
$$
XY + YZ \geq AC \quad \text{or} \quad XY + YZ \geq BD.
$$
b) Does the inequality $XY + YZ \geq \frac{AC + BD}{2}$ always hold?

negatives.text:
Points $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are marked on the sides $AD$, $AB$ and $BC$ of a parallelogram $ABCD$, respectively. It is known that $AX = CZ$.
a) Prove that at least one of the inequalities holds
$$
XY + YZ < AC \text{ or } XY + YZ < BD.
$$
b) Is it true that $XY + YZ < \frac{AC + BD}{2}$?

Points $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are marked on the sides $AD$, $AB$ and $BC$ of a parallelogram $ABCD$, respectively. It is known that $AX = CZ$.
a) Prove that at least one of the inequalities holds
$$
XY + YZ \geq AC^2 \text{ or } XY + YZ \geq BD^2.
$$
b) Is it true that $XY + YZ \geq \frac{AC^2 + BD^2}{2}$?

Points $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are marked on the sides $AD$, $AB$ and $BC$ of a parallelogram $ABCD$, respectively. It is known that $AX = CZ$.
a) Prove that at least one of the inequalities holds
$$
XY + YZ \geq AC \text{ and } XY + YZ \geq BD.
$$
b) Is it true that $XY + YZ \geq \frac{AC + BD}{2}$?

positive_text:
Let triangle $ABC$ have side lengths $AB = c$, $BC = a$, $CA = b$. Points $C_1, C_2$ lie on $AB$, $A_1, A_2$ lie on $BC$, and $B_1, B_2$ lie on $CA$, satisfying the relations:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{CA_1}{a} &= \frac{CB_2}{b} = \frac{a+b}{a+b+c}, \\
\frac{AB_1}{b} &= \frac{AC_2}{c} = \frac{b+c}{a+b+c}, \\
\frac{BC_1}{c} &= \frac{BA_2}{a} = \frac{a+c}{a+b+c}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Show that the intersection points of $A_1C_2$, $C_1B_2$, and $B_1A_2$ are concyclic with $A$, $B$, and $C$.

negatives.text:
Let triangle $ABC$ have side lengths $AB = c$, $BC = a$, $CA = b$. Points $C_1, C_2$ lie on $AB$, $A_1, A_2$ lie on $BC$, and $B_1, B_2$ lie on $CA$, satisfying the relations:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{CA_1}{a} &= \frac{CB_2}{b} = \frac{a-b}{a+b+c}, \\
\frac{AB_1}{b} &= \frac{AC_2}{c} = \frac{b-c}{a+b+c}, \\
\frac{BC_1}{c} &= \frac{BA_2}{a} = \frac{c-a}{a+b+c}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Prove that the points of intersection of the lines $A_1C_2$, $C_1B_2$, and $B_1A_2$ lie on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

Let triangle $ABC$ have side lengths $AB = c$, $BC = a$, $CA = b$. Points $C_1, C_2$ lie on $AB$, $A_1, A_2$ lie on $BC$, and $B_1, B_2$ lie on $CA$, satisfying the relations:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{CA_1}{a} &= \frac{CB_2}{b} = \frac{a+b}{a+b+c}, \\
\frac{AB_1}{b} &= \frac{AC_2}{c} = \frac{b+c}{a+b+c}, \\
\frac{BC_1}{c} &= \frac{BA_2}{a} = \frac{a+c}{a+b+c}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Prove that the points of intersection of the lines $A_1C_2$, $C_1B_2$, and $B_1A_2$ lie on the incircle of triangle $ABC$.

Let triangle $ABC$ have side lengths $AB = c$, $BC = a$, $CA = b$. Points $C_1, C_2$ lie on $AB$, $A_1, A_2$ lie on $BC$, and $B_1, B_2$ lie on $CA$, satisfying the relations:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{CA_1}{a} &= \frac{CB_2}{b} = \frac{a+b}{a+b+c}, \\
\frac{AB_1}{b} &= \frac{AC_2}{c} = \frac{b+c}{a+b+c}, \\
\frac{BC_1}{c} &= \frac{BA_2}{a} = \frac{a+c}{a+b+c}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Prove that the lines $A_1C_2$, $C_1B_2$, and $B_1A_2$ are concurrent.

positive_text: \text{Prove that } \frac{1}{a+b+1} - \frac{1}{(a+1)(b+1)} < \frac{1}{11} \text{ for all positive real numbers } a, b.

negatives.text: \text{Prove that } \frac{1}{x+y+1} - \frac{1}{(x+1)(y+1)} < \frac{1}{10} \text{ for all positive } x, y.
\text{Prove that } \frac{1}{x+y+1} - \frac{1}{(x+1)(y+1)} < -\frac{1}{11} \text{ for all positive } x, y.
\text{Prove that } \frac{1}{x^2+y^2+1} - \frac{1}{(x+1)(y+1)} < \frac{1}{11} \text{ for all positive } x, y.

positive_text: Consider the hyperbolae $H_1: xy = 1$ and $H_2: xy = -1$. A straight line intersects $H_1$ at points $A$ and $B$, and $H_2$ at points $C$ and $D$. The tangents to $H_1$ at $A$ and $B$ intersect at point $M$, and the tangents to $H_2$ at $C$ and $D$ intersect at point $N$. Show that the points $M$ and $N$ are symmetric with respect to the origin.

negatives.text: Let $H_1$ and $H_2$ be the hyperbolae $y = \frac{1}{x}$ and $y = -\frac{1}{x}$. A line intersects $H_1$ at points $A$ and $B$, and $H_2$ at points $C$ and $D$. The lines tangent to $H_1$ at $A$ and $B$ intersect at $M$, and the lines tangent to $H_2$ at $C$ and $D$ intersect at $N$. Prove that $M$ and $N$ are symmetric with respect to the x-axis.

Let $H_1$ and $H_2$ be the hyperbolae $y = \frac{1}{x}$ and $y = -\frac{1}{x}$. A line intersects $H_1$ at points $A$ and $B$, and $H_2$ at points $C$ and $D$. The lines tangent to $H_1$ at $A$ and $B$ intersect at $M$, and the lines tangent to $H_2$ at $C$ and $D$ intersect at $N$. Prove that $M$ and $N$ are symmetric with respect to the line $y = x$.

Let $H_1$ and $H_2$ be the hyperbolae $y = \frac{1}{x}$ and $y = -\frac{1}{x}$. A line intersects $H_1$ at points $A$ and $B$, and $H_2$ at points $C$ and $D$. The lines tangent to $H_1$ at $A$ and $B$ intersect at $M$, and the lines tangent to $H_2$ at $C$ and $D$ intersect at $N$. Prove that $M$ and $N$ are symmetric with respect to the origin, but only if the line passes through the origin.

positive_text: Let $H_1$ and $H_2$ be hyperbolas defined by $y = 1/x$ and $y = -1/x$, respectively. A line intersects $H_1$ at $A$ and $B$, and $H_2$ at $C$ and $D$. If $O$ is the origin, show that the areas of triangles $OAC$ and $OBD$ are equal.

negatives.text: Given two hyperbolas $H_1$ and $H_2$ with equations $y = 1/x$ and $y = -1/x^2$, respectively. A straight line meets $H_1$ at $A$ and $B$, and $H_2$ at $C$ and $D$. Let $O$ be the origin. Prove that the areas of triangles $OAC$ and $OBD$ are equal.

Let $H_1$ and $H_2$ be hyperbolas defined by $y = 1/x$ and $y = 1/x$, respectively. A straight line meets $H_1$ at $A$ and $B$, and $H_2$ at $C$ and $D$. Let $O$ be the origin. Prove that the areas of triangles $OAC$ and $OBD$ are equal.

Given two hyperbolas $H_1$ and $H_2$ with equations $y = 1/x$ and $y = -1/x$, respectively. A straight line meets $H_1$ at $A$ and $B$, and $H_2$ at $C$ and $D$. Let $O$ be the origin. Prove that the areas of triangles $OAC$ and $OBD$ are equal if the line passes through the origin.

positive_text: Let $H_1$ and $H_2$ be the hyperbolae given by $xy = 1$ and $xy = -1$, respectively. Let $M$ be a point on $H_1$, and let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be the points where the lines from $M$ are tangent to $H_2$. Prove that the line through $M_1$ and $M_2$ is tangent to $H_1$.

negatives.text: Let $H_1$ and $H_2$ be the hyperbolae $y = 1/x$ and $y = -1/x$, respectively. Let $M$ be a point on $H_1$, and let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be the intersection points of the lines $MM_1$ and $MM_2$ with $H_2$. Prove that the line through $M_1$ and $M_2$ is tangent to $H_1$.

Let $H_1$ and $H_2$ be the hyperbolae $y = 1/x$ and $y = -1/x$, respectively. Let $M$ be a point on $H_1$, and let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be the tangency points of the lines from $M$ to $H_2$. Prove that the line through $M_1$ and $M_2$ is tangent to $H_2$.

Let $H_1$ and $H_2$ be the hyperbolae $y = 1/x$ and $y = -1/x$, respectively. Let $M$ be a point on $H_1$, and let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be the points where the lines from $M$ intersect $H_2$ at right angles. Prove that the line through $M_1$ and $M_2$ is tangent to $H_1$.

positive_text: Determine all integers $n$ with $1 \leq n < 60$ for which the set $M = \{n, n+1, \dots, 60\}$ admits a partition into disjoint subsets where one element in each subset is the sum of the others.

negatives.text: Find all positive integers $n$ ($n < 60$) such that the set $M = \{n, n+1, \dots, 60\}$ can be partitioned into disjoint subsets so that in each subset the sum of all numbers is equal to the square of one of the numbers in the subset.

Find all positive integers $n$ ($n < 60$) such that the set $M = \{n, n+1, \dots, 60\}$ can be partitioned into disjoint subsets so that in each subset one of the numbers is equal to the product of all other numbers of this subset.

positive_text:
\text{Let } AB = p, BC = q, CD = r, DA = s, AC = m, BD = n \text{ be the sides and diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral } ABCD. \text{ Prove that} 

$$\left(\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{r}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{1}{q} + \frac{1}{s}\right)^2 \ge 8\left(\frac{1}{m^2} + \frac{1}{n^2}\right).$$

negatives.text:
\text{Let } a, b, c, d, x, y \text{ denote the sides and diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral } ABCD. \text{ Prove that} 

$$\left(\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{c}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{d}\right)^2 \le 8\left(\frac{1}{x^2} + \frac{1}{y^2}\right).$$

\text{Let } a, b, c, d, x, y \text{ denote the sides and diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral } ABCD. \text{ Prove that} 

$$\left(\frac{1}{a^2} + \frac{1}{c^2}\right) + \left(\frac{1}{b^2} + \frac{1}{d^2}\right) \ge 8\left(\frac{1}{x^2} + \frac{1}{y^2}\right).$$

\text{Let } a, b, c, d, x, y \text{ denote the sides and diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral } ABCD. \text{ Prove that} 

$$\left(\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{c}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{d}\right)^2 \ge 8\left(\frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y}\right)^2.$$

positive_text: \left(a^2 + \frac{c^2}{b^2}\right) \left(b^2 + \frac{a^2}{c^2}\right) \left(c^2 + \frac{b^2}{a^2}\right) \ge \frac{abc}{\sqrt{3}} \left(\frac{a^2 + 1}{a}\right) \left(\frac{b^2 + 1}{b}\right) \left(\frac{c^2 + 1}{c}\right) for all positive real $a, b, c$

negatives.text: \left(a^2 + \frac{c^2}{b^2}\right) \left(b^2 + \frac{a^2}{c^2}\right) \left(c^2 + \frac{b^2}{a^2}\right) < \frac{abc}{\sqrt{3}} \left(a + \frac{1}{a}\right) \left(b + \frac{1}{b}\right) \left(c + \frac{1}{c}\right) for all positive real $a, b, c$

\left(a^2 + \frac{c^2}{b^2}\right) \left(b^2 + \frac{a^2}{c^2}\right) \left(c^2 + \frac{b^2}{a^2}\right) \ge \frac{abc}{\sqrt{3}} \left(a + \frac{1}{a^2}\right) \left(b + \frac{1}{b^2}\right) \left(c + \frac{1}{c^2}\right) for all positive real $a, b, c$

\left(a^2 + \frac{c^2}{b^2}\right) \left(b^2 + \frac{a^2}{c^2}\right) \left(c^2 + \frac{b^2}{a^2}\right) \ge \frac{abc}{\sqrt{3}} \left(a + \frac{1}{a} + 1\right) \left(b + \frac{1}{b} + 1\right) \left(c + \frac{1}{c} + 1\right) for all positive real $a, b, c$

positive_text: Given real numbers $x, y, z, w$ such that $\sin x + y > \sin z + w$, $x + \sin y > z + \sin w$, prove that $x + y > z + w$.

negatives.text: Given real numbers $a, b, c, d$ such that $\sin a + b > \sin c + d$, $a + \sin b < c + \sin d$, prove that $a + b > c + d$.
Given real numbers $a, b, c, d$ such that $\sin a + b > \sin c + d$, $a + \sin b > c + \sin d$, prove that $a + b > c + d + 1$.
Given real numbers $a, b, c, d$ such that $\sin a + b > \sin c + d$, $a + \sin b > c + \sin d$, prove that $a + b^2 > c + d^2$.

positive_text:
Let $a, b, c$ be real numbers satisfying
$$
a + b + c = ab + bc + ca = -1.
$$
Show that $(ab - c^2)(bc - a^2)(ca - b^2) = abc - 1$.

negatives.text:
Given real numbers $x, y, z$ with
$$
x + y + z = xy + yz + zx = -1,
$$
prove that $(xy - z^2)(yz - x^2)(zx - y^2) = -xyz - 1$.

Given real numbers $x, y, z$ with
$$
x + y + z = xy + yz + zx = -1,
$$
prove that $(xy - z^2)(yz - x^2)(zx - y^2) = xyz + 1$.

Given real numbers $x, y, z$ with
$$
x + y + z = xy + yz + zx = -1,
$$
prove that $(xy - z^2)(yz - x^2)(zx - y^2) = xyz - 1$ and $(x + y + z)^2 = 0$.

positive_text: Determine all real numbers $a$ for which there exists a non-constant function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying $f(f(x)) = x f(x) - a x$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$, and such that the image of $f$ includes the value $a$.

negatives.text: Find all real numbers $a$ such that there exists a non-constant function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f(f(x)) = x f(x) + a x$ for all real $x$, and $f$ takes the value $a$.
Find all real numbers $a$ such that there exists a non-constant function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f(f(x)) = x f(x) - a$ for all real $x$, and $f$ takes the value $a$.
Find all real numbers $a$ such that there exists a non-constant function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f(f(x)) = x f(x) - a x$ for all real $x$, and $f$ never takes the value $a$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have points $K$ and $N$ on sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, such that $KB = KN$. Let the angle bisector of $\angle ACB$ intersect the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ again at point $R$. If the perpendicular from $R$ to $AB$ intersects $BN$ at $D$, prove that $A$, $K$, $D$, $N$ lie on a circle.

negatives.text: Points $K$ and $N$ are marked on the sides $AB$ and $AC$ of triangle $ABC$, respectively, such that $KB = KN$. The bisector of the angle $ACB$ meets the circumcircle of $ABC$ at points $C$ and $R$. The perpendicular from $R$ to $AB$ intersects the segment $BN$ at $D$. Prove that the points $A$, $K$, $D$, $B$ are concyclic.

Points $K$ and $N$ are marked on the sides $AB$ and $AC$ of triangle $ABC$, respectively, such that $KB = KN$. The bisector of the angle $ACB$ meets the circumcircle of $ABC$ at points $C$ and $R$. The perpendicular from $R$ to $AB$ intersects the segment $BN$ at $D$. Prove that the points $A$, $K$, $D$, $R$ are concyclic.

Points $K$ and $N$ are marked on the sides $AB$ and $AC$ of triangle $ABC$, respectively, such that $KB = KN$. The bisector of the angle $ACB$ meets the circumcircle of $ABC$ at points $C$ and $R$. The perpendicular from $R$ to $AB$ intersects the segment $BN$ at $D$. Prove that the points $A$, $K$, $D$, $N$ are collinear.

positive_text: Let $G$ be a graph with $n$ vertices ($n \ge 4$) such that for any pair of vertices $u$ and $v$, there exists a vertex $w$ which is not adjacent to either $u$ or $v$. Determine the maximum number of edges in $G$.

negatives.text: Given a graph with $n$ ($n \ge 4$) vertices. It is known that for any two of the vertices there is a vertex connected with both of these two vertices. Find the greatest possible number of the edges in the graph.

Given a graph with $n$ ($n \ge 4$) vertices. It is known that for any two of the vertices there is a vertex connected with at least one of these two vertices. Find the greatest possible number of the edges in the graph.

Given a graph with $n$ ($n \ge 4$) vertices. It is known that for any two of the vertices there is a vertex connected with at least one of these two vertices but not both. Find the greatest possible number of the edges in the graph.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $AB = 2AC$. Points $M$ and $N$ lie on $BC$ and $AB$ respectively such that the perimeter of trapezoid $CMNA$ equals $AB + AC$. Construct point $M$ using a ruler and compass.

negatives.text: Given triangle $ABC$ with $AB = 2AC$. If points $M$ and $N$ lie on $BC$ and $AB$ respectively and the perimeter of trapezoid $CMNA$ is the product of the lengths $AB$ and $AC$, construct $M$ using compasses and ruler.

Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $AB = 2AC$. Points $M$ and $N$ lie on $BC$ and $AB$ respectively such that the perimeter of trapezoid $CMNA$ is the sum of the squares of $AB$ and $AC$. Construct $M$ using compasses and ruler.

Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $AB = 2AC$. If points $M$ and $N$ lie on $BC$ and $AB$ respectively and the perimeter of trapezoid $CMNA$ is less than the sum of $AB$ and $AC$, construct $M$ using compasses and ruler.

positive_text: Let a trapezoid $ABCD$ be inscribed in the parabola $y = x^2$, with bases $AB$ and $CD$ parallel. Let the line passing through the midpoint of the non-parallel sides intersect the parabola at $K$ and $L$. Show that the distances from $K$ to $M$ and from $L$ to $N$ are equal.

Let $y = 1/x$ for $x > 0$ be intersected by a line $l$ at points $A$ and $B$. Two lines $l_1$ and $l_2$, parallel to $l$, intersect the left branch ($x < 0$) of the same hyperbola at points $E$, $F$ and $C$, $D$, respectively. Suppose $l_1$ meets the segments $AD$ and $BC$ at $G$ and $H$. Show that the segment $GE$ is congruent to $HF$.

negatives.text: Let a line $l$ intersect the right branch of the hyperbola $y = 1/x$ at $A$ and $B$. Two lines $l_1$ and $l_2$, parallel to $l$, intersect the left branch at $E, F$ and $C, D$, respectively. The line $l_1$ intersects the segments $AD$ and $BC$ at $G$ and $H$. Prove that $GE = HD$.

Let a line $l$ intersect the right branch of the hyperbola $y = 1/x$ at $A$ and $B$. Two lines $l_1$ and $l_2$, perpendicular to $l$, intersect the left branch at $E, F$ and $C, D$, respectively. The line $l_1$ intersects the segments $AD$ and $BC$ at $G$ and $H$. Prove that $GE = HF$.

Let a line $l$ intersect the right branch of the hyperbola $y = 1/x$ at $A$ and $B$. Two lines $l_1$ and $l_2$, parallel to $l$, intersect the left branch at $E, F$ and $C, D$, respectively. The line $l_1$ intersects the segments $AC$ and $BD$ at $G$ and $H$. Prove that $GE = HF$.

positive_text: Two quadratics $P(x) = x^2 + a x + b$ and $Q(x) = x^2 + c x + d$ are called *friendly* if they both have two distinct real roots, and the sum of the smallest root of $P(x)$ with the smallest root of $Q(x)$, and the sum of the largest root of $P(x)$ with the largest root of $Q(x)$, are the roots of $x^2 + (a + c)x + b + d$. Let $M$ be a set of at least three *friendly* trinomials. Prove that every trinomial in $M$ has $0$ as a root.

negatives.text: Two quadratic trinomials $P(x) = x^2 + a x + b$ and $Q(x) = x^2 + c x + d$ are called *friendly* if each of them has distinct real roots and $x_1 - x_3$, $x_2 - x_4$ are the roots of the quadratic trinomial $x^2 + (a + c)x + b + d$, where $x_1 < x_2$ are the roots of $P(x)$, $x_3 < x_4$ are the roots of $Q(x)$. Let $M$ be the set of pairwise *friendly* trinomials consisting of at least three trinomials. Prove that $0$ is a root of every trinomial from the set $M$.

Two quadratic trinomials $P(x) = x^2 + a x + b$ and $Q(x) = x^2 + c x + d$ are called *friendly* if each of them has distinct real roots and $x_1 + x_3$, $x_2 + x_4$ are the roots of the quadratic trinomial $x^2 + (a - c)x + b + d$, where $x_1 < x_2$ are the roots of $P(x)$, $x_3 < x_4$ are the roots of $Q(x)$. Let $M$ be the set of pairwise *friendly* trinomials consisting of at least three trinomials. Prove that $0$ is a root of every trinomial from the set $M$.

Two quadratic trinomials $P(x) = x^2 + a x + b$ and $Q(x) = x^2 + c x + d$ are called *friendly* if each of them has distinct real roots and $x_1 + x_3$, $x_2 + x_4$ are the roots of the quadratic trinomial $x^2 + (a + c)x + b - d$, where $x_1 < x_2$ are the roots of $P(x)$, $x_3 < x_4$ are the roots of $Q(x)$. Let $M$ be the set of pairwise *friendly* trinomials consisting of at least three trinomials. Prove that $0$ is a root of every trinomial from the set $M$.

positive_text: Let $P$ be a point on segment $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ (not coinciding with $B$ or $C$). Let $I_1$ and $I_2$ be the incenters of triangles $ABP$ and $APC$, respectively. If the circumcircle of triangle $I_1PI_2$ intersects $BC$ again at a point $Q$, show that $AB + QC = AC + QB$.

negatives.text: Let $P$ be a point on segment $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ (excluding $B$ and $C$). Let $I_1$ and $I_2$ be the incenters of triangles $ABP$ and $APC$. If the circumcircle of triangle $I_1PI_2$ intersects $BC$ again at $Q$, prove that $AB + QC > AC + QB$.

Let $P$ be a point on segment $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ (excluding $B$ and $C$). Let $I_1$ and $I_2$ be the incenters of triangles $ABP$ and $APC$. If the circumcircle of triangle $I_1PI_2$ intersects $BC$ again at $Q$, prove that $AB + QC = AC + QB$ when $Q = P$.

Let $P$ be a point on segment $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ (excluding $B$ and $C$). Let $I_1$ and $I_2$ be the incenters of triangles $ABP$ and $APC$. If the circumcircle of triangle $I_1PI_2$ intersects $BC$ again at $Q$, prove that $AB + QC = AC + QB$ when $Q$ lies on the extension of $BC$ beyond $C$.

positive_text: Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. Consider a $2n \times 2n$ grid with all cells initially white. In a single move, you can toggle the color of any three adjacent cells along a row or column (from white to black or black to white). Determine all values of $n$ for which it is possible to achieve a standard chessboard coloring (alternating black and white) using such moves.

negatives.text: Given a $2n \times 2n$ table all the cells being white. Per move it is allowed to change the color of any two consecutive cells in any row or in any column (white cell is replaced by black one and vice versa). Find all possible values of $n \ge 2$ for which one can obtain the chess coloring of the given table.

Given a $2n \times 2n$ table all the cells being white. Per move it is allowed to change the color of any three consecutive cells in any row or in any column (white cell is replaced by black one and vice versa). Find all possible values of $n \ge 2$ for which one can obtain the chess coloring of the given table using only row moves.

positive_text:
Consider a $(2n + 1) \times (2n + 1)$ grid, all cells initially white. Each move allows flipping the color (black to white or white to black) of any three adjacent cells aligned either horizontally or vertically.
a) Show that for all positive integers $n$, it is possible to achieve a checkerboard pattern with white cells in the corners.
b) Determine the minimal number of moves required to obtain such a pattern when $n = 3$.

negatives.text:
Given a $(2n + 1) \times (2n + 1)$ table, all its unit cells being white. Per move it is allowed to change the color of any three consecutive cells in any row or in any column (white cell is replaced by black one and vice versa).
a) Prove that for any positive integer $n$ one can obtain the chess coloring of the given table with black corner cells (the example of such coloring is shown in the figure for $n = 3$).
b) Find the minimum number of the moves one needs to obtain the chess coloring of the given table with black corner cells if $n = 3$.

Given a $(2n + 1) \times (2n + 1)$ table, all its unit cells being white. Per move it is allowed to change the color of any four consecutive cells in any row or in any column (white cell is replaced by black one and vice versa).
a) Prove that for any positive integer $n$ one can obtain the chess coloring of the given table with white corner cells (the example of such coloring is shown in the figure for $n = 3$).
b) Find the minimum number of the moves one needs to obtain the chess coloring of the given table with white corner cells if $n = 3$.

Given a $(2n + 1) \times (2n + 1)$ table, all its unit cells being white. Per move it is allowed to change the color of any two consecutive cells in any row or in any column (white cell is replaced by black one and vice versa).
a) Prove that for any positive integer $n$ one can obtain the chess coloring of the given table with white corner cells (the example of such coloring is shown in the figure for $n = 3$).
b) Find the minimum number of the moves one needs to obtain the chess coloring of the given table with white corner cells if $n = 3$.

positive_text: Consider a square grid of size $(2n + 1) \times (2n + 1)$, initially filled with white cells. A move consists of flipping the color (white to black or black to white) of any three adjacent cells in a single row or column. Determine all values of $n$ for which it is possible to achieve a checkerboard pattern with black cells at the four corners, such as the configuration depicted for $n = 2$.

negatives.text: Given a $(2n + 1) \times (2n + 1)$ grid with all white cells, define a move as flipping the color of any three consecutive cells in a row or column. Determine all $n$ for which it is possible to reach a checkerboard pattern with white corner cells.

Given a $(2n + 1) \times (2n + 1)$ grid with all white cells, define a move as flipping the color of any two consecutive cells in a row or column. Determine all $n$ for which it is possible to reach a checkerboard pattern with black corner cells.

Given a $(2n + 1) \times (2n + 1)$ grid with all white cells, define a move as flipping the color of any three consecutive cells in a row, but not in a column. Determine all $n$ for which it is possible to reach a checkerboard pattern with black corner cells.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = BC$. Let $K$ and $M$ be the midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. If the circumcircle of triangle $CKB$ intersects line $BM$ again at $N$, and a line through $N$ parallel to $AC$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at $A_1$ and $C_1$, show that triangle $A_1BC_1$ is equilateral.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = BC$. Let $K$ be the midpoint of $AB$ and $M$ the midpoint of $AC$. The circumcircle of triangle $CKB$ intersects the line $BM$ at a point $N$ different from $M$. A line through $N$ perpendicular to $AC$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at points $A_1$ and $C_1$. Prove that triangle $A_1BC_1$ is equilateral.

Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = BC$. Let $K$ be the midpoint of $AB$ and $M$ the midpoint of $AC$. The circumcircle of triangle $CKB$ intersects the line $BM$ at a point $N$ different from $M$. A line through $N$ parallel to $AB$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at points $A_1$ and $C_1$. Prove that triangle $A_1BC_1$ is equilateral.

Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = BC$. Let $K$ be the midpoint of $AB$ and $M$ the midpoint of $AC$. The circumcircle of triangle $CKB$ intersects the line $BM$ at a point $N$ different from $M$. A line through $N$ parallel to $AC$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at points $A_1$ and $C_1$. Prove that triangle $A_1BC_1$ is isosceles.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an isosceles right triangle with $\angle ABC = 90^\circ$, and let $X$ be any interior point. Show that $AX + BX + \sqrt{2}CX \ge \sqrt{5}AB$, and determine the configuration of $X$ when equality is achieved.

negatives.text: Let $X$ lie inside an isosceles right triangle $ABC$ with $\angle B = 90^\circ$. Prove that $AX + BX + CX \ge \sqrt{5}AB$ and determine when equality holds.
Let $X$ be a point in the interior of triangle $ABC$, where $\angle B = 90^\circ$ and $AB = BC$. Prove that $AX + BX + \sqrt{2}CX \le \sqrt{5}AB$ and determine when equality is achieved.

positive_text: Determine the smallest prime $q$ for which the inequality $\{\sqrt{q}\} < \frac{1}{501}$ holds true.

negatives.text: Find the minimum prime number $p$ such that $\{\sqrt{p}\} > \frac{1}{501}$.
Find the minimum prime number $p$ such that $\{\sqrt{p}\} < \frac{1}{501}$ and $p > 1000$.
Find the minimum prime number $p$ such that $\{\sqrt{p}\} < \frac{1}{500}$.

positive_text: \text{Show that for all integers } n \ge 2, \quad \sum_{k=2}^{n} \frac{2^{k-2}}{k!} \le \frac{3}{2}.

negatives.text: \text{For every integer } n \ge 2, \text{ prove the inequality} \quad \frac{1}{2!} + \frac{2}{3!} + \dots + \frac{2^{n-2}}{n!} \le \frac{1}{2}.
\text{For every integer } n \ge 2, \text{ prove the inequality} \quad \frac{1}{2!} + \frac{2}{3!} + \dots + \frac{2^{n-2}}{n!} \ge \frac{3}{2}.
\text{For every integer } n \ge 2, \text{ prove the inequality} \quad \frac{1}{2!} + \frac{2}{3!} + \dots + \frac{2^{n-2}}{n!} \le \frac{3}{2} + \frac{1}{n!}.

positive_text: Let $T_1T_2T_3$ be an acute triangle with altitudes $T_1H_1$, $T_2H_2$, $T_3H_3$ and internal angle bisectors $T_1L_1$, $T_2L_2$, $T_3L_3$. Prove that the area of triangle $L_1L_2L_3$ is at least as large as the area of triangle $H_1H_2H_3$.

negatives.text: Let $A_1H_1$, $A_2H_2$, $A_3H_3$ be altitudes and $A_1L_1$, $A_2L_2$, $A_3L_3$ be bisectors of an acute angled triangle $A_1A_2A_3$. Prove the inequality $S(L_1L_2L_3) < S(H_1H_2H_3)$ where $S$ stands for the area of a triangle.

Let $A_1H_1$, $A_2H_2$, $A_3H_3$ be altitudes and $A_1L_1$, $A_2L_2$, $A_3L_3$ be medians of an acute angled triangle $A_1A_2A_3$. Prove the inequality $S(L_1L_2L_3) \ge S(H_1H_2H_3)$ where $S$ stands for the area of a triangle.

positive_text: A figure $\Phi$ consists of three adjacent $n \times n$ squares arranged as shown in the figure, where adjacent squares share a full side of length $1$. Determine all values of $n > 1$ for which $\Phi$ can be tiled using only $1 \times 3$ and $3 \times 1$ tiles without overlaps.

negatives.text: Three $n \times n$ squares form the figure $\Phi$ on the checkered plane as shown in the figure. (Neighboring squares are touching along the segment of length $1$). Find all $n > 1$ for which the figure $\Phi$ can be covered with tiles $2 \times 3$ and $3 \times 2$ without overlapping.

Three $n \times n$ squares form the figure $\Phi$ on the checkered plane as shown in the figure. (Neighboring squares are touching along the segment of length $1$). Find all $n > 1$ for which the figure $\Phi$ can be covered with tiles $1 \times 2$ and $2 \times 1$ without overlapping.

Three $n \times n$ squares form the figure $\Phi$ on the checkered plane as shown in the figure. (Neighboring squares are touching along the segment of length $1$). Find all $n > 1$ for which the figure $\Phi$ can be covered with tiles $1 \times 3$ and $3 \times 1$ with overlapping allowed.

positive_text: Let $A, B, C, D$ be points on the curve $y = x^2$, forming a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$. Given that $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle with $AC$ as a diameter, and $M$, $N$ are the midpoints of $AC$ and $BD$, determine the magnitude of the vertical component of the vector $\vec{MN}$.

negatives.text: The vertices of the convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ lie on the parabola $y = x^2$. It is known that $ABCD$ is cyclic and $AC$ is a diameter of its circumcircle. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ respectively. Find the length of the projection of the segment $MN$ on the axis $Ox$.

The vertices of the convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ lie on the parabola $y = x^2$. It is known that $ABCD$ is cyclic and $AC$ is a radius of its circumcircle. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ respectively. Find the length of the projection of the segment $MN$ on the axis $Oy$.

The vertices of the convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ lie on the parabola $y = -x^2$. It is known that $ABCD$ is cyclic and $AC$ is a diameter of its circumcircle. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ respectively. Find the length of the projection of the segment $MN$ on the axis $Oy$.

positive_text:
Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be positive integers such that
$$
(a b)^3 + (b c)^3 + (c a)^3 = abc(a^3 + b^3 + c^3).
$$
Show that the product of two of these numbers is a perfect square.

negatives.text:
Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be positive integers such that
$$
a^3 b^3 + b^3 c^3 + c^3 a^3 = abc(a^3 + b^3 + c^3 + 1).
$$
Prove that the product of two of these numbers is the square of a positive integer.

Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be positive integers such that
$$
-a^3 b^3 + b^3 c^3 + c^3 a^3 = abc(a^3 + b^3 + c^3).
$$
Prove that the product of two of these numbers is the square of a positive integer.

Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be positive integers such that
$$
a^2 b^3 + b^2 c^3 + c^2 a^3 = abc(a^3 + b^3 + c^3).
$$
Prove that the product of two of these numbers is the square of a positive integer.

positive_text:
a) Determine all real values of $a$ for which the graph of $y = x^2 - a$ intersects the graph of $y = \frac{1}{x}$ at exactly three distinct points.

b) Characterize the set of all centers of the circumcircles formed by these intersection points as $a$ varies over all real values.

negatives.text:
a) Find all real numbers $a$ such that the parabola $y = x^2 - a$ and the hyperbola $y = -\frac{1}{x}$ intersect each other in three different points.

b) Find the locus of the centers of circumcircles of such triples of intersection points when $a$ takes all possible values.

a) Find all real numbers $a$ such that the parabola $y = x^2 - a$ and the hyperbola $y = \frac{1}{x}$ intersect each other in three different points.

b) Find the locus of the centers of incircles of such triples of intersection points when $a$ takes all possible values.

a) Find all real numbers $a$ such that the parabola $y = x^2 - a$ and the hyperbola $y = \frac{1}{x^2}$ intersect each other in three different points.

b) Find the locus of the centers of circumcircles of such triples of intersection points when $a$ takes all possible values.

positive_text: Given the quadratic $f(x) = x^2 + bx + 8$ with $b \neq 0$ and distinct real roots $x_1$ and $x_2$, let $g(x)$ be the monic quadratic with roots $x_1 + \frac{1}{x_2}$ and $x_2 + \frac{1}{x_1}$. Determine all values of $g(1)$ such that $g(1) = f(1)$.

negatives.text: Let $f(x) = x^2 + bx + 8$ with $b \neq 0$ and distinct real roots $x_1$ and $x_2$. Define $g(x)$ as the monic quadratic with roots $x_1 - \frac{1}{x_2}$ and $x_2 - \frac{1}{x_1}$. Find all values of $g(1)$ such that $g(1) = f(1)$.

Let $f(x) = x^2 + bx + 8$ with $b \neq 0$ and distinct real roots $x_1$ and $x_2$. Define $g(x)$ as the monic quadratic with roots $x_1 + \frac{1}{x_1}$ and $x_2 + \frac{1}{x_2}$. Find all values of $g(1)$ such that $g(1) = f(1)$.

Let $f(x) = x^2 + bx + 8$ with $b \neq 0$ and distinct real roots $x_1$ and $x_2$. Define $g(x)$ as the monic quadratic with roots $x_1 + 1$ and $x_2 + 1$. Find all values of $g(1)$ such that $g(1) = f(1)$.

positive_text:
a) Determine a positive integer $n$ such that $n = a^2 - b = c^2 - d$ for distinct divisors $a, c$ of $n$, and $b, d$ also divisors of $n$.

b) Show that there are infinitely many such $n$.

negatives.text:
a) Find a positive integer $n$ such that $n = a^2 + b = c^2 + d$ for distinct divisors $a, c$ of $n$, and $b, d$ also divisors of $n$.

b) Show that there are infinitely many such $n$.

a) Find a positive integer $n$ such that $n = a^2 - b = c^2 - d$ for distinct divisors $a, c$ of $n$, and $b, d$ also divisors of $n$ with $b = d$.

b) Show that there are infinitely many such $n$.

positive_text: Define a sequence $b_1, b_2, b_3, \dots$ of positive integers with $b_1 = 63$ and for all $n \ge 2$, $b_n$ is the smallest integer divisible by $n$ and greater than or equal to $b_{n-1}$. Show that no positive integer appears more than once in this sequence.

negatives.text: Define a sequence $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ of positive integers with $a_1 = 63$ and for each $n \ge 2$, $a_n$ is the smallest positive integer divisible by $n^2$, which is not less than $a_{n-1}$. Prove that each positive integer can occur in this sequence at most once.

Let $a_1 = 63$ and for each $n \ge 2$, define $a_n$ as the smallest positive integer divisible by $n$, which is not greater than $a_{n-1}$. Prove that each positive integer can occur in this sequence at most once.

positive_text:
Determine all functions $f(x): \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for every real number $x$, the following holds:
$$
\frac{3}{4}f(|x|) + |f(x)| = x.
$$

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f(x): \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$, the following holds:
$$
\frac{3}{4}f(|x|) + f(x) = x.
$$

Find all functions $f(x): \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$, the following holds:
$$
\frac{3}{4}f(|x|) + |f(x)| = -x.
$$

Find all functions $f(x): \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$, the following holds:
$$
\frac{1}{2}f(|x|) + |f(x)| = x.
$$

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with diagonals intersecting at $O$. If $P$, $Q$, $R$, and $S$ are the projections of $O$ onto the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively, show that $BD \ge SP + QR$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with diagonals intersecting at $O$. Let $P$, $Q$, $R$, and $S$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $O$ to the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively. Prove the inequality $BD \le SP + QR$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with diagonals intersecting at $O$. Let $P$, $Q$, $R$, and $S$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $O$ to the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively. Prove the inequality $BD^2 \ge SP^2 + QR^2$.

positive_text: Let $A = \{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\}$ be a set of positive integers such that $\gcd(a_k, \sum_{i \neq k} a_i) > 1$ for every $k = 1, 2, \dots, n$. Show that for any $c \in (0, 1)$, there exists a constant $M$ such that for all $K \ge M$, there exists a set $A$ with at least $cK$ elements, each at most $K$, satisfying the above condition.

negatives.text:
Call the set $\{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\}$ of positive integers good if
$$
\gcd(a_k, \sum_{i \neq k} a_i) = 1
$$
for each $k = \overline{1, n}$. Prove that for each $c \in (0, 1)$ there exists a positive integer $M$ such that for any positive integer $K \ge M$ one can find a good set with at least $cK$ elements all elements of which do not exceed $K$.

Call the set $\{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\}$ of positive integers good if
$$
\gcd(a_k^2, \sum_{i \neq k} a_i) > 1
$$
for each $k = \overline{1, n}$. Prove that for each $c \in (0, 1)$ there exists a positive integer $M$ such that for any positive integer $K \ge M$ one can find a good set with at least $cK$ elements all elements of which do not exceed $K$.

Call the set $\{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\}$ of positive integers good if
$$
\gcd(a_k, \sum_{i \neq k} a_i) > 1
$$
for each $k = \overline{1, n}$ and $\sum_{i = 1}^{n} a_i$ is even. Prove that for each $c \in (0, 1)$ there exists a positive integer $M$ such that for any positive integer $K \ge M$ one can find a good set with at least $cK$ elements all elements of which do not exceed $K$.

positive_text: Let $A_1, \dots, A_n$ be points with rational coordinates such that the distance between any two is an integer. Show that there exist points $B_1, \dots, B_n$ with integer coordinates satisfying $|B_iB_j| = |A_iA_j|$ for all $i \ne j$.

negatives.text: Suppose $A_1, \dots, A_n$ are points on the plane with rational coordinates and integer pairwise distances. Prove that there exist points $B_1, \dots, B_n$ with rational coordinates such that $|B_iB_j| = |A_iA_j|$ for all $1 \le i < j \le n$.

Given $n$ points $A_1, \dots, A_n$ with rational coordinates and all pairwise distances being integer, prove that there exist points $B_1, \dots, B_n$ with integer coordinates such that $|B_iB_j| < |A_iA_j|$ for all $1 \le i < j \le n$.

positive_text:
Let $n$ and $k$ be positive integers with $k \le n$. An equilateral triangular grid has side length $n$, with the $i$-th row containing $i$ circles for $1 \le i \le n$. Place checkers on the grid such that any line parallel to a side of the triangle (there are $3n$ such lines) contains at most $k$ checkers. Let $T(k, n)$ denote the maximum number of checkers that can be placed under these constraints.

a) Prove that:
$$
T(k, n) \le \left\lfloor \frac{k(2n + 1)}{3} \right\rfloor .
$$

b) Determine $T(1, n)$ and $T(2, n)$.

negatives.text:
Given positive integers $n$ and $k$ with $k \le n$, consider a triangular grid of circles with the $i$-th row containing $i$ circles. Place checkers such that any line parallel to a side of the triangle contains at least $k$ checkers. Let $T(k, n)$ be the minimum number of checkers required.

a) Prove that:
$$
T(k, n) \ge \left\lceil \frac{k(2n + 1)}{3} \right\rceil .
$$

b) Find $T(1, n)$ and $T(2, n)$.

Given positive integers $n$ and $k$ with $k \le n$, consider a triangular board with $n$ rows of circles, with the $i$-th row containing $i$ circles. Place checkers such that any line parallel to a side of the triangle contains at most $k^2$ checkers. Let $T(k, n)$ be the maximum number of checkers that can be placed.

a) Prove that:
$$
T(k, n) \le \left\lfloor \frac{k^2(2n + 1)}{3} \right\rfloor .
$$

b) Determine $T(1, n)$ and $T(2, n)$.

positive_text:
Determine all real-coefficient polynomials $p(x)$ satisfying
$$
 p(a+b-2 c)+p(b+c-2 a)+p(c+a-2 b)=3 p(a-b)+3 p(b-c)+3 p(c-a)
$$
for every real number $a, b, c$.

negatives.text:
Find all polynomials $p(x)$ with real coefficients such that
$$
 p(a+b-2 c)+p(b+c-2 a)+p(c+a-2 b)=3 p(a-b)+3 p(b-c)+3 p(a-c)
$$
for all $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$.

Find all polynomials $p(x)$ with real coefficients such that
$$
 p(a+b-2 c)+p(b+c-2 a)+p(c+a-2 b)=3 p(a-b)+3 p(b-c)+3 p(c-a)^2
$$
for all $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$.

Find all polynomials $p(x)$ with real coefficients such that
$$
 p(a+b-2 c)+p(b+c-2 a)+p(c+a-2 b)=3 p(a-b)+3 p(b-c)+3 p(c-a)+1
$$
for all $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$.

positive_text:
Two players, Alice and Bob, play a game on a number line from $ 1 $ to $ N $. Alice begins by placing a marker at $ 1 $. On each turn, a player moves the marker to either $ n+1 $ or $ 2n $, as long as the result does not exceed $ N $. The player who places the marker at $ N $ wins.
a. Which player has a winning strategy if $ N=2011 $?
b. How many integers $ N \leqslant 2011 $ result in Bob having a winning strategy?

negatives.text:
Two players take turns writing numbers on a board starting with $ 1 $. On each turn, a player writes $ n-1 $ or $ 2n $, but the number must not exceed $ N $. The player who writes $ N $ first wins.
a. Which player has a winning strategy when $ N=2011 $?
b. How many values of $ N \leqslant 2011 $ allow the second player to force a win?

Players take turns writing numbers starting with $ 1 $. On each turn, a player writes $ n+1 $ or $ 2n $, but the result must not exceed $ N $. The player who writes $ N-1 $ first wins.
a. Which player has a winning strategy when $ N=2011 $?
b. How many values of $ N \leqslant 2011 $ allow the second player to force a win?

Players take turns writing numbers starting with $ 1 $. On each turn, a player writes $ n+1 $ or $ 2n $, but the result must not exceed $ N $. The player who writes $ N $ first wins, but only if the number is odd.
a. Which player has a winning strategy when $ N=2011 $?
b. How many values of $ N \leqslant 2011 $ allow the second player to force a win?

positive_text: Find all quadruples $(x, y, z, w)$ of positive real numbers such that $xyzw = 1$, $x^{2012} + 2012y = 2012z + w^{2012}$, and $2012x + y^{2012} = z^{2012} + 2012w$.

negatives.text: Find all quadruples $(a, b, c, d)$ of positive real numbers such that $abcd = 1$, $a^{2012} - 2012b = 2012c + d^{2012}$, and $2012a + b^{2012} = c^{2012} + 2012d$.
Find all quadruples $(a, b, c, d)$ of positive real numbers such that $abcd = 1$, $a^{2012} + 2012b = 2012c + d^{2013}$, and $2012a + b^{2012} = c^{2012} + 2012d$.
Find all quadruples $(a, b, c, d)$ of positive real numbers such that $abcd = 1$, $a^{2012} + 2012b = 2012c + d^{2012}$, and $2012a + b^{2012} = 2012c^{2012} + d$.

positive_text:
Let $A, B, C, D$ be the vertices of a square. A point $P$ lies in the interior of the square such that $\angle PAB \geq 60^\circ$. Define $Q$ as the intersection of $AD$ with the line through $P$ perpendicular to $BP$. Define $R$ as the intersection of $BQ$ with the line through $C$ perpendicular to $BP$.

a. Prove that $|BP| \geq |BR|$.

b. For which point(s) $P$ does the inequality in (a) become an equality?

negatives.text:
Let $ABCD$ be a square. Let $P$ be a point inside the square such that $\angle PAB \geq 60^\circ$. Let $Q$ be the intersection of $AD$ with the line through $P$ parallel to $BP$. Let $R$ be the intersection of $BQ$ with the line through $C$ parallel to $BP$.

a. Prove that $|BP| \geq |BR|$.

b. For which point(s) $P$ does the inequality in (a) become an equality?

Let $ABCD$ be a square. Let $P$ be a point inside the square such that $\angle PAB \geq 60^\circ$. Let $Q$ be the intersection of $AD$ with the line through $P$ perpendicular to $AP$. Let $R$ be the intersection of $BQ$ with the line through $C$ perpendicular to $AP$.

a. Prove that $|BP| \geq |BR|$.

b. For which point(s) $P$ does the inequality in (a) become an equality?

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with circumcenter $O$. Consider a circle $\Gamma_{B}$ passing through $A$ and $B$ and tangent to $AC$, and a circle $\Gamma_{C}$ passing through $A$ and $C$ and tangent to $AB$. For any line $\ell$ through $A$, denote its second intersections with $\Gamma_{B}$ and $\Gamma_{C}$ as $X$ and $Y$, respectively. Prove that $OX = OY$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with circumcenter $O$. Let $\Gamma_{B}$ be the circle through $A$ and $B$ tangent to $AC$, and let $\Gamma_{C}$ be the circle through $A$ and $C$ tangent to $AB$. For any line through $A$, let $X$ and $Y$ be the second points of intersection with $\Gamma_{B}$ and $\Gamma_{C}$, respectively. Prove that $|OX| + |OY| = 2R$, where $R$ is the circumradius of triangle $ABC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with circumcenter $O$. Let $\Gamma_{B}$ be the circle through $A$ and $B$ tangent to $AC$, and let $\Gamma_{C}$ be the circle through $A$ and $C$ tangent to $AB$. For any line through $A$, let $X$ and $Y$ be the second points of intersection with $\Gamma_{B}$ and $\Gamma_{C}$, respectively. Prove that $\angle OX Y = \angle OY X$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with circumcenter $O$. Let $\Gamma_{B}$ be the circle through $A$ and $B$ tangent to $AC$, and let $\Gamma_{C}$ be the circle through $A$ and $C$ tangent to $AB$. For any line through $A$, let $X$ and $Y$ be the second points of intersection with $\Gamma_{B}$ and $\Gamma_{C}$, respectively. Prove that $|OX| = |OY|$ when the triangle $ABC$ is equilateral.

positive_text:
An integer $ m > 1 $ is rich if for every positive integer $ n $, there are positive integers $ x, y, z $ satisfying $ m x^{2} = n + y^{2} + z^{2} $. An integer $ m > 1 $ is poor if it is not rich.

a) Find a poor integer.

positive_text: Considere o triângulo $ABC$ com lados $AB = 13$, $BC = 15$ e $AC = 9$. Seja $r$ uma reta paralela ao lado $BC$ que passa pelo vértice $A$. A bissetriz do ângulo $\angle ACB$ intercepta $r$ no ponto $E$ e a bissetriz do ângulo $\angle ABC$ intercepta $r$ no ponto $F$. Determine o comprimento de $EF$.

negatives.text: Seja $ABC$ um triângulo com $AB = 13$, $BC = 15$ e $AC = 9$. Seja $r$ a reta perpendicular a $BC$ traçada por $A$. A bissetriz do ângulo $\angle BCA$ corta a reta $r$ em $E$ e a bissetriz do ângulo $\angle CBA$ corta $r$ em $F$. Calcular a medida do segmento $EF$.

Seja $ABC$ um triângulo com $AB = 13$, $BC = 15$ e $AC = 9$. Seja $r$ a reta paralela a $BC$ traçada por $A$. A bissetriz do ângulo $\angle BAC$ corta a reta $r$ em $E$ e a bissetriz do ângulo $\angle ABC$ corta $r$ em $F$. Calcular a medida do segmento $EF$.

positive_text:
Considere um eneágono regular com lado de comprimento $a$, menor diagonal $b$ e maior diagonal $d$.

a) Calcule a medida do ângulo $B\hat{A}E$.

b) Demonstre que $d = a + b$.

negatives.text:
Dado um polígono regular de 9 lados, com lado $a$, menor diagonal $b$ e maior diagonal $d$:

a) Determine a medida do ângulo $B\hat{A}E$.

b) Mostre que $d = a - b$.

Considere um polígono regular de 9 lados, com lado $a$, menor diagonal $b$ e maior diagonal $d$:

a) Determine a medida do ângulo $B\hat{A}E$.

b) Mostre que $d = a + b^2$.

Dado um polígono regular de 9 lados, com lado $a$, menor diagonal $b$ e maior diagonal $d$:

a) Determine a medida do ângulo $B\hat{A}C$.

b) Mostre que $d = a + b$.

positive_text: Dado que os círculos com centro em $B$ e $A$ são tangentes em $X$, e os círculos com centro em $C$ e $A$ são tangentes em $Y$, além disso, os círculos de centros $B$ e $C$ são também tangentes entre si. Se $AB = 6$, $AC = 5$ e $BC = 9$, determine o comprimento de $AX$.

negatives.text: Na figura a seguir, o círculo de centro $B$ é tangente ao círculo de centro $A$ em $X$. O círculo de centro $C$ é tangente ao círculo de centro $A$ em $Y$. Além disso, os círculos de centros $B$ e $C$ são tangentes internamente. Se $AB=6$, $AC=5$ e $BC=9$, quanto mede $AX$?

Na figura a seguir, o círculo de centro $B$ é tangente ao círculo de centro $A$ em $X$. O círculo de centro $C$ é tangente ao círculo de centro $A$ em $Y$. Além disso, os círculos de centros $B$ e $C$ são secantes. Se $AB=6$, $AC=5$ e $BC=9$, quanto mede $AX$?

positive_text: Considere um anel composto por $m$ polígonos regulares com $n$ lados cada, formado de acordo com as seguintes regras: cada polígono compartilha um lado com dois outros, adjacentes; o perímetro interno é formado por exatamente dois lados de cada polígono. Um exemplo é dado com $m=6$ e $n=9$. Quantos valores distintos de $n$ permitem a construção de tal anel?

negatives.text: Um anel simétrico com $m$ polígonos regulares de $n$ lados cada é formado de acordo com as regras: i) cada polígono no anel encontra dois outros; ii) dois polígonos adjacentes têm apenas um vértice em comum; iii) o perímetro da região interna delimitada pelos polígonos consiste em exatamente dois lados de cada polígono. O exemplo na figura a seguir mostra um anel com $m=6$ e $n=9$. Para quantos valores diferentes de $n$ é possível construir esse anel?

Um anel simétrico com $m$ polígonos regulares de $n$ lados cada é formado de acordo com as regras: i) cada polígono no anel encontra dois outros; ii) dois polígonos adjacentes têm apenas um lado em comum; iii) o perímetro da região interna delimitada pelos polígonos consiste em exatamente três lados de cada polígono. O exemplo na figura a seguir mostra um anel com $m=6$ e $n=9$. Para quantos valores diferentes de $n$ é possível construir esse anel?

Um anel simétrico com $m$ polígonos regulares de $n$ lados cada é formado de acordo com as regras: i) cada polígono no anel encontra dois outros; ii) dois polígonos adjacentes têm apenas um lado em comum; iii) o perímetro da região interna delimitada pelos polígonos consiste em exatamente dois lados de cada polígono, mas não mais que um por vértice. O exemplo na figura a seguir mostra um anel com $m=6$ e $n=9$. Para quantos valores diferentes de $n$ é possível construir esse anel?

positive_text: No triângulo $ABC$, sejam $M$, $N$ e $P$ pontos sobre $BC$, $CA$ e $AB$, respectivamente, tais que $BM = BP$ e $CM = CN$. Sejam $l_1$ a perpendicular de $B$ a $MP$ e $l_2$ a perpendicular de $C$ a $MN$. Se $I$ é o ponto de interseção de $l_1$ e $l_2$, mostre que $\angle IPA = \angle INC$.

negatives.text: No triângulo $ABC$, sejam $M$, $N$ e $P$ pontos sobre $BC$, $CA$ e $AB$, respectivamente, tais que $BM = CP$ e $CM = BN$. As perpendiculares de $B$ a $MP$ e de $C$ a $MN$ intersectam-se em $I$. Prove que $\angle IPA = \angle INC$.

No triângulo $ABC$, sejam $M$, $N$ e $P$ pontos sobre $BC$, $CA$ e $AB$, respectivamente, tais que $BM = BP$ e $CM = CN$. As perpendiculares de $B$ a $MP$ e de $C$ a $MN$ intersectam-se em $I$. Prove que $\angle IPB = \angle INC$.

No triângulo $ABC$, sejam $M$, $N$ e $P$ pontos sobre $BC$, $CA$ e $AB$, respectivamente, tais que $BM = BP$ e $CM = CN$. A perpendicular de $A$ a $MP$ e a perpendicular de $C$ a $MN$ intersectam-se em $I$. Prove que $\angle IPA = \angle INC$.

positive_text: Seja $ABCD$ um quadrilátero inscrito em um círculo, cuja diagonal $AC$ é um diâmetro. Considere as retas perpendiculares traçadas por $A$ e $C$ à diagonal $BD$, que intersectam $BD$ nos pontos $E$ e $F$, respectivamente. Prove que $$ DE = BF. $$

negatives.text: Seja $ABCD$ um quadrilátero inscritível no círculo, com $BD$ sendo um diâmetro. Se $E$ e $F$ são os pontos de interseção das perpendiculares a $AC$ passando por $A$ e $C$, respectivamente, demonstre que $$ DE = BF. $$

Seja $ABCD$ um quadrilátero inscritível no círculo, com $BD$ sendo um diâmetro. Se $E$ e $F$ são os pontos de interseção das perpendiculares a $BD$ passando por $A$ e $C$, respectivamente, demonstre que $$ DE > BF. $$

positive_text: Dado um retângulo $ABCD$ com $AB = \sqrt{3}$, e sabendo que o ângulo entre $AC$ e $CD$ é $75^{\circ}$, determine a medida da diagonal $AC$ e calcule $\cos 75^{\circ}$.

negatives.text: Seja $ABCD$ um retângulo com $AB = \sqrt{3}$, e $\angle ACD = 105^{\circ}$. Determine o comprimento de $AC$ e o valor de $\cos 105^{\circ}$.
Seja $ABCD$ um retângulo com $AB = \sqrt{3}$, e $\angle ACD = 75^{\circ}$. Determine o comprimento de $AC$ e o valor de $\sin 75^{\circ}$.
Seja $ABCD$ um quadrilátero convexo com $AB = \sqrt{3}$, e $\angle ACD = 75^{\circ}$. Determine o comprimento de $AC$ e o valor de $\cos 75^{\circ}$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a unit square. If $M$ and $N$ are midpoints of $AB$ and $BC$ respectively, and lines $CM$ and $DN$ intersect at $I$, compute the area of triangle $CIN$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a square of side length $1$. $M$ and $N$ are midpoints of $AB$ and $BC$, respectively. If lines $CM$ and $DN$ intersect at $I$, compute the area of triangle $CIN$ and the area of triangle $AIM$.
Let $ABCD$ be a square of side length $1$. $M$ and $N$ are midpoints of $AB$ and $CD$, respectively. If lines $CM$ and $DN$ intersect at $I$, compute the area of triangle $CIN$.
Let $ABCD$ be a rectangle of side lengths $1$ and $2$. $M$ and $N$ are midpoints of $AB$ and $BC$, respectively. If lines $CM$ and $DN$ intersect at $I$, compute the area of triangle $CIN$.

positive_text:
Prove that there are finitely many positive integer triples $(x, y, z)$ such that
$$
\frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{z} = \frac{1}{k},
$$
where $k = 1983$.

negatives.text:
Show that there are only finitely many solutions to
$$
\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c} = -\frac{1}{1983}
$$
in positive integers.

Show that there are only finitely many solutions to
$$
\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c} = \frac{1}{1983^2}
$$
in positive integers.

positive_text: \text{Let } k, m, n, p \text{ be integers. Prove that the equation } x^2 + k x + m = y^2 + n y + p \text{ admits infinitely many integer solutions if and only if } k^2 - 4m = n^2 - 4p.

negatives.text: \text{Let } a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{Z}. Show that } x^2 + a x + b = y^2 + c y + d \text{ has infinitely many integer solutions if and only if } a^2 + 4b = c^2 + 4d.
\text{Let } a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{Z}. Prove that } x^2 + a x + b = y^2 + c y + d \text{ has infinitely many integer solutions if and only if } a^2 - 4b = c^2 - 4d + 1.
\text{Let } a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{Z}. Show that } x^2 + a x + b = y^2 + c y + d \text{ has infinitely many integer solutions if and only if } a^2 - 4b > c^2 - 4d.

positive_text: Let $ f(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n) $ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. For each positive integer $ m $, define $ k(m) $ as the number of $ n $-tuples $ (b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n) $ such that $ 0 \le b_i < m $ and $ f(b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n) $ is relatively prime to $ m $. Prove that if $ m $ and $ n $ are coprime, then $ k(mn) = k(m)k(n) $, and if $ q $ is a prime number, then $ k(q^t) = q^{n(t-1)}k(q) $.

negatives.text: Let $ f(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n) $ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. For each positive integer $ r $, define $ k(r) $ as the number of $ n $-tuples $ (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) $ such that $ 0 \le a_i < r $ and $ f(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) $ is divisible by $ r $. Prove that if $ u $ and $ v $ are coprime, then $ k(uv) = k(u)k(v) $, and if $ p $ is prime, then $ k(p^s) = p^{n(s-1)}k(p) $.

Let $ f(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n) $ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. For each positive integer $ r $, define $ k(r) $ as the number of $ n $-tuples $ (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) $ such that $ 0 \le a_i < r $ and $ f(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) $ is congruent to 1 modulo $ r $. Prove that if $ u $ and $ v $ are coprime, then $ k(uv) = k(u)k(v) $, and if $ p $ is prime, then $ k(p^s) = p^{n(s-1)}k(p) $.

Let $ f(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n) $ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. For each positive integer $ r $, define $ k(r) $ as the number of $ n $-tuples $ (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) $ such that $ 0 \le a_i < r $ and $ f(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) $ is a perfect square modulo $ r $. Prove that if $ u $ and $ v $ are coprime, then $ k(uv) = k(u)k(v) $, and if $ p $ is prime, then $ k(p^s) = p^{n(s-1)}k(p) $.

positive_text: For $n > 4$, construct an example of a set of points $\{A_i\}_{i=1}^n$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ such that the point $P = (x, y, z)$ minimizing $\sum_{i=1}^n (|x - x_i| + |y - y_i| + |z - z_i|)$ is not contained in the convex hull of the $A_i$.

negatives.text: Let $P = (x, y, z)$ be the point minimizing $\sum_{i=1}^n (|x - x_i|^2 + |y - y_i|^2 + |z - z_i|^2)$ for a set of points $\{A_i\}_{i=1}^n$ in three dimensions. Construct, for each $n > 4$, a configuration of the $A_i$ such that $P$ is not in the convex hull of the $A_i$.

Let $P = (x, y, z)$ be the point minimizing $\sum_{i=1}^n (|x - x_i| + |y - y_i| + |z - z_i|)$ for a set of points $\{A_i\}_{i=1}^n$ in three dimensions. Construct, for each $n > 4$, a configuration of the $A_i$ such that $P$ is in the convex hull of the $A_i$.

Let $P = (x, y, z)$ be the point minimizing $\sum_{i=1}^n (|x - x_i| + |y - y_i| + |z - z_i|)$ for a set of points $\{A_i\}_{i=1}^n$ in three dimensions. Construct, for each $n > 4$, a configuration of the $A_i$ such that $P$ lies on the boundary of the convex hull of the $A_i$.

positive_text: Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. A function $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ satisfies $f(n) = n - 10$ for all $n > 100$, and $f(100) = f(f(111))$. Determine the image of $f$.

negatives.text: Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Define $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that $f(n) = n + 10$ for $n > 100$ and $f(100) = f(f(111))$. Determine the set of possible values of $f$.
Let $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ be defined as $f(n) = n - 10$ for $n > 100$ and $f(n) = f(f(n+11))$ for $n < 100$. Find the set of possible values of $f$.

positive_text: Prove that there exist infinitely many positive integers $a$, $b$, and $c$ such that $a^3 + 1990b^3 = c^4$.

negatives.text: Show that there are infinitely many positive integer solutions to $a^3 + 1990b^3 = c^3$.
Show that there are infinitely many positive integer solutions to $a^3 - 1990b^3 = c^4$.
Show that there are infinitely many positive integer solutions to $a^3 + 1990b^3 = c^4 + 1$.

positive_text: Let $k > 0$ and define the sequence $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ with initial values and recurrence $a_{n+2} = a_{n+1} + \frac{k}{n} a_n$. Determine for which values of $k$ the general term $a_n$ can be expressed as a polynomial in $n$. Also, find for which values of $k$ the ratio $\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}$ is a rational function in $n$.

negatives.text: Let $k > 0$ and define the sequence $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ with initial values and recurrence $a_{n+2} = a_{n+1} - \frac{k}{n} a_n$. For which $k$ can we write an $a_n$ as a polynomial in $n$? For which $k$ can we write $\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \frac{p(n)}{q(n)}$, where $p$ and $q$ are polynomials?

Let $k > 0$ and define the sequence $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ with initial values and recurrence $a_{n+2} = a_{n+1} + \frac{k}{n^2} a_n$. For which $k$ can we write an $a_n$ as a polynomial in $n$? For which $k$ can we write $\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \frac{p(n)}{q(n)}$, where $p$ and $q$ are polynomials?

Let $k > 0$ and define the sequence $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ with initial values and recurrence $a_{n+2} = a_{n+1} + \frac{k}{\sqrt{n}} a_n$. For which $k$ can we write an $a_n$ as a polynomial in $n$? For which $k$ can we write $\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \frac{p(n)}{q(n)}$, where $p$ and $q$ are polynomials?

positive_text: Prove that for some $n > 2$, the number $199\underbrace{9\dots 9}_{n \text{ times}}1$ is divisible by $1991$.

negatives.text: Show that there is a number of the form $199\dots 91$ (with $n$ 9s) with $n > 2$ which is divisible by $1993$.
Show that there is a number of the form $199\dots 91$ (with $n$ 9s) with $n > 2$ which is divisible by $1991^2$.
Show that there is a number of the form $199\dots 91$ (with $n$ 9s) with $n > 2$ which is divisible by $1991$ and $1993$.

positive_text: Suppose the cubic polynomial $x^3 + ax + b$ has three real roots that are all distinct. Prove that $a < 0$.

negatives.text: The polynomial $x^3 + px + q$ has three distinct real roots. Show that $p > 0$.
The polynomial $x^3 + px + q$ has three real roots (not necessarily distinct). Show that $p < 0$.
The polynomial $x^3 + px + q$ has three distinct complex roots. Show that $p < 0$.

positive_text: Given fixed lengths $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$, construct a polygon with sides of those lengths in order, such that the area is maximized.

negatives.text: Given positive real numbers $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$, find the polygon $A_0A_1 \dots A_n$ with $A_0A_1 = x_1$, $A_1A_2 = x_2$, $\dots$, $A_{n-1}A_n = x_n$ which has the smallest area.
Given positive real numbers $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$, find the polygon $A_0A_1 \dots A_n$ with $A_0A_1 = x_1^2$, $A_1A_2 = x_2^2$, $\dots$, $A_{n-1}A_n = x_n^2$ which has the greatest area.
Given positive real numbers $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$, find the polygon $A_0A_1 \dots A_n$ with $A_0A_1 = x_1$, $A_1A_2 = x_2$, $\dots$, $A_{n-1}A_n = x_n$ which has the greatest perimeter.

positive_text: Determine all values of $n > 5$ for which there exists a convex polyhedron consisting of $n$ congruent faces, each having a parallel counterpart among the faces.

negatives.text: Find all $n > 5$ for which it is possible to find a convex polyhedron with all $n$ faces congruent such that each face has another face perpendicular to it.
Find all $n > 5$ for which it is possible to find a convex polyhedron with all $n$ faces congruent such that each face has another face adjacent to it.
Find all $n > 5$ for which it is possible to find a convex polyhedron with all $n$ faces congruent such that each face has another face parallel to it, and all faces are triangles.

positive_text: Let a triangle have inradius $r$, circumradius $R$, and semi-perimeter $s$. Prove that the triangle is right-angled if and only if $s - 2R = r$.

negatives.text: A triangle has semi-perimeter $s$, circumradius $R$, and inradius $r$. Show that it is right-angled iff $2R = s + r$.
A triangle has semi-perimeter $s$, circumradius $R$, and inradius $r$. Show that it is right-angled iff $R = s - r$.
A triangle has semi-perimeter $s$, circumradius $R$, and inradius $r$. Show that it is right-angled iff $2r = s - R$.

positive_text: Let $a_n$ be a sequence defined by $a_1 = a_2 = 1$, $a_{n+2} = a_{n+1} + a_n$. Define $X_n = \sqrt{a_n^2 + a_{n+2}^2}$. Prove that $X_n$, $X_{n+1}$, $X_{n+2}$ form a triangle with area $\frac{1}{2}$.

negatives.text: Let $F_n$ be the Fibonacci sequence $F_1 = F_2 = 1$, $F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_n$. Put $V_n = \sqrt{F_n^2 - F_{n+2}^2}$. Show that $V_n$, $V_{n+1}$, $V_{n+2}$ are the sides of a triangle of area $1/2$.

Let $F_n$ be the Fibonacci sequence $F_1 = F_2 = 1$, $F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_n$. Put $V_n = \sqrt{F_n^2 + F_{n+2}^2}$. Show that $V_n$, $V_{n+1}$, and $V_{n+2}$ are the sides of a triangle with area greater than $1/2$.

positive_text: Let $\mathbb{N}_0 = \{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\}$. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{N}_0 \to \mathbb{N}_0$ such that $f(2f(n)) = n + 1998$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$.

negatives.text: Let $N = \{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\}$. Find all functions $f: N \to N$ which satisfy $f(2f(n)) = n - 1998$ for all $n$.
Let $N = \{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\}$. Find all functions $f: N \to N$ which satisfy $f(2f(n)) = n^2 + 1998$ for all $n$.
Let $N = \{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\}$. Find all functions $f: N \to N$ which satisfy $f(2f(n)) = n + 2000$ for all $n$.

positive_text:
Let $ A $ be a corner of a rectangular sheet of paper, and suppose a line $ r $ passes through $ A $, forming an angle $ \alpha $ with the horizontal edge. To trisect $ \alpha $, proceed as follows:

a) Select points $ B $ and $ C $ on the vertical edge such that $ AB = BC $. Draw a line $ s $ through $ B $ parallel to the horizontal edge.

b) Fold the paper such that $ C $ maps to a point $ C' $ on $ r $, and $ A $ maps to a point $ A' $ on $ s $. Let $ B' $ be the image of $ B $.

Prove that the lines $ AA' $ and $ AB' $ divide $ \alpha $ into three equal parts.

negatives.text:
Let $ A $ be a vertex of a rectangular sheet of paper, with a line $ r $ passing through it and forming an angle $ \alpha $ with the horizontal side. To trisect $ \alpha $, mark points $ B $ and $ C $ on the vertical side such that $ AB = 2BC $, then draw a line $ s $ through $ B $ parallel to the horizontal side. Fold the sheet so that $ C $ maps to a point $ C' $ on $ r $, and $ A $ maps to a point $ A' $ on $ s $. Let $ B' $ be the image of $ B $.

Prove that the lines $ AA' $ and $ AB' $ trisect angle $ \alpha $.

positive_text: Let $X$ be the set of all sequences $a = (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{2000})$ where $a_i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ for the first 1000 positions and $a_i \in \{0, 1\}$ for the next 1000 positions. For $a, b \in X$, define $d(a, b)$ as the number of indices $i$ such that $a_i \ne b_i$. Determine the number of functions $f: X \to X$ satisfying $d(f(a), f(b)) = d(a, b)$ for all $a, b \in X$.

negatives.text: Let $X$ be the set of all sequences $a = (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{2000})$ such that $a_i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ for $1 \le i \le 1000$ and $a_i \in \{0, 1\}$ for $1001 \le i \le 2000$. Define $d(a, b)$ as the number of indices $i$ for which $a_i + b_i$ is odd. Find the number of functions $f: X \to X$ such that $d(f(a), f(b)) = d(a, b)$ for all $a, b \in X$.

Let $X$ be the set of all sequences $a = (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{2000})$ such that $a_i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ for $1 \le i \le 1000$ and $a_i \in \{0, 1\}$ for $1001 \le i \le 2000$. Define $d(a, b)$ as the number of indices $i$ for which $a_i > b_i$. Find the number of functions $f: X \to X$ such that $d(f(a), f(b)) = d(a, b)$ for all $a, b \in X$.

Let $X$ be the set of all sequences $a = (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{2000})$ such that $a_i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ for $1 \le i \le 1000$ and $a_i \in \{0, 1\}$ for $1001 \le i \le 2000$. Define $d(a, b)$ as the number of indices $i$ for which $a_i = b_i$. Find the number of functions $f: X \to X$ such that $d(f(a), f(b)) = d(a, b)$ for all $a, b \in X$.

positive_text:
Prove that
$$
(b+a)(c+a) \ge 2\sqrt{abc(a+b+c)}
$$
for all positive real numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$.

negatives.text:
Prove that
$$
(a+b)(a+c) \ge 2\sqrt{abc(a-b+c)}
$$
for all positive real numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$.

Prove that
$$
(a+b)(a+c) \ge 2\sqrt{abc(a+b^2+c)}
$$
for all positive real numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$.

Prove that
$$
(a+b)(a+c) \ge 2\sqrt{abc(a+b+c)^2}
$$
for all positive real numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$.

positive_text: Let $g(x)$ be a strictly increasing real-valued function on the positive reals such that $g\left(\frac{2xy}{x+y}\right) = \frac{g(x)+g(y)}{2}$ for all $x$. Prove there exists $x$ such that $g(x) < 0$.

negatives.text: Let $f(x)$ be a strictly increasing function on the positive reals such that $f\left(\frac{2xy}{x+y}\right) = \frac{f(x)+f(y)}{2}$ for all $x$. Show that $f(x) > 0$ for all $x$.

a. What is the probability that $\text{span}_+(w_1, w_2, w_3, w_4) = \mathbb{R}^3$?

b. What is the probability that each vector is necessary in the cone, i.e., that $\text{span}_+(w_1, w_2, w_3) \neq \text{span}_+(w_1, w_2, w_3, w_4)$, and similarly for all subsets of three vectors?

b. What is the probability that no one vector can be removed without changing the cone?

positive_text: Un număr natural este rotund dacă are un număr de divizori egal cu un pătrat perfect. Pentru un astfel de număr $n$ cu $d^{2}$ divizori, construim o matrice pătratică $d \times d$ și o completăm cu toți divizorii lui $n$. La fiecare pas, alegem un rând și rotim elementele acestuia la stânga (de exemplu, elementul de pe coloana 1 trece pe coloana 2, etc.). O configurație este fezabilă dacă există o coloană în care elementele sunt într-o ordine astfel încât $a_{1}\mid a_{2}\mid \ldots \mid a_{d}$ sau $a_{d}\mid a_{d-1}\mid \ldots \mid a_{1}$. Determinați toate numerele rotunde $n \geq 2$ pentru care, oricum am completa inițial matricea, există o configurație fezabilă accesibilă printr-un număr finit de pași.

negatives.text: Un număr natural este rotund dacă numărul divizorilor săi este pătrat perfect. Pentru un astfel de număr $n$ cu $d^{2}$ divizori, construim un tablou $d \times d$ și completăm celulele cu divizorii lui $n$. La fiecare pas, putem alege un rând și executa o rotație circulară la stânga. O configurație este fezabilă dacă există o coloană în care toate elementele sunt divizibile cu elementul de pe poziția 1. Determinați toate numerele rotunde $n \geq 2$ pentru care, oricum am completa inițial tabloul, putem ajunge printr-un număr finit de pași la o configurație fezabilă.

positive_text: Let $ a \geq 3 $ and $ b \geq 2 $ be integers. positive_text: Let $k$ be an integer, $1 < k < 100$. Consider all permutations $\pi$ of $\{1, 2, \ldots, 100\}$, and define $\pi_{101} = 0$. negatives.text: Let $k$ be an integer, $1 < k < 100$. For every permutation $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{100}$ of $\{1, 2, \ldots, 100\}$, define $a_{101} = 0$. Choose the least integer $m > k$ such that $a_{m}$ is less than at most $k-1$ of the numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{k}$. Find all $k$ for which the number of permutations with $a_{m} = 1$ is equal to $\frac{100!}{4}$.
