We are given a triangle $ABC$. Find the locus of points $X$ in the plane of $ABC$ whose reflections through the lines $AB$, $BC$, and $CA$ are vertices of a triangle with area equal to the area of triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: Let $AB$ be a segment in the plane. For any interior point $X$ on $AB$, define a triangle $XYZ$ such that $\triangle XBY \sim \triangle XZA$ and $A$, $B$, $Y$, $Z$ lie on a circle in this order. Determine the set of midpoints of all segments $YZ$ as $X$ varies.

negatives.text: Let $AB$ be a segment in the plane. A triangle $XYZ$ is defined such that $\triangle XBY \sim \triangle XAZ$ and $A$, $B$, $Y$, $Z$ lie on a circle in this order. Find the locus of midpoints of $YZ$.

Given a segment $AB$ and a triangle $XYZ$ with $X$ an interior point of $AB$, suppose $\triangle XBY \sim \triangle XZA$ and $A$, $B$, $Y$, $Z$ lie on a line in this order. Determine the locus of midpoints of $YZ$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle such that the axis of the median from $C$ is not perpendicular to either $CA$ or $CB$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the points where this axis intersects $CA$ and $CB$, respectively. Determine all triangles $ABC$ for which $A, B, X, Y$ are concyclic. (Ján Mazák)

negatives.text: In any triangle $ABC$, in which the median from $C$ is not perpendicular to any of the sides $CA$ nor $CB$, let $X$ and $Y$ be the points where the axis of the median intersects $CA$ and $CB$. Find all such triangles $ABC$ for which the points $A, B, X, Y$ are collinear. (Ján Mazák)

In triangle $ABC$, let $X$ and $Y$ be the points where the axis of the median from $C$ intersects $CA$ and $CB$, respectively. Find all such triangles $ABC$ for which the points $A, B, X, Y$ lie on the same circle, assuming the median from $C$ is perpendicular to one of the sides $CA$ or $CB$. (Ján Mazák)

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have its shortest side $BC$. Points $X$, $Y$ lie on $AB$, $AC$ and $K$, $L$ lie on the rays opposite to $BC$, $CB$ such that $BX = BK = BC = CY = CL$. If lines $KX$ and $LY$ meet at $M$, show that the centroid of triangle $KLM$ is the incenter of triangle $ABC$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ have its shortest side $BC$. Points $X$, $Y$ lie on $AB$, $AC$ and $K$, $L$ lie on the rays opposite to $BC$, $CB$ respectively such that $BX = BK = BC = CY = -CL$. Line $KX$ intersects line $LY$ at point $M$. Prove that the centroid of triangle $KLM$ coincides with the incenter of triangle $ABC$.

Let triangle $ABC$ have its shortest side $BC$. Points $X$, $Y$ lie on $AB$, $AC$ and $K$, $L$ lie on the rays opposite to $BC$, $CB$ respectively such that $BX = BK = 2BC = CY = CL$. Line $KX$ intersects line $LY$ at point $M$. Prove that the centroid of triangle $KLM$ coincides with the incenter of triangle $ABC$.

Let triangle $ABC$ have its shortest side $BC$. Points $X$, $Y$ lie on $AB$, $AC$ and $K$, $L$ lie on the rays opposite to $BC$, $CB$ respectively such that $BX = BK = BC = CY = CL$. Line $KX$ intersects line $LY$ at point $M$. Prove that the centroid of triangle $KLM$ coincides with the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: Let $k$ be a positive integer and let $n = 2k$. There are $n$ real numbers on the blackboard. In each step, select two numbers, remove them, and replace each with their product. Prove that it is always possible to reach a configuration where all $n$ numbers are the same, regardless of the initial $n$-tuple.

negatives.text: Let $n$ be an even positive integer and suppose $n$ real numbers are written on the board. In each step, pick two numbers $a$ and $b$, remove both, and write $a + b$ in their place twice. Prove that, regardless of the initial configuration, it is possible to make all numbers equal after a finite number of such operations.

Let $n$ be an odd positive integer and suppose $n$ real numbers are written on the board. In each step, pick two numbers $a$ and $b$, remove both, and write $ab$ in their place twice. Prove that, regardless of the initial configuration, it is possible to make all numbers equal after a finite number of such operations.

positive_text: Paul alternately places crosses and circles in a $(2n + 1) \times (2n + 1)$ table, beginning with a cross. After the table is filled, he computes his score as the number of rows with more crosses than circles plus the number of columns with more circles than crosses. What is the maximum possible score he can obtain in terms of $n$?

negatives.text: Paul fills a $(2n + 1) \times (2n + 1)$ table with crosses and circles in an alternating pattern, starting with a circle. After the table is filled, he calculates his score as the number of rows with more crosses than circles plus the number of columns with more circles than crosses. What is the maximum possible score in terms of $n$?

Paul fills a $(2n + 1) \times (2n + 1)$ table with crosses and circles in an alternating pattern, starting with a cross. After the table is filled, he calculates his score as the number of rows with more circles than crosses plus the number of columns with more circles than crosses. What is the maximum possible score in terms of $n$?

Paul fills a $(2n + 1) \times (2n + 1)$ table with crosses and circles in an alternating pattern, starting with a cross. After the table is filled, he calculates his score as the number of rows with an equal number of crosses and circles plus the number of columns with an equal number of crosses and circles. What is the maximum possible score in terms of $n$?

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with orthocenter $H$. Let the internal angle bisector of $\angle BHC$ intersect $BC$ at point $D$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the reflections of $D$ across lines $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Show that the circumcircle of triangle $AEF$ contains the midpoint of the arc $BAC$ of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with orthocenter $H$. The external angle bisector of $\angle BHC$ intersects side $BC$ at $D$. Denote by $E$, $F$ the reflections of $D$ about $AB$, $AC$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircle of triangle $AEF$ passes through the midpoint of arc $BAC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with orthocenter $H$. The bisector of angle $BHC$ intersects side $BC$ at $D$. Denote by $E$, $F$ the reflections of $D$ about $BC$, $AC$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircle of triangle $AEF$ passes through the midpoint of arc $BAC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with orthocenter $H$. The bisector of angle $BHC$ intersects side $BC$ at $D$. Denote by $E$, $F$ the reflections of $D$ about $AB$, $AC$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircle of triangle $AEF$ passes through the midpoint of arc $BC$ of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle BAC = \alpha$. The angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets $BC$ at $D$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the centers of the circumcircles of triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$, respectively. If the circumcenter of triangle $AEF$ lies on $BC$, determine all possible values of $\alpha$. (Patrik Bak)

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle and let $AD$ be the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$, intersecting $BC$ at $D$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the incenters of triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$, respectively. If the circumcenter of triangle $AEF$ lies on $BC$, find all possible values of $\angle BAC$. (Patrik Bak)

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AD$ the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ intersecting $BC$ at $D$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the circumcenters of triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$, respectively. If the circumcenter of triangle $AEF$ lies on the line $AD$, find all possible values of $\angle BAC$. (Patrik Bak)

Let $ABC$ be a triangle and let $AD$ be the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$, intersecting $BC$ at $D$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the circumcenters of triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$, respectively. If the centroid of triangle $AEF$ lies on $BC$, find all possible values of $\angle BAC$. (Patrik Bak)

positive_text: Given an isosceles trapezoid $ABCD$ with $AB > CD$, let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$ and $J$ be the $C$-excenter of triangle $ACD$. Show that the line segment $IJ$ is parallel to $AB$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be an isosceles trapezoid with longer base $AB$. Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$ and $J$ the $C$-excenter of triangle $ACD$. Prove that $IJ$ and $AB$ are perpendicular.
Let $ABCD$ be an isosceles trapezoid with longer base $AB$. Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$ and $J$ the $C$-excenter of triangle $ABD$. Prove that $IJ$ and $AB$ are parallel.
Let $ABCD$ be an isosceles trapezoid with longer base $AB$. Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$ and $J$ the $C$-excenter of triangle $ACD$. Prove that $IJ$ and $CD$ are parallel.

positive_text: Given an acute triangle $ABC$ with orthocenter $H$ and incenter $I$, let $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $I$ to side $BC$. Let $E$ be the reflection of $A$ over $I$, and let $F$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $H$ to the line $ED$. Show that $B$, $H$, $F$, and $C$ are concyclic.

negatives.text: In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$, let $H$ be the orthocenter and $I$ the incenter. Let $D$ be the perpendicular projection of $I$ onto $BC$, and $E$ the reflection of $A$ across $I$. Let $F$ be the perpendicular projection of $H$ onto the line $ED$. Prove that the points $A$, $H$, $F$, and $I$ lie on one circle.

In an acute triangle $ABC$, let $H$ be the orthocenter and $I$ the incenter. Let $D$ be the perpendicular projection of $I$ onto $BC$, and $E$ the reflection of $A$ across $I$. If $F$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $I$ to line $ED$, prove that $B$, $H$, $F$, and $C$ lie on one circle.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with orthocenter $H$ and incenter $I$. Let $D$ be the perpendicular projection of $I$ onto $BC$, and $E$ the reflection of $A$ across $I$. Let $F$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $H$ to the line $ED$. Prove that the points $B$, $I$, $F$, and $C$ lie on one circle.

positive_text: Let $k$ and $n$ be odd positive integers. Martin wrote all fractions $\frac{i}{j}$ for $i, j$ satisfying $1 \le i \le k$ and $1 \le j \le n$. Find the median of these fractions, defined as the real number $q$ such that when the fractions are arranged in non-decreasing order, $q$ is the value of the central element in the list.

negatives.text: Let $k$ and $n$ be odd positive integers. Martin wrote all fractions $\frac{i}{j}$ for $1 \le i \le k$ and $1 \le j \le n$. Determine the median of the sum $i + j$ instead of the fractions.

Let $k$ and $n$ be odd positive integers. Martin wrote all fractions $\frac{i}{j}$ for $1 \le i \le k$ and $1 \le j \le n$. Determine the median of the absolute differences $|i - j|$ instead of the fractions.

positive_text:
Consider a $3 \times 3$ grid where each cell is filled with a unique natural number from $1$ to $9$. Compute the sum of each $2 \times 2$ subgrid and list them in non-decreasing order. Is it possible to achieve the following sets of four values:

a) $24$, $24$, $25$, $25$,

b) $20$, $23$, $26$, $29$?

negatives.text:
Suppose that we fill a $3 \times 3$ table with natural numbers from $1$ to $9$ using each of them precisely once. After that, we write down the sums in each of the four $2 \times 2$ squares in the ascending order. Determine whether it is possible to obtain the following quadruples of natural numbers:

a) $24$, $24$, $25$, $26$,

b) $20$, $23$, $26$, $29$.

Suppose that we fill a $3 \times 3$ table with natural numbers from $1$ to $9$ using each of them precisely once. After that, we write down the sums in each of the four $2 \times 2$ squares in the ascending order. Determine whether it is possible to obtain the following quadruples of natural numbers:

a) $24$, $24$, $25$, $25$,

b) $19$, $23$, $26$, $29$.

Suppose that we fill a $3 \times 3$ table with natural numbers from $1$ to $9$ using each of them precisely once. After that, we write down the sums in each of the four $2 \times 2$ squares in the ascending order. Determine whether it is possible to obtain the following quadruples of natural numbers:

a) $24$, $24$, $25$, $25$,

b) $20$, $23$, $26$, $30$.

positive_text: Let $T$ be the centroid of triangle $ABC$. Let $K$ and $L$ be points such that triangles $BTK$ and $CTL$ are isosceles and right-angled at $T$, with $K$ located in the half-plane defined by $BTC$ and $L$ in the half-plane defined by $CTA$. Let $D$ and $E$ denote the midpoints of $BC$ and $KL$, respectively. Find all possible values of the ratio $\frac{AT}{DE}$.

negatives.text: Let $T$ be the centroid of triangle $ABC$. Consider two isosceles right-angled triangles $BTK$ and $CTL$ so that $K$ lies in the half-plane $BTC$ and $L$ lies in the half-plane $CTA$. Let $D$ and $E$ denote the midpoints of $BC$ and $KL$, respectively. Determine all possible values of the ratio $\frac{BT}{DE}$.

Let $T$ be the centroid of triangle $ABC$. Consider two isosceles right-angled triangles $BTK$ and $CTL$ so that $K$ lies in the half-plane $BTC$ and $L$ lies in the half-plane $CTA$. Let $D$ and $E$ denote the midpoints of $BC$ and $KL$, respectively. Determine all possible values of the ratio $\frac{AT}{DE^2}$.

Let $T$ be the centroid of triangle $ABC$. Consider two isosceles right-angled triangles $BTK$ and $CTL$ so that $K$ lies in the half-plane $BTC$ and $L$ lies in the half-plane $CTA$. Let $D$ and $E$ denote the midpoints of $BC$ and $KL$, respectively. Determine all possible values of the ratio $\frac{AT^2}{DE}$.

positive_text: Let $ ABC $ be an acute triangle inscribed in a circle $ k $. Let $ P $ be a point on the minor arc $ BC $, and let $ O $ be the intersection point of $ AP $ and $ BC $. If $ O_1 $ and $ O_2 $ are the circumcenters of triangles $ PBQ $ and $ PCQ $, respectively, show that if the line $ O_1O_2 $ goes through a vertex of triangle $ ABC $, then one of $ O_1 $ or $ O_2 $ lies on the circle $ k $.

negatives.text: Let $ ABC $ be an acute triangle with circumcircle $ k $. Let $ P $ lie on the minor arc $ BC $ of $ k $, and let $ O $ be the intersection of $ AP $ with $ BC $. Let $ O_1 $ and $ O_2 $ be the incenters of triangles $ PBQ $ and $ PCQ $, respectively. Prove that if the line $ O_1O_2 $ passes through a vertex of triangle $ ABC $, then one of $ O_1 $ or $ O_2 $ lies on $ k $.

Let $ ABC $ be an acute triangle with circumcircle $ k $. Let $ P $ lie on the minor arc $ BC $ of $ k $, and let $ O $ be the intersection of $ AP $ with $ BC $. If $ O_1 $ and $ O_2 $ are the circumcenters of triangles $ PBC $ and $ PCB $, respectively, prove that if the line $ O_1O_2 $ passes through a vertex of triangle $ ABC $, then one of $ O_1 $ or $ O_2 $ lies on $ k $.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Solve the system
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_k^k &= n, \\
\sum_{k=1}^{n} kx_k &= n(n+1)
\end{aligned}
$$
in the set of nonnegative real numbers $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Solve the system
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_k^k &= n, \\
\sum_{k=1}^{n} kx_k &= \frac{n(n+1)}{2} + 1
\end{aligned}
$$
in the set of nonnegative real numbers $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$.

positive_text: Five distinct points $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$, $T$ are arranged in order on a circle of radius $r$, such that $PR = QS = RT = r$. Let $H_1$, $H_2$, $H_3$ be the orthocentres of triangles $PRS$, $QRS$, $QRT$, respectively. Prove that triangle $H_1H_2H_3$ is right-angled.

negatives.text: There are 5 distinct points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$ lying in this order on a circle with radius $r$ satisfying $AC = BD = CE = r$. There is a triangle having incentres of triangles $ACD$, $BCD$, $BCE$ as its vertices. Prove that this triangle is right-angled.

There are 5 distinct points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$ lying in this order on a circle with radius $r$ satisfying $AC = BD = CE = r$. There is a triangle having orthocentres of triangles $ABD$, $BCD$, $BCE$ as its vertices. Prove that this triangle is right-angled.

There are 5 distinct points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$ lying in this order on a circle with radius $r$ satisfying $AC = BD = CE = 2r$. There is a triangle having orthocentres of triangles $ACD$, $BCD$, $BCE$ as its vertices. Prove that this triangle is right-angled.

positive_text:
Let $A, B, C, D, E$ be the vertices of a regular pentagon. Find the minimum value of
$$
\frac{PA + PB}{PC + PD + PE}
$$
for any point $P$ in the plane of the pentagon.

negatives.text:
Let $A, B, C, D, E$ be the vertices of a regular pentagon. Determine the minimum value of
$$
\frac{PA^2 + PB^2}{PC^2 + PD^2 + PE^2}
$$
for any point $P$ in the plane.

Let $A, B, C, D, E$ be the vertices of a regular pentagon. Determine the maximum value of
$$
\frac{PA + PB}{PC + PD + PE}
$$
for any point $P$ in the plane.

positive_text: Let $ AB $ be a chord of a circle $ k $, not a diameter, and let $ C $ lie on the major arc $ AB $. Define $ K $ as the reflection of $ A $ over line $ BC $, and $ L $ as the reflection of $ B $ over line $ AC $. Prove that the distance between the midpoints of $ KL $ and $ AB $ is constant for all such points $ C $.

negatives.text: Let $ AB $ be a chord of a circle $ k $, not a diameter, and let $ C $ lie on the major arc $ AB $. Define $ K $ as the reflection of $ A $ over line $ BC $, and $ L $ as the reflection of $ A $ over line $ AC $. Prove that the distance between the midpoints of $ KL $ and $ AB $ is independent of the location of $ C $.

Let $ AB $ be a chord of a circle $ k $, not a diameter, and let $ C $ lie on the major arc $ AB $. Define $ K $ as the reflection of $ A $ over line $ BC $, and $ L $ as the reflection of $ B $ over line $ AB $. Prove that the distance between the midpoints of $ KL $ and $ AB $ is independent of the location of $ C $.

Let $ AB $ be a chord of a circle $ k $, not a diameter, and let $ C $ lie on the major arc $ AB $. Define $ K $ as the reflection of $ A $ over line $ BC $, and $ L $ as the reflection of $ B $ over line $ AC $. Prove that the distance between the midpoints of $ KL $ and $ AC $ is independent of the location of $ C $.

positive_text: Let $a$, $b$ be integers with $b$ not a square. Prove that the number of integer values of $x$ for which $x^2 + a x + b$ is a perfect square is finite.

negatives.text: Let $a$, $b$ be integers with $b$ not a perfect square. Show that $x^2 - a x + b$ can be a perfect square for infinitely many integers $x$.
Let $a$, $b$ be integers with $b$ not a perfect square. Show that $x^2 + a x + b$ can be a perfect square for all but finitely many integers $x$.
Let $a$, $b$ be integers with $b$ not a perfect square. Show that $x^2 + a x + b$ can be a perfect square for infinitely many integers $x$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be inscribed in a circle. Let $P$ be the midpoint of the arc $BAC$ not containing $B$ or $C$. The circle with diameter $CP$ intersects the internal angle bisector of $\angle A$ at two points $K$ and $L$, with $K$ closer to $A$. Let $M$ be the reflection of $L$ over $BC$. Prove that the circumcircle of triangle $BKM$ divides segment $BC$ in half.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be inscribed in a circle, and let $P$ be the midpoint of arc $BAC$. A circle with diameter $CP$ intersects the external angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ at points $K$ and $L$, with $K$ closer to $A$. If $M$ is the reflection of $L$ across $BC$, prove that the circumcircle of triangle $BKM$ bisects segment $BC$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be inscribed in a circle, and let $P$ be the midpoint of arc $BAC$. A circle with diameter $AP$ intersects the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ at points $K$ and $L$, with $K$ closer to $A$. If $M$ is the reflection of $L$ across $BC$, prove that the circumcircle of triangle $BKM$ bisects segment $BC$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be inscribed in a circle, and let $P$ be the midpoint of arc $BAC$. A circle with diameter $CP$ intersects the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ at points $K$ and $L$, with $K$ closer to $A$. If $M$ is the reflection of $K$ across $BC$, prove that the circumcircle of triangle $BKM$ bisects segment $BC$.

positive_text:
Let $k$ be a fixed positive integer. A finite sequence of integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_m$ is written on a blackboard. Pepa and Geoff play a game in rounds as follows:
* In each round, Pepa partitions the current sequence into at least two contiguous parts. If the number of parts exceeds two, each part must have a total sum divisible by $k$.
* Geoff then removes all but one of the parts.
The game ends when only one number remains. Show that Pepa can always force the game to end in at most $3k$ rounds, regardless of Geoff's choices.

negatives.text:
Let $k$ be a fixed positive integer. A finite sequence of integers $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ is written on a blackboard. Pepa and Geoff play a game:
* In each round, Pepa partitions the current sequence into two or more contiguous subsequences. However, if the number of subsequences is greater than two, then the sum of numbers in each of them has to be congruent to $-1$ modulo $k$.
* Then Geoff selects one of the subsequences and removes the rest.
The game ends when only one number remains. Prove that Pepa can force the game to end in at most $3k$ rounds.

Let $k$ be a fixed positive integer. A finite sequence of integers $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ is written on a blackboard. Pepa and Geoff play a game:
* In each round, Pepa partitions the current sequence into two or more contiguous subsequences. However, if the number of subsequences is greater than two, then the sum of numbers in each of them has to be divisible by $k^2$.
* Then Geoff selects one of the subsequences and removes the rest.
The game ends when only one number remains. Prove that Pepa can force the game to end in at most $3k$ rounds.

Let $k$ be a fixed positive integer. A finite sequence of integers $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ is written on a blackboard. Pepa and Geoff play a game:
* In each round, Pepa partitions the current sequence into two or more contiguous subsequences. However, if the number of subsequences is greater than two, then the sum of numbers in each of them has to be divisible by $k$.
* Then Geoff selects one of the subsequences and removes the rest.
The game ends when only one number remains. Prove that Pepa can force the game to end in at most $2k$ rounds.

positive_text: Given an acute triangle $ABC$, let $D$ be a point on the side of line $AB$ where $C$ lies, such that $DB \perp AB$ and $\angle ADB = 45^\circ + \frac{1}{2}\angle ACB$. Similarly, let $E$ be a point on the side of line $AC$ where $B$ lies, with $EC \perp AC$ and $\angle AEC = 45^\circ + \frac{1}{2}\angle ABC$. Let $F$ be the reflection of $A$ across the midpoint of the arc $BAC$ of the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ that contains $A$. Prove that $A, D, E, F$ lie on a common circle.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute. Point $D$ lies in the halfplane $AB$ containing $C$ and satisfies $DB \perp AB$ and $\angle ADB = 45^\circ - \frac{1}{2}\angle ACB$. Similarly, $E$ lies in the halfplane $AC$ containing $B$ and satisfies $EC \perp AC$ and $\angle AEC = 45^\circ - \frac{1}{2}\angle ABC$. Let $F$ be the reflection of $A$ in the midpoint of arc $BAC$ containing $A$. Prove that points $A, D, E, F$ are concyclic.

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute. Point $D$ lies in the halfplane $AB$ containing $C$ and satisfies $DB \perp AB$ and $\angle ADB = 45^\circ + \frac{1}{2}\angle ACB$. Similarly, $E$ lies in the halfplane $AC$ containing $B$ and satisfies $EC \perp AC$ and $\angle AEC = 45^\circ + \frac{1}{2}\angle ABC$. Let $F$ be the reflection of $A$ in the midpoint of arc $BC$ not containing $A$. Prove that points $A, D, E, F$ are concyclic.

positive_text: Let a basic L-shape be defined as three unit squares joined in an L-configuration. Show that for every positive integer $k$, an L-shape scaled by a factor of $k$ in both dimensions can be partitioned into multiple unit L-shapes.

negatives.text: A unit L-shape consists of three unit squares. Prove that for any positive integer $k$, it is possible to cut a similar L-shape with side lengths $k + 1$ times larger into unit L-shapes.
A unit L-shape consists of three unit squares. Prove that for any positive integer $k$, it is possible to cut a similar L-shape with side lengths $k$ times smaller into unit L-shapes.

positive_text: Three players $P_1$, $P_2$, and $P_3$ each begin with a card labeled with their own name. On their turn, a player selects one of the other two and replaces the name on that card with their own. The sequence of turns is $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$, and then repeats in that order. The game ends when all three cards have the same name, and the player whose name appears is the winner. Is there a player who can guarantee a win, regardless of the moves of the others?

negatives.text: Three players $A$, $B$, and $C$ each begin with a card labeled with their own name. On their turn, a player selects one of the other two and appends their own name to the selected card (instead of replacing it). The game ends when all three cards contain the same name, and the player whose name appears is the winner. Does any of the players have a winning strategy?

Three players $A$, $B$, and $C$ each begin with a card labeled with their own name. On their turn, a player selects one of the other two and replaces the name on that card with their own. The game ends when all three cards have the same name, and the winner is the player who makes the final move. Does any of the players have a winning strategy?

Three players $A$, $B$, and $C$ each begin with a card labeled with their own name. On their turn, a player selects one of the other two and replaces the name on that card with their own. However, each player is only allowed to perform this action once. The game ends when all three cards have the same name, and the winner is the player whose name appears. Does any of the players have a winning strategy?

positive_text: Let $D$ be the midpoint of segment $BC$ in triangle $ABC$. Let $G_1$ and $G_2$ be the centroids of triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$, respectively. Prove that the perpendicular distances from $G_1$ and $G_2$ to the line $AD$ are equal.

negatives.text: Let $D$ be the midpoint of side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$. Prove that the intersection point of medians of triangle $ABD$ and that of triangle $ACD$ are equidistant from line $BC$.
Let $D$ be the midpoint of side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$. Prove that the intersection point of medians of triangle $ABD$ and that of triangle $ACD$ are equidistant from point $A$.

positive_text: Given a regular $n$-gon with each vertex labeled $0$ or $1$, Juku triangulates it with non-crossing diagonals and writes the sum of the vertex labels in each triangle. Show there exists a triangulation such that the difference between the largest and smallest triangle sums is at most $1$.

negatives.text: In a regular $n$-gon, either $0$ or $1$ is written at each vertex. Juku divides it into triangles using non-intersecting diagonals and writes the product of the vertex numbers in each triangle. positive_text: A $n \times n$ grid is colored using two colors, red and blue, such that all $2 \times 2$ subgrids exhibit all $16$ distinct colorings (where rotations and reflections are considered different). Determine the smallest possible $n$ and then the minimum number of red cells for that $n$.

negatives.text: A $n \times n$ board is colored red or blue such that all $2 \times 2$ subgrids contain at least one red and one blue cell. a) Find the minimal $n$. b) For that $n$, find the minimal number of red cells.

A $n \times n$ board is colored red or blue such that all $2 \times 2$ subgrids contain at most 2 red squares. a) Find the minimal $n$. b) For that $n$, find the minimal number of red cells.

positive_text:

The resulting composition was $25\%$ ugly and $45\%$ useless. What percentage of the original satchel items were both beautiful and useful?

*Answer:* $4\%$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral such that each side is the diameter of a circle. Suppose all four circles share a common point $O$ (distinct from the vertices of $ABCD$) and intersect only at $O$. Prove that $ABCD$ is a rhombus.

negatives.text: Each side of a convex quadrangle $ABCD$ is a diameter of a circle. All four circles pass through the same point $O$, different from the vertices of the quadrangle, and no two circles have common points other than those mentioned. Prove that $ABCD$ is a square.

Each side of a convex quadrangle $ABCD$ is a diameter of a circle. All four circles pass through the same point $O$, different from the vertices of the quadrangle, and no two circles have common points other than those mentioned. Prove that $ABCD$ is a rectangle.

Each side of a convex quadrangle $ABCD$ is a diameter of a circle. All four circles pass through the same point $O$, different from the vertices of the quadrangle, and no two circles have common points other than those mentioned. Prove that $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have integer side lengths. Suppose the internal angle bisector from $B$ and the perpendicular from $C$ intersect at a point $P$ within the triangle. Show that the ratio $[APB]/[APC]$ is rational.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ have integer side lengths. The angle bisector from $B$ and the median from $C$ intersect at point $P$. Prove that the ratio of areas of triangles $APB$ and $APC$ is a rational number.

Let triangle $ABC$ have integer side lengths. The angle bisector from $B$ and the altitude from $C$ intersect at point $P$. Prove that the ratio of areas of triangles $APB$ and $ABC$ is a rational number.

positive_text: \text{Given a parallelogram } ABCD, \text{ show that if the incenter of triangle } ABC \text{ lies on the diagonal } BD, \text{ then } ABCD \text{ is a rhombus.} \text{ Additionally, determine whether the condition that the circumcenter of } ABC \text{ lies on } BD \text{ also implies } ABCD \text{ is a rhombus.}

negatives.text: \text{Consider a parallelogram } ABCD.\text{ a) Prove that if the incenter of the triangle } ABC \text{ is located on the diagonal } AC, \text{ then the parallelogram } ABCD \text{ is a rhombus.} \text{ b) Is the parallelogram } ABCD \text{ a rhombus whenever the circumcenter of the triangle } ABC \text{ is located on the diagonal } AC?

\text{Consider a parallelogram } ABCD.\text{ a) Prove that if the incenter of the triangle } ABC \text{ is located on the diagonal } BD, \text{ then the parallelogram } ABCD \text{ is a square.} \text{ b) Is the parallelogram } ABCD \text{ a square whenever the circumcenter of the triangle } ABC \text{ is located on the diagonal } BD?

\text{Consider a parallelogram } ABCD.\text{ a) Prove that if the incenter of the triangle } ABC \text{ is located on the diagonal } BD, \text{ then the parallelogram } ABCD \text{ is a rectangle.} \text{ b) Is the parallelogram } ABCD \text{ a rectangle whenever the circumcenter of the triangle } ABC \text{ is located on the diagonal } BD?

positive_text: Let $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5A_6$ be a convex hexagon. If the hexagon formed by the intersection points of the diagonals $A_1A_3$, $A_2A_4$, $A_3A_5$, $A_4A_6$, $A_5A_1$, and $A_6A_2$ is regular, does this imply that $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5A_6$ is regular?

negatives.text: Consider the diagonals $A_1A_3$, $A_2A_4$, $A_3A_5$, $A_4A_6$, $A_5A_1$ and $A_6A_2$ of a convex hexagon $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5A_6$. The hexagon whose vertices are the points of intersection of the diagonals is equilateral. Can we conclude that the hexagon $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5A_6$ is also regular?

Consider the diagonals $A_1A_3$, $A_2A_4$, $A_3A_5$, $A_4A_6$, $A_5A_1$ and $A_6A_2$ of a convex hexagon $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5A_6$. The hexagon whose vertices are the points of intersection of the diagonals is cyclic. Can we conclude that the hexagon $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5A_6$ is also regular?

Consider the diagonals $A_1A_3$, $A_2A_4$, $A_3A_5$, $A_4A_6$, $A_5A_1$ and $A_6A_2$ of a convex hexagon $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5A_6$. The hexagon whose vertices are the points of intersection of the diagonals is equiangular. Can we conclude that the hexagon $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5A_6$ is also regular?

positive_text: A triangle composed of $9$ small equilateral triangles, each of side length $1$, is formed from a larger equilateral triangle of side length $3$. Each vertex of the small triangles (colored in the diagram) is labeled with a unique integer from $1$ to $10$. If the sum of the numbers at the vertices of each small triangle is written within it, prove that at least three of these sums exceed $11$.

negatives.text: An equilateral triangle with side length $3$ is divided into $9$ equilateral triangles with side length $1$. An integer from $1$ to $10$ is written into every point that is a vertex of a small triangle, such that all numbers are used exactly once. For every small triangle, the product of the numbers in its three vertices is written inside it. Prove that at least three of those products are greater than $11$.

An equilateral triangle with side length $3$ is divided into $9$ equilateral triangles with side length $1$. An integer from $1$ to $10$ is written into every point that is a vertex of a small triangle, such that all numbers are used exactly once. For every small triangle, the sum of the numbers in its three vertices is written inside it. Prove that at least three of those sums are greater than or equal to $11$.

An equilateral triangle with side length $3$ is divided into $9$ equilateral triangles with side length $1$. An integer from $1$ to $10$ is written into every point that is a vertex of a small triangle, such that all numbers are used exactly once. For every small triangle, the sum of the numbers in its three vertices is written inside it. Prove that at least two of those sums are greater than $11$.

positive_text: Let $ k $ be a positive integer. positive_text: A group of hikers wishes to walk around a lake that is enclosed by a circular path. They identify two points on the shoreline that are farthest apart and decide to follow a circular route with these two points as the endpoints of a diameter. Is it guaranteed that, regardless of the lake's shape, the entire route lies along the shoreline and does not require crossing the water?

negatives.text: A hiking club wants to walk around a lake along a circular route. They identify two points on the shoreline that are the farthest apart and construct a circle with these points as the center and radius. Is it guaranteed that the entire route lies along the shoreline and no part of the path requires crossing the water, regardless of the lake's shape?

A hiking club wishes to walk around a lake along a circular route. They identify two points on the shoreline that are the closest to each other and construct a circle with these points as the endpoints of its diameter. Can they be sure that, regardless of the lake's shape, they do not have to swim across the lake on any part of their route?

A hiking club wants to hike around a lake along an exactly circular route. They determine two points on the shoreline that are the most distant from each other and start to walk along the circle, which has these two points as the endpoints of its radius. Can they be sure that, independent of the shape of the lake, they do not have to swim across the lake on any part of their route?

positive_text: A train was delayed by 12 minutes at the start. If it could travel continuously at the same average speed as it would have between stops (according to the schedule), it would arrive on time. However, if it were to stop at each station for the full duration it was scheduled to stop, it would need to increase its average speed by 40\% between stations to arrive on time. Determine the total scheduled travel time (excluding stops).

negatives.text: A train departed 12 minutes later than planned. If it could travel continuously at the same average speed as it would between stops, it would arrive on time. But if it stopped at each station for the same amount of time it was supposed to, it would have to travel with average speed 40\% less than before in order to arrive on time. Find the scheduled travel time.

A train departed 12 minutes later than planned. If it could travel continuously at the same average speed as it would between stops, it would arrive on time. But if it stopped at each station for twice the amount of time it was supposed to, it would have to travel with average speed 40\% higher than before in order to arrive on time. Find the scheduled travel time.

positive_text: In an acute triangle $ABC$, let the altitude from $B$ and the angle bisector from $C$ intersect at point $D$. Reflect $D$ over line $AC$ to obtain point $E$. If $A$, $B$, $C$, and $E$ lie on a circle, show that triangle $ABC$ is isosceles.

positive_text: Let $D$, $E$, and $F$ be the midpoints of sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ of triangle $ABC$, respectively. Show that the circumcircles of triangles $AEF$, $BFD$, and $CDE$ have a common point of intersection.

positive_text: Consider a board with squares labeled from 1 to 10 arranged in a row. A player can move the button from a square to another square that is either 2 less or twice as large. Is there a starting position from which the player can reach every square on the board at least once?

negatives.text: A boardgame board consists of 10 squares in a row that are numbered 1 to 10. On some square there is a button. Does there exist an initial location for the button that allows the player to visit all squares of the board? It is allowed to visit one square several times.

A boardgame board consists of 10 squares in a row that are numbered 1 to 10. On some square there is a button. In one move it is allowed to move the button to a square whose number is either smaller by 2 or 2 times bigger, but the button cannot revisit any square. Does there exist an initial location for the button that allows the player to visit all squares of the board?

A boardgame board consists of 10 squares in a row that are numbered 1 to 10. On some square there is a button. In one move it is allowed to move the button to a square whose number is either smaller by 2 or 2 times bigger. positive_text:
Find all prime numbers $p$ for which there exists a positive integer $m$ and digits $d_0, d_1, \dots, d_m$ in base $p$ such that
$$
\begin{cases} d_0 + d_1 p + \dots + d_{m-1} p^{m-1} + d_m p^m = 2013, \\ d_0 + d_1 + \dots + d_{m-1} + d_m = 11. \end{cases}
$$

negatives.text:
Find all prime numbers $p$ for which one can find a positive integer $m$ and non-negative integers $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_m$ less than $p$ such that
$$
\begin{cases} a_0 + a_1 p + \dots + a_{m-1} p^{m-1} + a_m p^m = 2013, \\ a_0 + a_1 + \dots + a_{m-1} + a_m = 12. \end{cases}
$$

Find all prime numbers $p$ for which one can find a positive integer $m$ and non-negative integers $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_m$ less than $p$ such that
$$
\begin{cases} a_0 + a_1 p + \dots + a_{m-1} p^{m-1} + a_m p^m = -2013, \\ a_0 + a_1 + \dots + a_{m-1} + a_m = 11. \end{cases}
$$

Find all prime numbers $p$ for which one can find a positive integer $m$ and non-negative integers $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_m$ less than $p$ such that
$$
\begin{cases} a_0 + a_1 p + \dots + a_{m-1} p^{m-1} + a_m p^m = 2013^2, \\ a_0 + a_1 + \dots + a_{m-1} + a_m = 11. \end{cases}
$$

positive_text: Consider a sequence of $125$ distinct positive integers where for any three consecutive terms $a_{i-1}, a_i, a_{i+1}$, the inequality $a_i > \frac{a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}}{2}$ holds. Determine the minimal possible value of the largest number in the sequence.

negatives.text: There are $125$ distinct positive integers in a row such that among every three consecutive numbers the second one is less than the arithmetic mean of the first and the third one. Find the largest number in the row, given that it is as small as possible under such conditions.

There are $125$ distinct positive integers in a row such that among every three consecutive numbers the second one is equal to the arithmetic mean of the first and the third one. Find the largest number in the row, given that it is as small as possible under such conditions.

There are $125$ distinct positive integers in a row such that among every three consecutive numbers the second one is greater than the geometric mean of the first and the third one. Find the largest number in the row, given that it is as small as possible under such conditions.

positive_text: Consider a grid of $n \times m$ lamps, all initially off. Each operation toggles the state of three consecutive lamps in a row or column. Determine all positive integer pairs $(n, m)$ for which it is possible to turn on all the lamps.

negatives.text: A grid of $n \times m$ lamps is initially all off. A move consists of flipping the state of two consecutive lamps in a row or column. For which values of $n$ and $m$ can all lamps be turned on?

negatives.text: Angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are such that $\frac{\tan \alpha}{\tan \beta} = k \neq 1$. Express $\frac{\cos(\alpha + \beta)}{\cos(\alpha - \beta)}$ in terms of $k$.

positive_text: Suppose a finite set of points is given in the plane, with no three collinear, and there exists a non-convex polygon whose vertices are among these points. Show that there is a non-convex quadrilateral with all its vertices chosen from the same set.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have medians $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$ intersecting at centroid $G$. Consider the circles centered at $G$ with radii $GD$, $GE$, and $GF$. Suppose that the figure obtained by deleting one of the four rectangles can be tiled using $2 \times 3$ and $4 \times 3$ tiles. Prove that one of the four sub-rectangles is also tileable by $2 \times 3$ and $3 \times 2$ tiles.

A rectangle is divided into four smaller rectangles with integer dimensions using two perpendicular lines. Suppose that the figure obtained by removing one of the four rectangles can be tiled using $2 \times 3$ and $3 \times 2$ tiles. Prove that the remaining three rectangles can be tiled using $1 \times 3$ and $3 \times 1$ tiles.

positive_text: Two players, Ats and Pets, alternately write distinct triplets of single-digit positive integers that add up to $15$. Each new triplet must share exactly one number with the previous triplet, none with the one before that, and not share all three numbers with any earlier triplet. Ats begins with any valid triplet, and the player unable to write a valid triplet loses. Who can guarantee a win regardless of the opponent's strategy?

negatives.text: Ats and Pets take turns to write representations of the number $15$ as the sum of three distinct single-digit positive integers. Each new sum must share exactly one addend with the previous sum, at least one addend with the second previous sum, and less than three common addends with any sum written earlier. Ats starts and can choose the first sum arbitrarily. The player who cannot write a sum loses. Who can win regardless of the opponent's play?

Ats and Pets take turns to write representations of the number $15$ as the sum of three distinct single-digit positive integers. Each new sum must share exactly one addend with the previous sum, no common addends with the second previous sum, and less than two common addends with any sum written earlier. Ats starts and can choose the first sum arbitrarily. The player who cannot write a sum loses. Who can win regardless of the opponent's play?

positive_text: Three people prepare fruit drinks. The first person creates $a$ litres of drink by mixing water and syrup in the ratio $a : 1$, the second person makes $b$ litres in the ratio $b : 1$, and the third person produces $c$ litres in the ratio $c : 1$. The total volume of drink is $6$ litres. Show that the total amount of syrup used does not exceed $2$ litres.

negatives.text: Anna, Berta, and Carol make $a$, $b$, and $c$ litres of drink respectively by mixing water and syrup in the proportions $a : 1$, $b : 1$, and $c : 1$. They make a total of $6$ litres of drink. Prove that they use at least $2$ litres of syrup.

Anna, Berta, and Carol make $a$, $b$, and $c$ litres of drink by mixing water and syrup in the proportions $a : 1$, $b : 1$, and $c : 1$. They make $6$ litres of drink in total. Prove that they use at most $2$ litres of syrup, given that $a, b, c$ are integers.

Anna, Berta, and Carol make $a$, $b$, and $c$ litres of drink by mixing water and syrup in the proportions $1 : a$, $1 : b$, and $1 : c$ respectively. The total volume of drink is $6$ litres. Prove that they use at most $2$ litres of syrup.

positive_text: Given a positive integer $n$, determine the smallest integer $k$ such that an $n \times n$ grid can be filled with integers from $1$ to $k$ so that the sum of each pair of adjacent (horizontally or vertically) cells is unique. Repetition of numbers is allowed.

negatives.text: Let $n$ be any natural number. Find the least natural number $k$ such that it is possible to write a natural number from $1$ through $k$ into every cell of an $n \times n$ table in such a way that the product of every two adjacent cells differs from all other such products.

Let $n$ be any natural number. Find the least natural number $k$ such that it is possible to write a natural number from $1$ through $k$ into every cell of an $n \times n$ table in such a way that the sum of every two adjacent cells is unique and the numbers in the cells are all distinct.

Let $n$ be any natural number. Find the least natural number $k$ such that it is possible to write a natural number from $1$ through $k$ into every cell of an $n \times n$ table in such a way that the sum of every two adjacent cells is less than or equal to all other such sums.

positive_text: Given 5 arbitrary points in a plane, determine the maximum number of unique right triangles that can be formed using these points as vertices.

negatives.text: On a plane, 5 points are chosen arbitrarily. Find the largest possible number of distinct acute triangles with all vertices in the chosen points.
On a plane, 5 points are chosen arbitrarily. Find the largest possible number of distinct isosceles triangles with all vertices in the chosen points.
On a plane, 5 points are chosen arbitrarily. Find the largest possible number of distinct right triangles with all vertices in the chosen points, where all three vertices lie on a circle.

positive_text: Let quadrilateral $ABDE$ have diagonals intersecting at point $C$. It is given that $AB = CE = 8$ cm and $AE = CD$. The perimeter of triangle $CDE$ is 35 cm, and the condition $\angle BAC = \angle AEC$ holds. Determine the perimeter of the pentagon $ABCDE$.

negatives.text: The diagonals of quadrilateral $ABDE$ meet at $C$. Given that $AB = CE = 8$ cm and $AE = CD$, the perimeter of triangle $CDE$ is 35 cm. If $\angle BAC = 2\angle AEC$, find the perimeter of the pentagon $ABCDE$.

The diagonals of quadrilateral $ABDE$ meet at $C$. Given that $AB = CE = 8$ cm and $AE = 2CD$, the perimeter of triangle $CDE$ is 35 cm. If $\angle BAC = \angle AEC$, find the perimeter of the pentagon $ABCDE$.

The diagonals of quadrilateral $ABDE$ meet at $C$. Given that $AB = CE = 8$ cm and $AE = CD$, the perimeter of triangle $CDE$ is 35 cm. If $\angle BAC = 90^\circ$ and $\angle AEC = 90^\circ$, find the perimeter of the pentagon $ABCDE$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with an interior point $P$. Let $A'$, $B'$, $C'$ be the points such that $P$ is the midpoint of segments $AA'$, $BB'$, and $CC'$, respectively. Determine the area ratio between the hexagon $AB'CA'BC'$ and triangle $ABC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle and $P$ a point on its perimeter. Let $A'$, $B'$, $C'$ be the reflections of $A$, $B$, $C$ from point $P$, respectively. Find the ratio of the areas of the hexagon $AB'CA'BC'$ and the triangle $ABC$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle and $P$ a point inside it. Let $A'$, $B'$, $C'$ be the reflections of $A$, $B$, $C$ from line $AP$, respectively. Find the ratio of the areas of the hexagon $AB'CA'BC'$ and the triangle $ABC$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle and $P$ a point inside it. Let $A'$, $B'$, $C'$ be the projections of $A$, $B$, $C$ onto point $P$, respectively. Find the ratio of the areas of the hexagon $AB'CA'BC'$ and the triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: A snail family is trying to reach a friend located $75$ cm away. Each hour, they spend $\frac{3}{4}$ of the time moving and $\frac{1}{4}$ resting. In the $n$-th hour, their movement is $\frac{1}{n^2+1}$ m forward, but the child reverses it by $\frac{1}{n+1}$ of that hour's forward distance. Will they arrive at their destination, and if so, in how many hours?

negatives.text: A snail family is trying to reach a neighbor who is $75$ cm away. Each hour, they move for $45$ minutes and rest for $15$. In the $n$-th hour, they travel $\frac{1}{n^2+1}$ m forward, but the child pulls them back by $\frac{1}{n-1}$ of this hour's progress. Will they ever reach the neighbor, and if so, when?

A snail family wants to visit a neighbor $75$ cm away. Every hour, they move forward $\frac{1}{n^2+1}$ m, but the child pulls them back by $\frac{1}{n+1}$ of this hour's progress. However, the snails can only move for $30$ minutes and rest for $30$ minutes in each hour. Will they ever reach their destination, and if so, when?

A snail family is traveling to a neighbor $75$ cm away. Each hour, they move for $45$ minutes and rest for $15$. In the $n$-th hour, they move $\frac{1}{n^2+1}$ m forward, and the child pulls them back by $\frac{1}{n+1}$ of the total distance they have already covered. Will they ever reach the neighbor, and if so, when?

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a rectangle. The internal bisector of $\angle CAD$ intersects side $CD$ at point $L$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AL$. The line $DM$ intersects the diagonals and sides $AC$ and $AB$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively. If $AE = AF$, show that $ABCD$ is a square.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a rectangle. The bisector of the angle $\angle CAD$ meets the side $CD$ at point $L$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the line segment $AL$. The line $DM$ meets lines $AC$ and $AB$ at points $E$ and $F$, respectively. Given that line segments $AE$ and $BF$ are equal, prove that $ABCD$ is a square.

Let $ABCD$ be a rectangle. The bisector of the angle $\angle CAD$ meets the side $CD$ at point $L$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the line segment $AL$. The line $DM$ meets lines $AC$ and $AB$ at points $E$ and $F$, respectively. Given that line segments $AE$ and $AF$ are equal, prove that $ABCD$ is a rectangle with sides in a $2:1$ ratio.

Let $ABCD$ be a rectangle. The bisector of the angle $\angle CAD$ meets the side $CD$ at point $L$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the line segment $AL$. The line $DM$ meets lines $AC$ and $AB$ at points $E$ and $F$, respectively. Given that line segments $AE$ and $AF$ are equal, prove that $ABCD$ is an isosceles trapezoid.

positive_text:
ext{A set of web pages can link to each other. A *natural* list is one in which, if page } A 	ext{ links to page } B, 	ext{ then } A 	ext{ appears before } B.
Given a natural list, a new list is formed by first listing all pages with no incoming links, followed by all pages linked to by the first page in the original list, then all pages linked to by the second page not yet listed, and so on.

a. Suppose each page has at most one incoming link. Is the new list guaranteed to be natural?
b. Without knowing the incoming link constraints, is it possible to construct a natural new list?}

negatives.text:
ext{A set of web pages is connected by links. A *natural* list is one where a page appears before any it links to.
Given a natural list, a new list is formed by first listing all pages with no incoming links, followed by the pages pointed to by the *last* page of the original list, then the pages pointed to by the second-to-last page not yet listed, and so on.

a. If each page has at most one incoming link, is the new list guaranteed to be natural?
b. If no such constraint is given, is it possible to construct a natural list?}

positive_text: An alien civilization informs us that the highest two points on their planet, measured from sea level, are $h$ units high, and the lowest point on the continent is $l$ units below sea level, where $h \ge 0 \ge l$. Given the planet's radius $r$ from the center to sea level, calculate the maximum possible distance between two points on the planet such that one is visible from the other.

negatives.text: According to a message from an advanced civilization, the highest point of their planet is $h$ above sea level, and the lowest point is $l$ below sea level, where $h \ge 0 \ge l$. The radius of the planet is $r$. What is the maximum distance between two points on the planet that are not visible from each other?

According to an alien message, the highest two points on their planet are $h$ above sea level and the lowest point is $l$ below sea level, where $h \ge 0 \ge l$. The radius of the planet is $r$. Determine the maximum distance between two points on the surface of the planet that are at the same height above sea level.

According to an extraterrestrial communication, the highest point of their planet is $h$ above sea level, and the lowest point is $l$ below sea level, where $h \ge 0 \ge l$. The radius of the planet is $r$. Find the maximum distance between two points on the surface of the planet such that one is visible from the other, assuming the planet is perfectly flat.

positive_text: Consider $2017$ lines in a plane with no three concurrent. A snail moves along these lines starting on one and continuing until it reaches an intersection of two lines. At each intersection, it turns left or right, alternating direction at each such point. Is it possible for the snail to traverse the same line segment twice, once in each direction?

negatives.text: There are $2017$ lines in a plane such that no $3$ of them go through the same point. Turbo the snail can slide along the lines in the following fashion: she initially moves on one of the lines and continues moving on a given line until she reaches an intersection of $2$ lines. At the intersection, she follows her journey on the other line turning left or right, but always turning in the same direction at each intersection point. Can it happen that she slides through a line segment for a second time in her journey but in the opposite direction as she did for the first time?

There are $2017$ lines in a plane such that no $3$ of them go through the same point. Turbo the snail can slide along the lines in the following fashion: she initially moves on one of the lines and continues moving on a given line until she reaches an intersection of $2$ lines. At the intersection, she follows her journey on the other line turning left or right, alternating the direction she chooses at each intersection point she passes. Can it happen that she slides through a line segment for a second time in her journey but in the same direction as she did for the first time?

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with circumcircle $\Gamma$ and orthocenter $H$. Let $K$ lie on $\Gamma$ on the side of $\Gamma$ opposite $A$ with respect to $BC$. Let $L$ be the mirror image of $K$ across line $AB$, and let $M$ be the mirror image of $K$ across line $BC$. Let $E$ be the second point where the circumcircle of triangle $BLM$ intersects $\Gamma$. Prove that the lines $KH$, $EM$, and $BC$ are concurrent.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with circumcircle $\Gamma$ and orthocenter $H$. Let $K$ be a point on $\Gamma$ on the same side of $BC$ as $A$. Let $L$ be the reflection of $K$ in the line $AB$, and let $M$ be the reflection of $K$ in the line $BC$. Let $E$ be the second point of intersection of $\Gamma$ with the circumcircle of triangle $BLM$. Show that the lines $KH$, $EM$, and $BC$ are concurrent.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with circumcircle $\Gamma$ and orthocenter $H$. Let $K$ be a point on $\Gamma$ on the other side of $BC$ from $A$. Let $L$ be the reflection of $K$ in the line $AB$, and let $M$ be the reflection of $K$ in the line $AC$. Let $E$ be the second point of intersection of $\Gamma$ with the circumcircle of triangle $BLM$. Show that the lines $KH$, $EM$, and $BC$ are concurrent.

positive_text: Let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, and let $\omega$ be a circle tangent to $AC$ and $BC$ and tangent internally to $\Omega$ at point $P$. A line through $Q$, tangent to $\omega$ and parallel to $AB$, lies entirely within triangle $ABC$. Show that $\angle ACP = \angle QCB$.

negatives.text: Let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, and let $\omega$ be a circle tangent to $AC$ and $BC$, and tangent externally to $\Omega$ at point $P$. A line parallel to $AB$ and intersecting the interior of triangle $ABC$ is tangent to $\omega$ at $Q$. Prove that $\angle ACP = \angle QCB$.

Let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, and let $\omega$ be a circle tangent to $AC$ and $BC$, and tangent internally to $\Omega$ at point $P$. A line perpendicular to $AB$ and intersecting the interior of triangle $ABC$ is tangent to $\omega$ at $Q$. Prove that $\angle ACP = \angle QCB$.

Let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, and let $\omega$ be a circle tangent to $AC$ and $BC$, and tangent internally to $\Omega$ at point $P$. A line parallel to $AB$ and intersecting the interior of triangle $ABC$ is tangent to $\omega$ at $Q$. Prove that $\angle ACP = \angle QBA$.

positive_text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. There are $n$ containers, each containing a nonnegative number of stones. In each operation, you may remove two stones from one container, discard one, and place the remaining one into a different container. A configuration is termed solvable if it is possible to achieve a state where no container is empty after a finite number of such operations. Characterize all configurations that are not solvable on their own, but become solvable if one stone is added to any single container.

negatives.text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. There are $n$ boxes, each containing a nonnegative number of pebbles. In each move, you may take two pebbles from one box, throw away both, and place a new pebble in another box. A configuration is solvable if it is possible to reach a configuration with no empty boxes in a finite number of such moves. Determine all configurations that are not solvable, but become solvable when an additional pebble is added to any box.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. There are $n$ boxes, each containing a nonnegative number of pebbles. In each move, you may take one pebble from a box and place it in another box. A configuration is solvable if it is possible to reach a configuration with no empty boxes in a finite number of such moves. Determine all configurations that are not solvable, but become solvable when an additional pebble is added to any box.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. There are $n$ boxes, each containing a nonnegative number of pebbles. In each move, you may take two pebbles from one box, throw away one of the pebbles, and put the other pebble in the same box. A configuration is solvable if it is possible to reach a configuration with no empty boxes in a finite number of such moves. Determine all configurations that are not solvable, but become solvable when an additional pebble is added to any box.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle CAB > \angle ABC$, and let $I$ be its incenter. Let $D$ be a point on $BC$ such that $\angle CAD = \angle ABC$. Let $\omega$ be a circle tangent to $AC$ at $A$ and containing $I$. Let $X$ be the second intersection point of $\omega$ with the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Prove that the internal angle bisectors of $\angle DAB$ and $\angle CXB$ intersect on the line $BC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle CAB > \angle ABC$, and let $I$ be its incenter. Let $D$ be a point on segment $BC$ such that $\angle DAC = \angle ABC$. Let $\omega$ be a circle tangent to $AC$ at $A$ and passing through $I$. Let $X$ be the second intersection point of $\omega$ with the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Prove that the internal bisectors of $\angle DAB$ and $\angle CXB$ meet on the line $AB$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle CAB > \angle ABC$, and let $I$ be its incenter. Let $D$ be a point on segment $BC$ such that $\angle DAC = \angle ABC$. Let $\omega$ be a circle tangent to $AC$ at $A$ and passing through $I$. Let $X$ be the second intersection point of $\omega$ with the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Prove that the internal bisectors of $\angle DAB$ and $\angle CXB$ intersect on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: Suppose $ABCDEF$ is a convex hexagon with $\angle A = \angle C = \angle E$ and $\angle B = \angle D = \angle F$. If the internal angle bisectors of $\angle A$, $\angle C$, and $\angle E$ intersect at a single point, show that the internal angle bisectors of $\angle B$, $\angle D$, and $\angle F$ are also concurrent.

negatives.text: Let $ABCDEF$ be a convex hexagon such that $\angle A = \angle C = \angle E$ and $\angle B = \angle D = \angle F$, and the (interior) angle bisectors of $\angle A$, $\angle C$, and $\angle E$ are parallel. Prove that the (interior) angle bisectors of $\angle B$, $\angle D$, and $\angle F$ must also be parallel.

Let $ABCDEF$ be a convex hexagon such that $\angle A = \angle C = \angle E$ and $\angle B = \angle D = \angle F$, and the (interior) angle bisectors of $\angle A$, $\angle C$, and $\angle E$ are concurrent. Prove that the (interior) angle bisectors of $\angle B$, $\angle D$, and $\angle F$ must also be parallel.

Let $ABCDEF$ be a convex hexagon such that $\angle A = \angle C = \angle E$ and $\angle B = \angle D = \angle F$, and the (exterior) angle bisectors of $\angle A$, $\angle C$, and $\angle E$ are concurrent. Prove that the (exterior) angle bisectors of $\angle B$, $\angle D$, and $\angle F$ must also be concurrent.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ have an obtuse angle at vertex $A$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the points where the external bisector of $\angle A$ meets the altitudes from $B$ and $C$, respectively. Points $M$ and $N$ lie on $EC$ and $FB$ such that $\angle EMA = \angle C$ and $\angle ANF = \angle B$. Show that $E, F, M, N$ are concyclic.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with an obtuse angle at $A$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the intersections of the internal bisector of angle $A$ with the altitudes through $B$ and $C$ respectively. Let $M$ and $N$ be points on $EC$ and $FB$ such that $\angle EMA = \angle BCA$ and $\angle ANF = \angle ABC$. Prove that the points $E, F, N, M$ lie on a circle.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with an obtuse angle at $A$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the intersections of the external bisector of angle $A$ with the altitudes through $B$ and $C$ respectively. Let $M$ and $N$ be points on $EC$ and $FB$ such that $\angle EMA = \angle ABC$ and $\angle ANF = \angle BCA$. Prove that the points $E, F, N, M$ lie on a circle.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with circumcircle $\Gamma$. Let $D$ be the point on $\Gamma$ such that $AD$ is a diameter. Suppose points $K$ and $L$ are located on $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, and $DK$, $DL$ are tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $AKL$. Prove that the line $KL$ passes through the orthocentre of triangle $ABC$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with circumcircle $\Gamma$. Let $D$ be the point on $\Gamma$ such that $AD$ is a diameter. Suppose points $K$ and $L$ lie on segments $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, and $DK$ and $DL$ are tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $AKL$. Show that the line $KL$ passes through the centroid of triangle $ABC$.

positive_text:
Let $\mathbb{N}$ be the set of positive integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $x, y \in \mathbb{N}$:
- The number of positive divisors of $x$ is equal to the number of positive divisors of $f(x)$.
- If neither $x$ divides $y$ nor $y$ divides $x$, then
$$
\operatorname{gcd}(f(x), f(y)) > f(\operatorname{gcd}(x, y))
$$

negatives.text:
Let $\mathbb{N}$ denote the set of positive integers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $x, y \in \mathbb{N}$:
- $x$ and $f(x)$ have the same number of positive divisors.
- If $x$ does not divide $y$ and $y$ does not divide $x$, then
$$
\operatorname{gcd}(f(x), f(y)) < f(\operatorname{gcd}(x, y))
$$

Let $\mathbb{N}$ denote the set of positive integers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $x, y \in \mathbb{N}$:
- $x$ and $f(x)$ have the same number of positive divisors.
- If $x$ does not divide $y$ and $y$ does not divide $x$, then
$$
\operatorname{lcm}(f(x), f(y)) > f(\operatorname{gcd}(x, y))
$$

Let $\mathbb{N}$ denote the set of positive integers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $x, y \in \mathbb{N}$:
- $f(x)$ has one more positive divisor than $x$.
- If $x$ does not divide $y$ and $y$ does not divide $x$, then
$$
\operatorname{gcd}(f(x), f(y)) > f(\operatorname{gcd}(x, y))
$$

positive_text: Soient $\omega$ et $\Omega$ deux cercles concentriques, avec $\omega$ strictement à l'intérieur de $\Omega$. Soient $X$ et $Y$ deux points distincts sur $\omega$. Soient $P$ et $Q$ les points d'intersection de $\Omega$ avec les tangentes issues respectivement de $X$ et $Y$ à $\omega$, tels que $P$ et $Q$ soient situés dans la même demi-plan délimité par $(XY)$. Démontrer que $X$, $Y$, $P$ et $Q$ appartiennent à un même cercle.

negatives.text: Soient $\omega$ et $\Omega$ deux cercles concentriques, avec $\omega$ strictement contenu dans $\Omega$. Soient $X$ et $Y$ deux points sur $\omega$, et soient $P$ et $Q$ les points d'intersection du cercle $\Omega$ avec les tangentes respectives issues de $X$ et $Y$ à $\omega$, tels que $P$ et $Q$ soient situés dans des demi-plans opposés par rapport à $(XY)$. Montrer que les points $X$, $Y$, $P$ et $Q$ sont cocycliques.

Soient $\omega$ et $\Omega$ deux cercles concentriques, avec $\omega$ strictement contenu dans $\Omega$. Soient $X$ et $Y$ deux points sur $\omega$, et soient $P$ et $Q$ les points d'intersection du cercle $\Omega$ avec les droites $(XZ)$ et $(YZ)$, où $Z$ est un point extérieur à $\omega$. Montrer que les points $X$, $Y$, $P$ et $Q$ sont cocycliques.

positive_text:
Soit $ABCD$ un trapèze isocèle tel que les côtés $(AD)$ et $(BC)$ sont parallèles.
a. Démontrer que $ABCD$ est inscriptible.
b. Soit $O$ le centre du cercle circonscrit à $ABCD$ et $E$ le point d'intersection des diagonales $[AC]$ et $[BD]$. Montrer que $O$ appartient au cercle circonscrit du triangle $AEB$.

negatives.text:
Soit $ABCD$ un trapèze isocèle avec $(AD)//(BC)$.
a. Montrer que $ABCD$ admet un cercle circonscrit.
b. Soit $O$ le centre du cercle circonscrit de $ABCD$ et $E$ l'intersection des diagonales. Montrer que $O$ est sur le cercle circonscrit de $AEC$.

Soit $ABCD$ un trapèze isocèle avec $(AD)//(BC)$.
a. Montrer que $ABCD$ admet un cercle circonscrit.
b. Soit $O$ le centre du cercle circonscrit de $ABCD$ et $E$ l'intersection des diagonales. Montrer que $O$ est sur le cercle circonscrit de $AEB$, sachant que $ABCD$ est rectangle.

Soit $ABCD$ un trapèze isocèle avec $(AD)//(BC)$.
a. Montrer que $ABCD$ admet un cercle circonscrit.
b. Soit $O$ le centre du cercle circonscrit de $ABCD$ et $E$ l'intersection des diagonales. Montrer que $O$ est à l'intérieur du cercle circonscrit de $AEB$.

positive_text: Soit $ABC$ un triangle isocèle et obtus en $A$. Soit $\Gamma$ le cercle centré en $B$ passant par $A$, et $\Omega$ le cercle centré en $C$ passant par $A$. Soit $D$ le point d'intersection de $\Gamma$ avec le segment $[BC]$, $E$ le point d'intersection, distinct de $A$, de la droite $(AD)$ avec $\Omega$, et $F$ l'autre point d'intersection de $\Omega$ avec la droite $(BC)$. Démontrer que le triangle $DFE$ est isocèle en $F$.

negatives.text: Soit $ABC$ un triangle isocèle et obtus en $A$. Soit $\Gamma$ le cercle de centre $B$ passant par $A$, et $\Omega$ le cercle de centre $C$ passant par $A$. Soit $D$ le point d'intersection de $\Gamma$ avec le segment $[BC]$, $E$ le deuxième point d'intersection de la droite $(AD)$ avec le cercle $\Gamma$, et $F$ le point d'intersection de la droite $(BC)$ avec le cercle $\Omega$ qui n'est pas sur le segment $[BC]$. Montrer que le triangle $DFE$ est isocèle en $F$.

Soit $ABC$ un triangle isocèle et aigu en $A$. Soit $\Gamma$ le cercle de centre $B$ passant par $A$, et $\Omega$ le cercle de centre $C$ passant par $A$. Soit $D$ le point d'intersection du cercle $\Gamma$ avec le segment $[BC]$, $E$ le deuxième point d'intersection de la droite $(AD)$ avec le cercle $\Omega$, et $F$ le point d'intersection de la droite $(BC)$ avec le cercle $\Omega$ qui n'est pas sur le segment $[BC]$. negatives.text: Sei $ABCD$ ein konvexes Parallelogramm mit einem stumpfen Winkel in $A$. Die Spiegelungen von $A$ an $BC$ und $CD$ seien $P$ und $Q$. Die Diagonale $BD$ schneide $\overline{AP}$ und $\overline{AQ}$ in $R$ und $S$. Zeigen Sie, dass die Umkreise von $\triangle BRP$ und $\triangle DQS$ sich berühren.
